caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1442 of 2008
lawyer:
Abul Kalam Chowdhury, Advocate instructed by A. K. M. Shahidul Huq, Advocate -on-Record ----- For the Petitioner 
M. A. Samad, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on record ----- For the Respondent no. 1. 
For respondent nos. 2-7 ----- Not represented
parties:
Golam Mostafa Bhuiyan ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Abu Taller and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 21st May, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2334 of 2005)
full_judgment:
S. K. Sinha J.:- This petition for leave to appeal arise from the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 21st May 2008 in Civil Revision No. 1442 of 2008. 

2. Petitioner instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1999(Preemption) in the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Noakhali for preemption of the case land claiming as co-sharer as well as holding lands contiguous to the lands transferred under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Petitioner's case in short is that Rashed Miah Bhuiyan, Tanu Miah Bhuiyan, Abdur Razzaque , sons of Soa Miah Bhuiyan were the owners of lands in D. S. kh/Khatian no. 657 corresponding to M. R. R. khatian No. 729 of mouja 314 Kasherpar Senbagh, Noakhali. Preemptor being the son of Rashed Miah Bhuiyan is a co-sharer by inheritance in the lands of D. S. khatian nos. 651 and 657 corresponding to M. R. R. khatian nos. 729 and 721 respectively of plot no. 2261. The Pre-emptor-Petitioner is also holding lands contiguous south of plot no. 2261 being plot no. 2326 of M. R. R. khatian no. 204. Rashed Miah Bhuiyan and Abdur Razzaque Bhuiyan purchased some lands of plot no. 2259 of D. S. khatian no. 587 corresponding to M. R. R. khatian no. 640 by a registered deed dated 9th February, 1968 from Montaj, Miah and therefore, the petitioner is also a co-sharer in the said holding. In the lands of D. S. khatian no. 657 corresponding to M.R.R. khatian no.729, D. S. khatian no. 651 corresponding to M. R. R. khatian no. 721, D. S. khatian no. 587 corresponding to M.R.R. khatian no. 640 the petitioner is a tenant holding lands contiguous to the lands of plot no. 2326. Said Abdur Razzaque Bhuiyan, the opposite party no.2 in the preemption case sold .291/2 acres of land of D. S. khatian no. 657 corresponding to M. R. R. khatian no. 729 and D. S. khatian no. 587 at a consideration of Tk. 30,000/- to the pre-emptee-respondent by registered deed dated 1st September, 1988. The respondent no.3 Abdullah, another co-sharer sold .201/2 acres of land out of D. S. khatian no. 657 corresponding to M. R. R. khatian no. 729 on the same date to the respondent no.1 at a consideration of Tk. 22,000/-; the respondent no. 4 Abul Kashem by registered deed dated 5th September, 1998 transferred .161/2 acres of land out of M. R. R. khatian no.729 at a consideration of Tk. 25,000/- to the respondent no.1 by registered deed dated 5th August, 1988. The respondents no. 5 and 6 Shamsul Huq and Setara Begum sold .181/2 acres of land out of lands of D.S. khatian no. 657 corresponding to M. R. R. khatian nos. 729 and 204 to the respondent no.1 at a consideration of Tk. 20,000/- by registered deed dated 3rd September, 1988. The respondents with a malafide motive to defeat the right of preemption mentioned the deeds as deeds of exchange but in fact by these s deeds the respondents no. 2-6 sold the case lands to the respondent no. 1. The respondent no. 3 executed deed no. 5254 in favour of the respondent no. 1. The respondent no.5 executed deed no. 5297 in favour of the respondent no.1; and the respondent no. 2 executed deed no. 5251 in favour of respondent no. 6; the respondent no. 4 created deed no. 4786 in favour of respondent no. 7, the brother-in-law of the respondent no. 1; the respondent no.1 also created deeds no. 5460 and 5502 for the same land through the respondent no.7. These deeds were created within a space of 15 days with a view to defeat the right of preemption. 

3. The respondent no.1 contested the case by filing a written objection. His case is that the preemption case is not legally maintainable, inasmuch as, the deeds in question being deeds of exchange, the lands covered with the deeds are not pre-emptible. His further case is that the respondent no. 2 to 6 sold lands to the respondent no. 7 who in turn transferred the same to the respondent nil and these deeds being separate transactions can not be claimed for preemption in the same case. He further claimed that he improved the case land by constructing houses and the case is, therefore, liable to be dismissed. 

4. The learned Assistant Judge upon hearing the parties by judgment and order dated 8th November, 2003 allowed the preemption in part in respect of .33 acres of land of S. A. plot no. 2261 of S. A. khatian no. 729 holding that the deeds are out and out sale and that the petitioner is a co-sharer in M. R. R. khatian no. 729 of plot no. 2261. The learned Assistant Judge also noticed that on the same date of execution of the deed of exchange, the respondent nos. 2-6 transferred the said lands to the respondent no.7 and thereafter the respondent no. 7 again transferred the same land to the respondent no.1- and these transactions sufficiently indicated that these deeds were created with a view to deprive the right of preemption and that these deeds were colorable deeds. The learned Assistant Judge however rejected the petitioner's claim of pre-emption as contiguous owner of plot no. 2261 with his plot no.  2326. 

5. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order, the petitioner filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 89 of 2003 and the respondent no.1 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 83 of 2003 before the learned District Judge, Noakhali. The learned Joint District Judge, Artharin Adalat, Noakhali heard both the appeals analogously and by judgment and order dated 24th January 2005 allowed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 83 of 2003 and set aside the judgment of the learned Assistant Judge and allowed pre-, emption in part in respect of .23 acres of land of plot no. 2261 of D. S. Khatian No. 657 corresponding to S. A. Khatian no. 721; .14 acres of land of plot no. 2261 of D. S. khatian no. 657 and .61/2 acres of land of plot no. 2259 of D. S. Khatian No. 587 corresponding to S.A. khatian no. 640. The learned Joint District Judge, however, set aside the judgment of the learned Assistant Judge allowing preemption in respect of .33 acres of land of plot no. 2261 of S. A. khatian no. 729. 

6. The respondent no.1 moved this Court in Civil Revision No. 2334 of 2005 against the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 89 of 2003 allowing preemption in respect of 43th acres of land. The petitioner also moved Civil Revision No. 1350 of 2005 against the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 83 of 2003 by which judgment, the learned Joint District Judge set aside the judgment and order of the learned Assistant Judge allowing pre-emption emption in respect of .33 acres of land of At plot no. 2261. The petitioner also preferred Civil Revision No. 1417 of 2005 against the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 89 of 2003 dis-missing the petitioner's claim of preemption in respect of .411/2 acres of land as co-sharer tenant and tenant holding land contiguous to the lands transferred. A Single Bench of the High Court Division heard all these revision petitions analogously and by judgment and order dated 21st May, 2008 made the rule in Civil Revision No. 2334 of 2005 absolute and discharged other rules without, however, making any order in the operating portion of the judgment as to whether the pre-emptor's claim for preemption was allowed or dismissed. It may be presumed that the High Court Division set aside the judgment of the lower appellate Court allowing pre-emption in respect of .431/2 acres of land as co-sharer. The High Court Division held that partial preemption of a holding allowed by the Court of appeal below is not permissible in law, that a transfer of land by way of exchange is not pre-emptible and that the preemptor-petitioner is not the tenant holding lands contiguous to the lands transferred. 

7. Mr. Abul Kalam Chowdhury, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner submits that the learned Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in not interfering with the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge in failing to consider that the preemptor is a contiguous owner of plot no.  2326 with plot no. 2261. It is argued that the Courts below failed to consider the admission of O.P.W. No. 2 Zainal Abedin that the pre-emptor is a contiguous owner of plots no. 2261 and 2326 and that P.W. 2 corroborated him. 

8. Mr. M. A. Samad, learned Counsel entering caveat, however supports the judgment of the High Court Division and submits that the Courts below concurrently found that the petitioner is not a tenant holding lands contiguous to the lands transferred. 

9. I have perused the judgment of the High Court Division and those of the Courts below and heard the learned Counsels. The Court of appeal below on cons iteration of the documentary evidence has held that it is not clear as to in which portion of plot no. 2261 the pre-emptor is in possession and that he has not specifically mentioned in the preemption petition in support of the claim as contiguous owner. The trial Court also found that the pre-emptor is not a contiguous owner of the lands transferred. In the leave petition also the pre-emptor has failed to take any specific ground in support of his claim as contiguous owner. The Courts below have con-currently found that the petitioner is not a tenant holding lands contiguous to the lands transferred and this finding is based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record. In view of the above, the learned Judge of the High Court Division is perfectly justified in affirming the judgments of the Courts below that the pre-emptor is not a tenant holding lands contiguous to the lands transferred. 

10. I find no merit in this petition. This Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1442 of 2008 is therefore dismissed. 

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1996 & 2029 of 2009
lawyer:

case_source: (Prom the judgment and order dated the 6th day of July, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original Decree No.387 of 2003 with Civil Rule No. 697(f) of 2003).
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim CJ: These Petitions for Leave to Appeal are directed against the judgment and order dated the 6th day of July, 2009 passed by the High Court Division in Appeal from Original') Decree No. 387 of 2003 with Civil Rule No. 697(f) of 2003 allowing the appeal.

<u>2. The facts involved in the case, in short, are that 'Ka' schedule property was leased out with one Faizul Huque and after his death to his wife Amina Hoque. As the lessee violated the terms of lease, the deed was cancelled and the Government took possession of the 'Ka' schedule property and thereafter it was leased out to the defendant Nos. 3-5. The defendant Nos. 3-5 thereupon instituted Title Suit No. 70 of 1998 for permanent injunction disclosing about the existence of deeds mentioned in schedule 'Kho' to the plaint. Mona Mohan Mondal or his song Adhor Chand and Amor Chand were not the owners of the 1 suit lands. 'They never possessed the same and therefore the deeds executed by Adhor Chand and Amor Chand in favour of the appellants predecessor were forged and collusive.</u>

3. The defendant Nos. 3-5 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all material allegations contending, inter-alia, that Nil Kanta Mondal was the owner  of the schedule,-'Ka' property and the C.S. Khatian was also prepared in his name. Nil Kanta Mondal died leaving his son, Mohim Chandra Mondal and the said 'Mohim Chandra Mondal while possessing the suit land died leaving his sons namely Krishna Mohan Mondal and Mona Mohan Mondal. Krishna Mohan Mondal died unmarried in 1964 leaving his brother Monti Mohan Mondal. Thereafter, Mono Mohan Monal died unmarried in 1964 leaving his brother Mona Mohan Mondal. Thereafter, Mona Mohan Mondal died leaving sons namely Amor Chand and Adhor Chand. Amor Chand and Adhor Chand by registered deeds dated 8th September, 1980 transferred the schedule-'Ka' property to their predecessor Abdul Baset Miah. After such purchase their predecessor went to the Revenue Officer for mutation of his name but the Revenue Officer refused to mutate his name on the  plea that the said property were enlisted as vested And non-resident property. Thereafter, their predecessor prayed before the then Sub-Division Officer for releasing the suit property from the list of vested property. The Sub-Divisional Officer on being satisfied recommended for releasing the property to the Deputy Commissioner. There was an inquiry into the matter and ultimately the Land Administration Board by order dated 17th November, 1983 released the property from the list of the vested and Non-resident property. Thereafter, one Amina Hoque filed an application before the Land Administrative Board for review of the judgment and order dated 23rd October, 1991 which allowed the review petition and cancelled the earlier order dated 17th November, 1983. Thereafter, their predecessor instituted Writ Petition No. 2718 of 1991 in the High Court Division challenging the reviewing order of the Land Administrative Board. The High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule absolute declaring the older of the Land Administration Board as had been made without lawful authority. Thereafter, the then Additional Deputy Commissioner (Review) unsuccessfully moved Civil Petition No. 166 of 1998 before this Court. Their predecessor there upon mutated his name, paid rent to the Government and possessed the suit property till his death. The suit properties are not vested and non-resident properly and the suit is not legally maintainable.

4. Mr. Biswajit Das, learned Deputy Attorney General, appearing for 'the petitioners submitted that 'Ka' schedule property having been leased Out to one Fazlul Haque and after his death to his wife Amina Haque and the said lessee having violated the terms of the lease, the lease was cancelled and the Government took possession of the 'Ka' schedule property and thereafter, it was leased out to the defendant Nos. 3-5; that the defendant Nos. 3-5 instituted Title Suit No. 70 of 1998 for permanent injunction in respect of the suit property and in that suit appellants 'predecessor filed a written statement disclosing about the existence of deeds mentioned in schedule 'Kha' to the plaint;  Mono Mohan Mondal or his sons Adhor Chand and Amor Chand were not owners of the suit lands and they never possessed the same; that deeds executed by Adhor Chand and Amor Chand in favour of the predecessor of the appellants were forged and collusive, the suit of the plaintiff was maintainable: that Ext-Ga and Ga(1), the disputed deeds proved that the original.; defendant No. 1 purchased the suit property with full knowledge that Krishna Mohan Mondal was the recorded owner of the suit property and inspite of that he purchased the lands from Adhor Chand and Amor Chand. The learned Deputy Attorney General further submitted that in view of the specific findings of the Joint District Judge that the defendants failed to adduce any reliable evidence that Adhor Chand Mondal ever possessed the suit property. The learned Deputy Attorney General also submitted that the documents of the defendants proved that Krishna Mohan Mondal was the recorded owner of the suit property and he, was not a resident of this country, the suit property was enlisted as vested and non-resident property and the Government is in possession of the suit property though its lessees, the High Court Division erred in law in allowing the appeal.

5. It appears that the suit property belonged on Nil Kanta Mondal. The plaintiffs did not say anything regarding the recording of the suit property in the C.S.Khatian in the name of Nil Kanta. Their basis of claim is S.A. Khatian which has no presumptive value. Krishna Mohan Mondal and Mona Mohan Mondal are the sons of Nil Kanta Mondal. The defendants have purchased the suit property from their heirs of Mona Mohan Mondal who is admittedly a co-sharer in the suit plot. Even if the defendants failed to prove that Krishna Mohan Mondal died in 1964 in this country, Mona Mohan Mondal being a co-sharer in the said Khatian his sons legally inherited at least half share of the suit property. Since Amor Chand and Adhor Chand are the legal heirs of Mona Mohan Mondal; the defendants have acquired title on the strength of Ext. Ga' series and therefore, the plaintiff cannot claim that they are not hound by the said deeds. It further appears that after the execution of the deeds, their predecessor went to the local revenue office mutation and payment of rent when the revenue officer disclosed that the suit property was enlisted as vested and non-resident property and refused to accept the rent. Thereafter, their predecessor filed an application before the then Sub-Divisional Officer 'for releasing the suit property from the list of vested and non-resident property and that on the recommendation of the then Sub-Divisional officer through the Additional Deputy Commissioner, the Land Administration Board released the suit property from the list of vested and non-resident  property On 17th November, 1987. It appears from the ext-'Gha' that the High Court Division declared the cancellation of the order releasing the suit property from the list of vested and non-resident property as illegal and void. P.W.1 in course of cross-examination admitted the said facts.

<u>6. The High Court Division observed that the Government is in possession of the suit property is based, upon proper appreciation of the evidence on record. Admittedly, the defendant Nos. 3-5 instituted Title Suit No. 70 of 1998 for permanent injunction on the ground that they were lessees under the Government and that they were in possession of the suit property against the predecessor of the defendants. Both the Courts below concurrently found that the lessees of the Government i.e. defendant Nos. 3-5 failed to prove their possession in the suit property by a competent civil Court in a properly constituted suit between the same parties binding upon the plaintiffs. The plaintiffs are claiming possession 'through their lessees who have been found out of possession. Their positive case is that their lessees instituted the suit when the defendants disclosed about the deeds mentioned in schedule-'Kha' to the plaint and their lessees are in possession of the suit property.</u>

<u>7. The High Court Division further observed that the lessees failed to establish their possession in the suit property. Therefore, neither vested property Authority nor its lessees are in possession of the suit property and therefore, the suit for declaration without seeking consequential relief is not legally maintainable. The Joint District Judge without adverting to that aspect of the matter upon a superficial consideration of the evidence on record has erroneously decreed the suit holding that the Government is in possession of the suit property. In the premises, the suit as framed is not legally maintainable and the plaintiffs are not entitled to any relief claimed in the suit.</u>

8. In view of the above, we find no Substance in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioners.

9. Accordingly, the petitions are dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Review Petition Nos. 4 and 5 of 2009
lawyer:
A. K. Badrul Huq, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md. Abu Siddique, Advocate-On-Record ----- For the Petitioner (in both the petitions) 
For the Respondents (in both the petitions) ----- Not Represented
parties:
Abdul Gafur ----- Petitioner (in both the petitions)
Vs.
Preemptor No. 1 Md. Nuru Miah being dead his heirs: Md. Muklesur Rahman and others ----- Respondents (in both the petitions)
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 29.07.2008 passed by this Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 602 of 2007)
full_judgment:
Md. Muzammel Hossain J:- These two civil review petitions arising out of the same judgment and order taken up together for hearing analogously are directed against the judgment and order dated 29.07.2008 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 602 of 2007 and 604 of 2007 by which leave petitions were dismissed a single judgment.

2. The facts relevant for disposal of the review petitions arc that the predecessor of respondent Nos. 1(a)-1(g) Md. Nuru Miah and predecessor of respondent No. 2(a) Bazlu Miah as petitioners filed a petition in the Court of Assistant Judge, Shahrasti, Chandpur under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for an order of pre-emption in respect of land conveyed through sale deed dated 20.01.1990 in favour of the petitioner Abdul Gafur which was numbered as Pre-emption Case No. 3 of 1991. The land covered in Preemption Case is the land of Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17 corresponding to State Acquisition Khatian No. 10 under Mouza-Ishapura, Police Station-Shahrasti, District-Chandpur. Another Pre-emption case being number 4 of 1991 between the respondents and petitioners had been filed in respect of another deed of conveyance dated 21.01.1990. Land covered in the sale deed is also the land of Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17 corresponding to State Acquisition Khatian No. 10 under aforesaid Mouza, Police Station and District.

3. That essence of the case projected in the Pre-emption Cases is that Holding of Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17 with an area of 28.94 acres originally belonged to Abu Miah, Yakub Ali, Hasna Banu, Saburrennessa and Salima Khatun to the extent of Six(6) annas share, Four (4) annas share, Two (2) annas share, Two(2) annas share and Two(2) annas share respectively. Yukub Ali out of his 7.23½ acres of land transferred 2.20 acres of land in favour of Ibrahim Khalil Majumder and others. Out of remaining 4.53½ acres of land by two registered sale deeds dated 17.04.1926 in favour of Karimuddin Bepari, father of Pre-emptee-Petitioner and others and Karimuddin Bepari got only 0.5766 acres of land. Karim Uddin Bepari died leaving behind four sons including pre-emptee-Petitioner and two daughters and Pre-emptee-Petitioner got only 0.113 acres in his share from his father Karimuddin Bepari. The Pre-emptee-Petitioner, also purchased .0188 acres from his two brothers and one sister. The Pre-emptor transferred .10 acres of land to one Abdul Ghani Master by registered sale deed dated 13.12.1953, and, also, sold .07 acres of land to one Nurul Islam by registered deed of transfer dated 06.07.1987 and the Pre-emptee-petitioner sold more then his share in Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17. The Pre-emptee-Petitioner is a stranger to the transferred holding.

4. That Pre-emptor-Respondent-side, thereafter, by way of an amendment dated 16.05.1996 put forth the case that heirs of Yukub Ali Munshi had shown transfer in respect of an area of 3 kanis, two (2) gondas two (2) karas and two (2) krantees equivalent to 3.76 acres out of land of disputed Cadastral Survey Khatian Nos. 17 and 18, 19, 20 and 21 along with khas khatian No. 1 and schedule of sale deed had shown that Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17 meant for transfer of 2.63 acres of land and pre-emptee-petitioner got no interest in respect of case holding. The Pre-emptor-respondents are co-sharers by way of inheritance and also by purchase.

<u>5. The pre-emptee-petitioner is a co-sharer of the case holding by way of inheritance and pre-emption case against him is not at all maintainable. Stand taken by pre-emptee-petitioner is that Karimuddin Bepari, predecessor of the pre-emptee-petitioner and his three brothers purchased 3.76 acres of land from heirs of Cadastral Survey recorded tenant Yukub Ali by registered deed of conveyance dated 17.04.1926 and Karimuddin got .94 acres in the case holding in his share. Karimuddin Bepari breathed his last leaving behind four sons, namely, Abdul Gani Master, pre-emptee-petitioner Abdul Gafur, Abdul Kader and Nurul Hoque, two daughters, Zinnatunnessa and Arabannessa and one wife Faridunnessa. Faridunnessa breathed her last leaving behind four sons, namely, Abdul Gani Master, Abdul Gafur, pre-emptee-petitioner, Abdul Kader and Nurul Hoque, two daughters Zinnatunnessa and Arabennessa. The Pre-emptee-petitioner from his father Karimuddin Bepari inherited 18¾ acres of land. The Pre-emptee-petitioner, thereafter, purchased .02¾ acres from his sister Zinnatunnessa. The Pre-emptee-petitioner in the above stated way became owner and possessor in respect of .21/(2/15) acres of land. The Pre-emptee-Petitioner sold out .17 acres of property by two sale deeds and he remained owner and possessor in respect of .21/(2/15) acres of land as a co-sharer in the case holding. Further positive stand taken by Pre-emptor-Petitioner is that Pre-emptor-Bazlu Miah and others got the holding separated on mutation in Mutation Case and Sub-Division of Holding Case No. 303 of 1987-88 and 296 of 1987-88 and opened new khatians, being Khatian No. 195 in respect of 4.30 acres of land and khatian No. 188 in respect of 4.13 acres of land and paid Rent separately and obtained rent receipts. The Pre-emptor-Respondent side, thus, no longer remained a co-sharer in the lands transferred of State Acquisition Khatian No. 10 covered by Sale deed dated 20.01.1990 Shamsuddin and his brothers FazIur Rahman and Khorshed Alam, also got their 2.18 acres of land, subdivided on mutation and separated the land from State Acquisition Khatian No. 10 in Mutation and Sub-Division of Holding Case No. 301 of 1987-88 and paid rents separately and got rent receipts. That further case of Pre-emptee-petitioner was that after purchase of land under Pre-emption proceeding the Pre-emptee-Petitioner caused much improvement on the purchased land and has excavated pond, raised land and constructed house and thereby incurred expenditure of an amount of Tk. 1,22,500/.</u>

6. The Miscellaneous Pre-emption Case Nos. 3 of 1991 and 4 of 1991 were dismissed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Shahrasti, Chandpur by the judgment and order dated 16.09.1992. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order the pre-emptee-respondent preferred Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 64 of 1992 and 65 of 1992 in the Court of District Judge, Chandpur. The pre-emptee-petitioner presented cross appeals and the learned Sub-Ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 2nd Court, Chandpur by the judgment and order dated 13.02.1996 allowed both the Miscellaneous Appeals and dismissed cross appeals of the pre-emptee-petitioner setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge and sent both the cases to the trial court on remand.

7. The learned Assistant Judge, Shahrasti, Chandpur by the judgment and order dated 11.01.1997 again dismissed the Miscellaneous Pre-emption Cases. Being aggrieved the pre-emptor-respondent preferred Miscellaneous Appeal Nos. 2 of 1997 and 3 of 1997 before the Court of District Judge, Chandpur, and the learned District Judge, Chandpur by the judgment and order dated 02.08.1998 dismissed both the Miscellaneous Appeals and affirmed those passed by the learned Assistant Judge of the Trial Court.

8. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order dated 02.08.1998 passed by the learned District Judge, Chandpur the pre-emptor-respondent preferred Civil Revision Nos. 4787 of 1998 and 4793 of 1998 before the High Court Division and a Single Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 09.11.2006 made the Rules absolute. Then the pre-emptee-petitioner preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 602 of 2007 and 604 of 2007 before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division by the judgment and order dated 29.07.2008 dismissed both the petitions. Thereafter the pre-emptee-petitioner being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order preferred these two Civil Review Petitions before the Appellate Division.

9. Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in both the petitions submits that though land of Cadestral Survey Khatian Nos. 18-21 had been shown as tenanted land in the sale deed dated 17.04.1926 under Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17 but the said under-tenancies subsequently got no existence as under tenancies and the said land went to khas holding of Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17 and those land of under-tenancies stood recorded in State Acquisition Khatian No. 10 in the names of tenants or heirs of transferors of Cadastral Survey Khatian No. 17 and not in the names of heirs of any under tenants of Cadestral Survey Khatian Nos. 18-21 and the deed of conveyance dated 17.04.1926 is a positive proof that Karim Uddin and his three (3) brothers purchased 3.76 acres of land from sons of Yakub Ali and Karim Uddin got .94 acres of land in the case holding and pre-emptee-Petitioner inherited .18¾ acres of land from his father Karimuddin and pre-emptee-Petitioner still remains owner and co-sharer by way of inheritance in respect of .1¾ acres of land after transfer of .17 acres of land and pre-emptee-Petitioner having been a co-sharer by way of inheritance, pre-emption cases by Pre-emptor-Respondent is not at all maintainable and both the Trail Court and the Lower Appellate Court concurrently found that the Pre-emptee-Petitioner is a co-sharer by inheritance and those findings rested upon correct construction and reading of the sale deed dated 17.04.1926, share of Yakub Ali in the Case holding and materials on record but the learned Single Judge of High Court Division totally misdirected himself in his approach in resolving the legal battle involved in Pre-emption cases and committed a substantial error in holding that pre-emptee-Petitioner inherited .13 acres of land and transferred .17 acres of land and thereby exhausted all his interest in case holding and became a stranger and this Hon'ble Division did not at all explore the legal controversy and in a summary way dismissed the leave petitions and Judgment under challenge in Civil Review petition may kindly be reviewed in the interest of Justice.

10. Mr. Huq submits that the Pre-emptor-Respondent-side in Mutation and Sub-Division of Joint Tenancy and Holding case Nos. 303 of 1987-1988 and 296 of 1987-1988 got original Joint Tenancy and Holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No. 10 separated and sub-divided and got their names mutated in separate Khatians in respect of 4.13 acres and 4.30 acres respectively and predecessor vendors of Pre-emptee-Petitioner Shamsuddin and others in Mutation and Sub-Division of Holding case No. 301 of 1987-1988 got their Holdings Sub-divided and separated on opening of new Khatian in respect of 2.18 acres of land and the original Joint Tenancy and holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No. 10 got no existence and Pre-emptor-Respondent-side and predecessor vendors of Pre-emptee-Petitioner who stepped into shoes of predecessor vendor-Respondents, no longer remained co-sharer of the transferred holding and the Pre-emptor-Respondent-side ceased to be co-sharer of the tenancy and holding i.e. State Acquisition Khatian No. 10, and, thus, had no legal character and locus standi to exercise right of Pre-emption against Pre-emptee-Petitioner and though the learned High Court Judge and the Appellate Court Judge took into stock this fundamental aspect of the matter neither the High Court Division nor the Appellate Division took into consideration the same and ruminated the vital and core legal aspect of the matter and that in the event of consideration and meditation of this important aspect of the matter, the fate of Civil Revisions and Civil Petitions For Leave To Appeal would have been otherwise and Pre-emptee-Petitioner would have been graced with favourable verdict and, as such, impugned Judgment may kindly be reviewed to secure ends of justice.

11. We have heard Mr. A.K. Badrul Huq, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner and perused the impugned judgment of this Division and also perused the other judgments in question and also other materials available on record.

12. The submissions of the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners merit consideration. Accordingly, leave is granted to consider the ground Nos. 1 and 2.

13. The petitioners in both the petitions are permitted to prepare paper books out of Court in accordance with Rules.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2141 of 2009
lawyer:
Dr. M. Zahir, Senior Advocate Instructed by Sufia Khatun, Advocate -on-Record ----- For the Petitioners 
Ahul Kashem, Advocate-on-Record ----- For Respondent Nos. 1-3 
Respondent Nos. 4-20 ----- Not represented
parties:
Sher Mohammad being dead his heir Most Tara Bibi and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Md. Munsur Ali and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 5.8.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1776 of 2000)
full_judgment:
B. K. Das J.:- This Petition for leave to appeal has arisen against an order dated 5.8.2009 of a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1776 of 2000 making the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court in Title Appeal No. 188 of 1998 of the 1st Court of the Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) Nawabganj upon restoring those of the trial court in other class Suit No. 38 of 1987. 

2. The respondents as plaintiffs instituted other class Suit No. 38 of 1987 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Gomestapur, Nawabgonj for declaration that the Heba-1 Bil-Ewaz deed dated 13.1.1974 allegedly given by the predecessor of the plaintiffs in favour of the defendant Nos. 1-6 is forged, collusive, illegal and created by false personification and as such the same is ineffective and not binding upon the plaintiffs and also for partition of the property as given in ka, kha, and Ga schedule of the plaint stating, inter-alia, that the suit land, as given in schedule ka, kha, and Ga of the plaint, originally belonged to Bilat Ali Mondal, the predecessor of the plain-tiffs and the defendants; that Bilat Ali Mondal married seven times, who died leaving behind his last wife Fakimon Bibi, the mother of the plaintiffs; that before his death he transferred some properties measuring 1.23 acres of land on 12.01.1961 in favour of the mother of the plaintiffs in lieu of her dower, besides this he did not transfer any land to any body that the defendants claimed land by two Heba-Bil-Ewaz deeds were created after the death of their father Bilat Ali Mondal by false personification. Hence the suit. 

3. The present petitioner as defendants contested the suit by filing written statement denying the case of the plaintiffs stating, inter alia, that the suit of the plaintiffs is not maintainable inasmuch as there was no cause of action to institute the suit; that the suit is barred by limitation and bad for defect of parties; that the defendants case is that the suit land originally belonged to Bilat Ali Mondal, who transferred the suit land to defendant Nos. 1-6 by executing two Heba-Bil-Ewaz deeds; that the alleged deed dated 12.1.1961 in favour of the mother of the plaintiffs is false, forged and fabricated and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. The trial court upon taking evidence and on hearing the parties decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 26.10.1998 in preliminary form. Being aggrieved thereby the defendant Nos. 1-6 as appellants filed Title Appeal No. 188 of 1998 before the learned District Judge, Nawabganj. The learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 1st Court, Nawabganj by judgment and decree dated 27.01.2000 reversed the decision of the trial court, allowed the appeal and dismissed the plaintiffs suit.

5. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiffs as petitioners moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1776 of 2000 and a learned Single Judge upon hearing the parties made the rule absolute, set aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court and restored those of the trial court. 

6. Being aggrieved thereby the defendants as petitioners filed the instant petition seeking leave to appeal.

7. Dr. M. Zahir, the learned Senior Advocate appears on behalf of the petitioners while Mr. Abul Kashem, Advocate-on-record appears on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1-3. 

8. We have heard the lengthy submissions of the learned Senior Counsel Dr. M. Zahir for the petitioners and also Mr. Abul Kashem, Advocate on record for the respondent. Dr. M. Zahir submits that the High Court Division committed serious error of law in failing to consider the facts that Haji Bilat Ali Mondal during his life time partitioned his properties amongst his legal heirs amicably and as a result of amicable partition plaintiffs got 5.23 acres of land of R.S. Khatians 400 and 108 and 0.3188 acres was given to his wife Faki Bibi and defendants got their share by registered deeds No. 75/46 and 75/47 and received their respective possession which shows that the partition was complete. Dr. M. Zahir then submits that a partition suit is not maintainable because the ejmali properties of co-sharers was not brought to hotchpotch and the High Court Division accordingly committed gross error in decreeing the suit. Mr. Abul Kashem, the learned Advocate-on-record supported the decision of the High Court Division. It appears that there is no evidence to conclude that there was any partition by metes and bounds between the parties. It further appears that the defendant though raised a plea of maintainability of partition suit for non-impleading of concerned co-sharers and for not bringing the entire properties of deceased owner Haji Bilat Ali Mondal in the hotchpotch of the suit but utterly failed to bring to record as to who are co-sharers who have been left out of the suit and which properties have not been brought to the hotchpotch of the suit. The lower appellate court being the final court of facts considered the evidence and held "On an analyses of the evidence on record, it appears to me that the above observation of the Court of appeal below is not only being based upon gross misreading of evidence on record also being based on misinterpretation of material evidences on record. I, therefore, find that there is a good deal of substance in the contentions raised by Mr. Abul Quasem and the view taken by the appellate Court below cannot be legally sustained." It therefore appears that the High Court Division noticed that the lower appellate court reversed the decision of the trial court on consideration of the evidence upon assigning cogent reason. The learned Judge of the High Court Division came to the finding "On consideration of the materials adduced by the parties, find sufficient reasons to hold that Fakimon Nesssa, the mother of the plaintiff-petitioners having been put into possession over 1.32 acres of land by Haji Bilat Ali on the strength of kabala dated 11.02.61. 

9. Having given my best consideration the materials on record both oral and documentary, I hold that the impugned judgment and decree of the appellate Court below suffers from illegalities in many folds, it cannot be sustained in law and is liable to be set aside and the findings arrived at by the trial court below have been rested upon consideration and discussion of legal evidences and materials of the legal aspect involved in the suit." 

10. Thus, it appears that the impugned judgment of the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division considered all the aspects of the case and found no illegality or irregularity committed by the appellate court being the final court of fact in granting a decree in favour of the plaintiff. We do not therefore find any substance in any of the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners. 

11. Accordingly this leave petition is dismissed. 

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2401 of 2009
lawyer:
Chowdhury Md. Zahangir Advocate-on-Record. ------ For the Petitioners 
A.S.M Khalequzzaman, Advocate, instructed by Mrs. Shahanara Begum, Advocate-on-Record.  ------ For the Respondent
parties:
Md. Daliluddin and others ------ Petitioners.
VS
Md. Mokarram Hossain ------ Respondent.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 27.10.2009 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.352 of 2008).
full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 27.10.2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court in Civil Revision No. 352 of 2008 discharging the Rule and thereby affirming the judgment and decree dated 16.09.2007 (decree signed on 23.09.2007 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in Other Appeal No. 44 of 2006, reversing the judgment and decree dated 26.06.2006 (decree signed on 02.07.2006) passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Baliadangi, Thakurgaon in Other Class Suit No. 15 of 2004 dismissing the suit.

2. The facts leading to the filing of this petition for leave to appeal, in short, are:

3. Respondent No.1 instituted Other Class Suit No. 15 of 2004 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Baladangi, Thakurgaon for recovery of khas possession by removing kachha houses.

4. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit land appertaining to C.S. khatian  No. 297/3 corresponding to S.A. khatians No. 283 of mouza Thumnia within the Police Station Baliadangi, District-Thakurgaon originally belonged to Ashi Md. Sheikh and Jutu Mohammad, the two brothers. They partitioned their joint property with their other sharers, vide registered partition deed No. 3003 dated 07.08.1956. According to the partition deed, Ashi Md. Sheikh alias Asiruddin got 10 decimals of land of plot No. 8066 and 22 decimals of land of plot No. 8067, in total, 32 decimals of land and he sold the said 32 decimals of land to Md. Jahedul Hoq and Md. Mazedul Hoq by two registered deeds. After that, Md. Mazedul Hoq transferred 44½ decimals of land to the plaintiff, vide registered sale deed No. 5433 dated 02.07.2000. It is mentionable that he transferred 2½, decimals out of 10 decimals of land of suit plot No.8066. Jahanul Hoq  transferred 5 decimals of land of the suit plot No.8066. Thus the plaintiff had been enjoying and possessing 7½, decimals of land out of 10 decimals of land of the suit plot No.8066 within the knowledge of all including the defendants. The plaintiff filled up the land with earth but on 12.05.2004, the defendants illegally took possession of the suit land by erecting house made of corrugated iron and bamboo fences in the absence of the plaintiff. On 22.05.2004, the plaintiff requested the defendants to hand over possession but the defendants threatened the plaintiff and refused to hand over possession. Consequently, the plaintiff lodged General Diary No.784, dated 22.05.2004.

5. The petitioners (defendant Nos. 1 to 4 in the suit) contested the suit by filing written statement denying all the material allegations of the plaint.

6. The case of defendant Nos. 1 to 4, in short, is:

7. Asim Mohammad Sheik and Mozibor Rahman, Khatibuddin, minor sons of late Chuto Mohammad were 3rd party to the partition deed. According to the terms of the partition deed, Foraj Ashi Mohammad obtained 5 decimals of land, minor sons of late Chuto Mohammad also got 5 decimals of land from plot No.8066 and also got 11 decimals of land of non suited plot No.8067. Mozibur Rahman sold his share to Matiar Rahman on 16.03.1982 and Motiar Rahman sold 6 decimals of land of suit plot No.8066 along with other land on 27.03.1985 to defendant No. 1 and delivered possession in his favour. On A 16.03.1993, Mazedul Hoq transferred 2½,  decimals of land of suit plot No.8066 to defendant No.1. Defendant No.1 has been possessing 8½, decimals of land by erecting house anti shop. He has been possessing the shop through tenant. Ashi Mohammad obtained 1/2 share, that is, 5 decimals of land of suit plot No.8066 and he had no saleable right to transfer 10 decimals of land to Jaherul Hoq and Mazedul Hoq. The plaintiff was never in possession of the suit land.

8. The learned Assistant Judge by his judgment and decree dated 26.06.2006 dismissed the suit being Other Class Suit No. 15 of 2004.

9. Defendant Nos. 1 to 4 being aggrieved, by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 26.06.2006 preferred Other Appeal No. 44 of 2006 in the Court of District Judge, Thakurgaon. The appeal was transferred to the Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon for hearing.

10. After hearing the parties, the Appellate Court allowed the appeal by the judgment and decree dated 16.09.2007 reversing the judgment and decree of the trial court.

11. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 16.09.2007 passed by the Additional District Judge, Thakurgaon in other Appeal No. 44 of 2006, the petitioners filed Civil Revision No. 352 of 2008 before the High Court Division and obtained Rule and stay of the operation of the impugned judgment and decree.

12. A single Bench of the High Court Division discharged the Rule by the judgment and order dated 27.10.2009.

13. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 27.10.2009 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 352 of 2008 discharging the Rule, the petitioners have preferred this petition for leave to appeal.

14. We have heard Mr. Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, learned Advocate-On-Record appearing for the petitioners and Mr. A.S.M. Khalequzzaman, learned Advocate for the respondent and perused the petition and the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other papers on record.

<u>15. The High Court Division found that the Trial Court's finding that the plaintiff could not prove his possession and dispossession in the suit land appeared to be inconsistent with the, material evidence on record.</u>

<u>16. The High Court Division on detailed consideration of the judgments of the Courts below found that the Appellate Court arrived at a correct finding that the plaintiff had been able to prove his possession prior to his dispossession and the date of dispossession in the suit property. The High Court Division has also found that the plaintiff exhibited documentary evidence including the original sale deeds and proved his title to suit land.</u>

<u>17. Therefore, the High Court Division concurred with the findings of the Court of appeal below. The findings arrived at and the decision made by the High Court Division are based on proper appreciation of the materials on record and as such no interference is called for.</u>

18. We find no substance in this petition which is accordingly dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Appeal No. 90 of 2004
lawyer:
Khondakar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Senior Advocate instructed by Md. Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record. ----- For the Appellant. 
Mr. Mahbubey Alam, Attorney General. ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Mohammad Abdul Alim ------ Appellant.
VS
Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents.
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 20th day of April, 2002 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.3916 of 2000).
full_judgment:
Mohammad Fazlul Karim J: This appeal by is directed against the judgment and order dated 20.04.2002 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3916 of 2000 discharging the Rule relating to the Building and Premises situated within 922 Ajutangsha of land of Dhaka City Corporation, bearing Holding No. 94, Nawabpur Road under Police Station Sutrapur, Dhaka, having been enlisted in the 'Ka' list of Abandoned Buildings published in Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.09.1986 under serial. No. Sutrapur-9 at page No.  9762(9) under the provisions of Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No.  LIV of 1985).

<u>2. The facts involved in the case; in short, are that the appellant, Mohammad Abdul Alim alleged to have purchased the disputed land and building bearing holding No. 94 of Nawabpur Road, under Sutrapur Police Station, Dhaka from one Abdus Sattar and Khorshed Anwar, the admitted owners of the property in question at a consideration of TK. 5,00,000.00 on 18.02.1999 (Annexure-C to the writ petition) in pursuance of the agreement dated 12.10.1984 entered into on 'payment of advance amount of TK. 3,00,000.00 (three lacs). Since original owners Abdus Sattar and Khorshed Anwar did not leave the country for any moment and also did never fail to manage the property in question the same cannot he declared as abandoned property allowing the authority to list it in the 'Ka' list under the provisions of Section 5(1) of the Ordinance No.  LIV of 1985. Filing a supplementary affidavit the appellant has further stated that since the property in question being a commercial one the respondent No. 1, Ministry of Housing and Works has no authority to entrust that same in the impugned list (Annexure-11 to the writ petition) rather, it is to be prepared and published by the Ministry of Commerce and Industries only under the provision of rule 6(3), of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking Over Possession) Rules, 1972.</u>

3. The respondent No. 1 contested the writ petition filing an affidavit-in-opposition  alleging, inter-alia, that the property in question has rightly been vested in the Government as abandoned property under Articles 4 and 5 of the provision of P.O. No. 16 of 1972 and thereafter it has been incorporated in the 'Ka' list under Section 5(1)(a) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 known as Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 since admitted original non-Bengali owners Abdus Sattar and Khorshed Anwar have left the country during the war of liberation leaving the property in question uncared for and subsequently treating the property as a commercial building it has been put in auction for the purpose of disposal. After long 25 years where some of the occupants have also brought two cases being Title Suit Nos. 137 of 1985 and 149 of 1989 which are still pending. It is further stated that since the building was initially constructed for residential purpose, out of which part was being used as shop, could not be treated as commercial building as contemplated in rule 6(3) of the Abandoned Property (Taking Over Possession) rules, 1972. Moreover, it is further submitted that the High Court Division has got no jurisdiction to release the property in favour of the appellant because it comes within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement constituted under Section 7 of the Ordinance No.  LIV of 1985.

<u>4. Leave was granted to consider the sub-missions of the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant that "no proof of Government's possession in the concerned property after the effective date 28.02.1972 having been brought on record and the admitted original owners Abdus Sattar and Khorshed Anwar (predecessors of the appellant) being in possession of the premises partly as their residence and on monthly basis rented as shops and possessed through their tenants, listing of the property in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property is without lawful authority and as such, the rule nisi issued by the High Court Division should have been made absolute. The learned Counsel further submitted that in view of the admitted position that the property in question was mostly used for commercial purpose (shops and godowns) the Ministry of Public Works had no authority to deal with the same in view of the provisions of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking Over Possession) Rules, 1972, as such, its listing as abandoned property at the instance of the said Ministry of the Government is without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.</u>

5. Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant submitted that the respondent could neither prove the possession of the Government of the alleged abandoned property effective from 28.02.1972 on the plea that the whereabouts or otherwise of the admitted original owners Abdus Sattar and Khorshed Anwar (predecessors of the appellant) being in possession partly as their residence and mostly as shops through their tenants, listing of the property in the 'Ka' list of abandoned property is without lawful authority. The learned Counsel further submitted that the original owners Abdus Sattar and Khorshed Anwar, admitted predecessors of the appellant sold the suit land by a kabala dated 18.02.1999 pursuant to an agreement dated 12.10.1984 and thus, the case land belonged to the appellant, a Bangladeshi national, the listing of the property as abandoned building was of no legal consequence.

6. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney General, has appeared for the respondents with leave of the Court and supported the impugned judgment referring positively to the record of the case, provision of law and sought to controvert the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant with reference to the findings and decisions of the Court below.

<u>7. There is nothing on the record to show that the alleged owners were Bangladeshi or in Bangladesh or their whereabouts were known at a point of time when the property became an abandoned property under the provisions of P.O.No. 16 of 1972 i.e. there is no material on record to show that Abdus Sattar and Khorshed Anwar, the original owners were in Bangladesh when the property became an abandoned or their whereabouts were known. Admittedly the property attracts the character of abandoned property under the provision of P.O.No. 16 of 1972 and absolutely vested in the Government. It appears that long thereafter, an application was filed by the alleged Khorshed Anwar only on 1996 for release of the property from the list of abandoned property when admittedly the property as well stood recorded in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned property under Section 5(1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 and before that period no attempt was ever made by the alleged owners to get the property released or there is nothing on record to show that the owners i.e. the petitioners were in possession when the property became an abandoned property in 1972 i.e. on 28.02.1972, on the contrary, the property has vested in the Government on declaration in the abandoned property in 1972 and upon promulgation of the Ordinance 55 of 1985 and it was accordingly listed in the 'Ka' list of the Abandoned Buildings.</u>

<u>8. The petitioner, an alleged transferee of the abandoned property, alleged to have obtained a kabala from the alleged owners on 18.02.1999. The High Court Division has found that the said deed is absolutely malafide and void as it is contrary to the provisions of Article 6 of P.O.No. 16 of 1972 which reads as under;</u>

<u>"No person shall except in accordance with the provisions of this order or any rules made, thereunder transfer any abandoned property in any manner or create any charge or encumbrance on such property; or any transfer made or change or encumbrance created in contravention of the order shall he null and void."</u>

9. Since the property was declared as abandoned property pursuant to Article 2(1) of the PO.No. 16 of 1972 thereby vested in the Government and subsequently was included in 'Ka' list prepared under Section 5(1) of the Ordinance, 1985 and there is nothing 19 show that the transfer was in accordance with the provisions of P.O.No. 16 of 1972 the alleged purchase was of no avail to the appellant and the same is void being a purported deed of transfer of an abandoned property contrary to the provisions of The Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972.

<u>10. The building was constructed as a residential building but simply letting out the same for alleged commercial purpose could not attract the provision regarding the commercial building under rule 6(3) of the Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules, 1972 and the alleged purchase was of no avail to the petitioner and have not acquired any locus standi. Moreover, as the alleged purchase was made at a time when the property has already been declared abandoned and accordingly vested in the Government as abandoned properly rendering the deed of transfer in favour of the petitioner as void and the alleged transferee have not acquired any interest in the abandoned property, as such, the appellant-petitioner has no locus standi to file the writ petition and thereby writ petition and consequently, this appeal at the instance of the alleged purchaser during the continuance of the property as abandoned is not maintainable.</u>

11. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: CIVIL APPEAL NO.163 OF 2009.
lawyer:
For Appellant: Mr. Mahbubey Alam, Attorney General, instructed by Mr. Nurul Islam Bhuiyan, Advocate-on-Record.  
For Respondent No.2: Mr. Probir Neogi, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Zainul Aabedin Advocate-on-Record. 
For Respondent Nos.9-10: (on added) Mr Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record. 
For Respondent Nos.1 & 3-8: N.R.
parties:
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of land, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dhaka ------ Appellant
Versus
Abdul Hye and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha, C.J. This appeal by leave is directed from a judgment of the High Court Division making the rule nisi absolute declaring the letters under memos dated 12th September, 2005 and 31st October, 2005 issued by the Ministry of Land, Section 8, government of Bangladesh to be without lawful authority. It also quashed the proceedings in Sylhet Kotwali P.S. Case Nos.117 dated 27th September, 2005 and 12 dated 2nd November, 2005 initiated against the writ petitioners Abdul Hai and Ragib Ali.

2. Facts relevant for the disposal are as under:

<u>3. Tarapur Tea Estate originally belonged to C.K. Hurdson. After his death, his son, W.R. Hurdson, inherited the tea estate who transferred it to Baikuntha Chandra Gupta by a registered deed dated 10th June, 1882. Thereafter, Baikuntha Chandra Gupta gifted the tea estate in favour of the Deity Sree Sree Radha Krishna Jieu on 2nd July 1892. In order to look after the tea estate for the said Deity a trust was formed in the name of the said Deity. Baikuntha Chandra Gupta appointed his son Radha Lal Gupta as the Shebait of the trust. Accordingly, during S.A. operation the record was correctly published in the name of Shebait Radha Lal Gupta. In the year, 1968, the tea estate was declared as enemy property by the then Government of Pakistan. In 1971 the then Shebait Rabindra Lal Gupta, his brother Rejendra Lal Gupta and other family members were killed by the Pakistani army except the minor boy Pankoj Kumar Gupta. In the circumstances, on behalf of the only alive minor Pankoj Kumar Gupta, the then Shebait Sabita Rani Gupta, Mukul Bala Gupta and Chhaya Gupta filed Title Suit No. 55 of 1971 in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet, for a declaration that the tea estate is not an enemy property. In the said suit Bangladesh Government was one of the parties. The tea estate was ultimately declared as the property of the Deity. The Shebait took control over the tea estate and subsequently, the said Pankoj Kumar Gupta attained majority, and he was appointed as the sole Shebait of the tea estate.</u>

4. While he was acting as such, on 16th September, 1988 he applied to the Government for permission to transfer the tea estate to the writ petitioners in the interest of the Deity. The office of the writ respondent No.1 by its Memo No.Bhu: Mi/Sha-8/Khajoj/53/89/446 dated 12th October 1989 accorded permission to the Shebait to grant a long term lease of the tea estate. Pursuant to the said permission the Shebait executed a deed of lease for 99 years in favour of writ-petitioner No.1 by registered deed dated 12th February, 1990. By dint of the lease deed, the writ-petitioner No.1 became the absolute owner and possessor of the tea estate being a lessee for 99 years. Since taking over the ownership and possession of the tea estate, the writ-petitioner No.1 invested huge amount of money for developing the tea estate in order to produce quality tea in the garden for earning foreign currency by exporting.

5. Some interested persons brought some false and frivolous allegations against the writ-petitioners before the Government of Bangladesh in the year 1994 alleging that they grabbed the tea estate by fraudulent and illegal means. Writ-petitioner No.1 applied to the government for allowing him to mutate his name in the revenue record. The Ministry of Law by its Office Notes opined that writ-petitioner No.1 was legally entitled to the mutation.

6. Writ-respondents at the behest of some influential people, are abstaining from mutating the name of the writ-petitioners to dispossess them from the tea estate with the help of writ-respondent Nos. 5-7. Writ-petitioner No.1 filed Title Suit No. 91 of 2005 with a prayer for a permanent injunction against the appellants. The Government had acquired 32.91 acres of land of the aforesaid tea estate for constructing the Sylhet Divisional Stadium and Shahajalal University of Science and Technology for which an amount of Tk. 30,76,189.20 was paid as compensation in 1990.

7. The writ-petitioner No. 2 who was then the constituted attorney of the Shebait received the compensation on behalf of the Shebait and the money was invested for the development of the tea estate. The writ-respondents are barred by the principles of estoppel from questioning the transfer of the tea estate and receipt of the compensation. While the said suit for permanent injunction was pending, the appellant No. 1 issued the impugned Memo dated 12th September, 2005.

8. Upon receiving the said instruction, writ-respondent No. 6 by his Memo No.SA/ Bondo/Chaa/5-599- 05/222 dated 27th September,2005 instructed writ-respondent No. 7 to file a criminal case against the writ-petitioners consequent upon which Kotwali Police Station Case No. 117 dated 27th September, 2005 under Section 419/420/ 406/467/468/471/109 of the Penal Code was filed by him. Subsequent to filing of the said F.I.R, the writ-respondent No.1 again directed writ-respondent No. 5 to file a criminal case against the writ-petitioners by Memo dated 31st October, 2005.

9.  The High Court Division made the rule nisi absolute on the reasoning’s that the government had acquired 32.91 acres of land of the tea estate for constructing Sylhet Divisional Stadium and Shahajal Science and Technology University; that the writ petitioner No. 2 received the compensation of Tk. 30,76,189.20 which he invested for the development of the tea estate; that since the said acquisition was legal, the government is debarred from questioning the transfer of the remaining area of the tea estate; that the impugned memos have been issued without lawful authority and that the criminal proceedings initiated against the writ petitioners are also unlawful.

10. Learned Attorney General has taken us to the orders impugned in the writ petition and the judgment and submits that tea estate being a Debutter property, it cannot be alienated in favour of the writ petitioners for 99 years. He further submits that disputed facts having been raised in the writ petition challenging the legality of annexure 'A' series, the High Court Division erred in law in declaring the said memos without lawful authority.

11. Admittedly, the tea estate in question is a debutter property. The government conducted an inquiry regarding the transfer of the debutter tea estate and upon such inquiry it was detected about the creation of forged permission from the government and made the following recommendations:

(ক) ভূমি মন্ত্রণালয়ের ভূয়া পত্রের বরাতে সেবাইত কর্তৃক তারাপুর চা বাগানের জমি হস্তান্তর ছিল একটি বড় ধরনের জালিয়াতির ঘটনা।ইহাতে সরকারের বিপুল পরিমান মূল্যবান জমি হাত ছাড়া হওয়ার উপশম করিয়াছে ৷ ভূয়া পত্রের বরাতে দলিল রেজিট্রিকরণ, জমির দখল গ্রহন, মেডিকেল কলেজ স্হাপন, হাউজিং এষ্টেট নির্মাণ এবং মার্কেট নির্মাণসহ অন্যান্য প্রক্রিয়া সরকারী জমি আত্মাসাতের ঘটনায় জড়িতদের বিরুদ্ধে অবিলম্বে ফৌজদারী মামলা রুজু করিতে হইবে৷

(গ) তারাপুর চা বাগান একটি দেবোত্তর সম্পত্তি ৷ দেবতাই দেবোত্তর সম্পত্তির মালিক ৷ কোন সেবায়েত দেবোত্তর সম্পত্তি নিজের বলিয়া দাবী করিতে পারে না। কাজেই হস্তান্তর দলিল সম্পূর্ণরূপে অবৈধ ৷ ইহা অবিলম্বে বাতিল করিয়া তারাপুর চা বাগানের ব্যবস্হাপনা ও পরিচালনার দায়িতৃ জেলা প্রশাসক সিলেট কর্তৃক নিয়োজিত কোন সেবায়েত বা কমিটিকে অর্পণের প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্হা গ্রহন করিতে হইবে।

(ঘ) দেবোত্তর সম্পত্তি অধিগ্রহনের ফলে জনাব রাপীব আলীকে ক্ষতিপূরণ বাবদ প্রদত্ত ৩০,৭৬,১৮৯.২০ টাকা প্রদান বিধি সমমত হয় নাই ৷ বিষয়টি পরীক্ষা করিয়া ক্ষতিপূরণ বাবদ প্রদত্ত টাকা বিধ��� মোতাবেক আদায়ের প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যবস্হা করিতে হইবে ৷

ঙ) তারাপুর চা বাগান নিয়া বিভিনড়ব আদালতে যে সকল মামলা বিচারাধীন রহিয়াছে সেইগুলিতে সরকারী স্বার্থ সংরক্ষণের উদ্দেশ্যে অবিলম্বে জেলা প্রশাসনকে পক্ষভূক্ত হইবার প্রয়োজনীয় পদক্ষেপ গ্রহন করিতে হইবে ৷

(চ) যে সকল সম্পত্তি ইতিমধ্যে বিভিনড়ব আদালতের রায় ডিস্মি মাধ্যমে বিভিন্ন ব্যক্তির অনুকুলে হস্তাম্ভরিত হইয়াছে তাহা পুনরুদ্ধার করিবার প্রয়োজনীয় আইনগত ব্যবস্হা গ্রহন করিতে হইবে I

12. It was found that the permission for transfer of the tea estate by Shebait was a product of forgery and that the writ petitioners established a Medical College, a housing estate and a market by removing tea plantations; that Tarapur Tea Estate should be taken over possession by the government; that it being a debutter property, the Deity is the owner of the property, and therefore, the transfer was totally unlawful; that the compensation money of Tk.30,76,189.20 received by Ragib Ali should be recovered and that the Deputy Commissioner should be directed to take steps for hearing of the proceedings relating to the tea estate.

13. Some facts are admitted in this appeal. Tarapur Tea Estate is a debutter property and it was being managed by the Shebait of the Deity before it was grabbed by the writ petitioners. Another admitted fact is that the respondents managed to obtain a long term lease deed of 99 years in respect of Tarapur Tea Estate. The respondents thereupon established a Medical College, a housing estate and a super market by damaging the tea plantations and utilized a portion of the tea estate for purposes other than the purposes for which the property was dedicated to the Deity.

14. The first question to be looked into is whether a debutter property can be leased out for 99 years by the Shebait even if it is assumed that the Shebait has agreed to transfer it with prior permission of the concerned Ministry. This takes us to consider the powers of a Shebait to alienate the debutter property. The mere fact that an idol has been established does not itself create a debutter. A religious trust by way of debutter can come into existence only when a property is dedicated for worship or service of the idol. When there is an endowment in favour of an established idol, no trust in the legal sense of the term can possibly come into being it is only the moral duty of the person who founds the Deity or his heirs to carry on the worship in such a way as they think proper in accordance with the deed of endowment.

15. Therefore, if the ancestor makes no endowment, there is no legal obligation on the descendants to spend money for the worship of the idol; and if one of them spends money, he cannot bring a suit for contribution against his co-heirs. A property can be given to an idol either at the time when it is consecrated or at any subsequent period. So, question comes in about the dedication of the property. When a property is given absolutely by a pious Hindu for worship of an idol, the property vests in the idol itself as a juristic person. This is quite in accordance with Hindu ideas and has been uniformly accepted in a long series of decisions by different courts including the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and also in the case of Kalanka Devi Sansthan V. M.R.T. Nagpur, AIR 1970 SC 439. In this case it has been observed that the 'properties of the law vest in the trustee whereas in the case of an idol or a Sansthan they do not vest in the manager or the Shebait.'

16. In province of East Pakistan V. Kshiti Dhar, 16 DLR (SC) 457, it was held that under the Hindu Law no particular form or mode of creating a dedication is prescribed, but if such a dedication is not evidenced by a document of dedication it must, as pointed out by the High Court itself, by quoting from a judgment of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Manakuru Das Matharami Reddi V. Duddukuni Shubba Rao, AIR 1957 S.C. 797, be established 'by cogent and satisfactory evidence of conduct of the parties and user of the property which show the extinction of the private secular character of the property and its complete dedication to charity. What is necessary to be established is that not only there is a clear and unequivocal intention to dedicate but also that such intention was in fact carried into effect.'

17. A trust would be denominated a religious or charitable trust if it is created for purposes of religion or charity. Two things, therefore, require to be considered in this connection are, (a) what are religious and charitable purposes? and (b) what is a trust? Religion is absolutely a matter of faith with individuals or communities, and it is not necessarily theistic, i.e Buddhism. The expression 'religious purpose' is understood in a case where the purpose or object is to secure the spiritual well-being of a person or persons according to the tenets of the particular religion which he believe in (B.K. Mukherjea on The Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts).

18. The conception of 'trust' in its technical sense was devised by the Chancery Courts in England which as Courts of Conscience attempted to supply the deficiencies of the English Common Law, by administering what were known as principles of equity and natural justice. Lewin in his well-known treatise on the Law of Trusts defines 'Trust' to be a "confidence reposed in some other, not issuing out of the land, but as a thing collateral, annexed in privity to the estate of the land; for which cestui que trust has no remedy but by Subpoena in the Chancery'.

19. Hindu concepts of religious and charitable gifts have been operative under two head 'Istha' and 'Purtta'. The compound word Istha-Purtta has been retained in the writings of all Brahminical sages and commentators down to modern days. `Istha' meant Vedic sacrifices, and rites and gifts in connection with the same. Turtta' on the other hand, means other pious and charitable acts which are unconnected with any one or Vedic sacrifice. The meaning of the two expressions has been discussed elaborately by Pandit Pran Nath Saraswati in his Tagore Law Lectures on the Hindu Law of Endowments.

20. In the Hindu Law system, there is no line of demarcation between religion and charity. The Hindu religion recognizes the existence of a life after death, and it believes in the law of 'karma' according to which the good or bad deeds of a man produce corresponding results in the life to come. If we look into the essentials of dedication for religious and charitable purposes, we will find that there are various works of this kind where the subject of gift or dedication has been elaborately discussed, among others, of Danakhanda by Hemadri, two works of Danakhanda by Hemadri, namely Purta kamalakar and Dana Kamalakar by Kamalakar Bhatta; Pratistha Mayukha of Nikantha and Pratistha Tattwa of Raghunandan (B.K. Mukherjea, ibid). In every act of dedication, there are two essential parts, one of which is called 'Sankalpa' or the formula of resolve, and the other 'Utsarga' or renunciation. The ceremonies, as Mandalik points out, always being with a `Sankalpa', which after reciting the time of gift with reference to age, year, season, month etc. states what object the founder has in making the gift. 'Utsarga', on the other hand, completes a gift by renouncing the ownership of the founder in the thing given.

21. If we examine the details on how Debutter is managed and administered, there is no doubt that it is in an ideal sense that the dedicated property vests in an idol. In Prosonna Kumari Debya V. Golab Chand Baboo, (1875) LR 2 IA 145, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council observed that "the person so entrusted must, of necessity, be empowered to do whatever may be required for the service of the idol and for the benefit and preservation of its property, at least to as great as the manager of an infant heir. If this were not so, the estate of the idol might be destroyed or wasted, and its worship discontinued for want of necessary funds to preserve and maintain them".

22. This human ministrant of the Deity, who is its manager and legal representative, is known by the name of 'Shebait' in Bengal and Northern India. He is the person entitled to speak on behalf of the Deity on earth and is endowed with authority to deal with all its temporal affairs. As regards the temple property, the manager is in the position of a trustee, but as regards the service of the temple and the duties that appertain to it he is rather in the position of the holder of an office of dignity. Reference in this connection is the case of Ramanathan Chetti V. Murugappa Chetti, (1906) LR 33 IA 139. In this connection it should be remembered that a Poojari' is a servant of the Shebait, and no part of the rights and obligations of the latter are transferred to him. When the appointment of a `Purohie has been at the will of the founder, the mere fact that the appointee has performed the worship for several generations will not confer an independent right upon the members of the family so appointed and will not entitle them as of right to be continued in office as priests. (Kalikrishna Ray V. Makhanlal Mookerjee, ILR 50 Cal 233).

<u>23. The exact position of a `Shebait' or manager cannot be said to be altogether beyond the range of controversy, though much of the earlier theories has now been discarded. It is now settled by the opinions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in Vidyavarathi Thirtha V. Balusami Ayyar, LR 48 IA 302 and we find no reason to depart from the same that the relation of a Shebait to the debutter property is not that of a trustee to trust property under the English law. It is held that the "endowments of a Hindu Math are not 'conveyed in trust', nor is the head of the math a 'trustee' to regard to them, save as to specific property proved to have been vested in him for a specific object." In English law the legal estate in the trust property vests in the trustee who holds it for the benefit of the cestui que trust. In a Hindu religious endowment, the entire ownership of the dedicated property is transferred to the Deity or the institution itself as a juristic person, and the Shebait is mere a manager. The Judicial Committee further held that a trust in the sense in which the expression is used in English law, is unknown in the Hindu system pure and simple. Hindu piety found expression in gifts to idols and images consecrated and installed in temples, to religious institutions of every kind, and for all purposes considered meritorious in the Hindu social and religious system. Under the Hindu law the image of a Deity of the Hindu pantheon is a juristic entity, vested with the capacity of receiving gift and holding property.</u>

24. In Sreepati Chatterjee V. Krishna Chandra Banarjee, 41 CLJ 22, it was held that as the Shebait has no right to property, and is a mere holder of an office with the rights and limitations applicable to the guardian of a minor, the rule in Tagore's case could not properly be extended to appointment of a Shebait. The controversy has been set at rest by the Full Bench decision in Monohar Mukherjee V. Bhupendra Nath Mukherjee, 37 CWN 29 (FB), where it has been held that shebaitship is not merely an hereditary office, and the ruling in Tagore V. Tagore, 9 BLR 377 has been made applicable to an hereditary office.

25. If the founder of the debutter lays down any mode of devolution of the office of Shebait, the office devolve according to that mode and in the absence of such laying down of the mode of devolution, the office devolves in accordance with the Hindu Law of succession, that is, the office of Shebait is a hereditary one. Anath Bandhu V. Krishna Lal, AIR 1979 Cal 168.

26. Under the Hindu law apostasy was certainly a disqualification in the heir and excluded him from inheritance. This was removed by the Cast Disabilities Removal Act, 1850 (Act XXI of 1850), with regard to ordinary property, the fact that a Hindu has become a convert to some other religion does not entail forfeiture of his heritable rights. This Act XXI of 1850 has been repealed by section 2 of Act VIII of 1973. By this Act, namely the Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act, 1973, some Laws promulgated in British India have been repealed including Act XXI of 1850. So, the consequence of such repeal is that a convert from Hinduism could inherit the property of Hindu Law by Act XXI of 1850; but after the repeal by Act VIII of 1973 he disinherits. The position stands now is that a Hindu apostasy is disqualified in the heir and succession of his paternal property. If that being so, a non-Hindu cannot become a Shebait or pujari of the Deity. He cannot carry on the worship or the management of the property of the Deity.

27. The same principle would apply to devolution of shebaitship as well. In the matter of carrying on the worship of a Deity, the intentions of the founder have got to be given effect to as far as practicable. When a pious Hindu establishes a Deity cannot possibly conceive of its `sheba' and `puja' being carried on under the supervision of a non-Hindu. Usages do exist in Hindu religious institutions and if succession of a non-Hindu Shebait is contrary to such usage, it cannot be allowed. Reference in this connection is the case of Venkatachalapati V. subbarayadu, ILR 13 Mad 293.

<u>28. The founder of an endowment can always confer upon a Shebait appointed by him the right of nominating his successor. Without such authority expressly given to him, no Shebait can appoint a successor to succeed to him in his office. The power of nomination can be exercised by the shebait either during his lifetime or by a will, but he cannot transfer the right of exercising this power to another person. This view will find support in the case of Rup Narain V. Junko, 3 CLR 112. If the line of Shebaits laid down by the founder is extinct, or when the Shebait to whom a power of nomination is given does not exercise the power, the shebaitship reverts to the founder who endowed the property or his heirs. Reference in this connection is the case of Jagannath Prasad Gupta V. Runjit Singh, ILR 25 CAL 354.If the founder has left no heirs, the founder's property may escheat to the state together with the endowed property. The right of the state under such circumstance would be same as those of the founder himself, and it would for the state to appoint a Shebait for the debutter Property. It cannot be said that the state receiving a dedicated property by escheat can put an end to the trust and treat it secular property (B .K. Mukherjea, ibid).</u>
