29. From the above discussions we may conclude as under:

(a) An idol is a juristic person in whom the title to the property of the endowment vests; but it is only in an ideal sense that the idol is the owner. It has, to act through human agency and that agent is the Shebait, who is, in law, the person entitled to take proceedings on its behalf. The personality of the idol might, therefore, in one sense, be said to be merged in that of the Shebait.

(b) Where, however, the Shebait refuses to act for the idol, or where the suit is to challenge the act of a Shebait himself as prejudicial to the interests of the idol then there must be some other agency which must have the right to act for the idol. In such cases, the law accordingly recognises a right in persons interested in the endowment to take proceedings on behalf of the idol.

30. A Shebait, like a trustee in English law, cannot delegate his duty to another, no matter whether such other is a stranger or a co-trustee. The rule is founded on the maxim "Delegatus non potest delegare". This has been explained by Bowen, L.J. in Re, Speight. Speight V. Gaunt, 22 Ch.D. 727.

31. "The proposition as to trustees or agents that they cannot delegate means this simply that a man employed to do a thing himself has not the right to get somebody else to do it, but when he is employed to get it done through others, he may do so".

Therefore, where a trustee is entrusted to do a particular thing himself, he cannot authorize somebody else to exercise judgment on his behalf. It is open to a trust to appoint a sub-agent or avail himself of the services of others, whenever such employment is according to the normal course of business, but such appointment must only be as a means of carrying out his own duties himself and not for the purpose of delegating those duties by means of such appointment. This will find support in Shree Shree Gopal Shreedhar V. Shashee Bhusan Sarkar, ILR 60 Cal 1.11. So, a Shebait cannot delegate his authority even to a co-Shebait.

32. The next question is whether the Shebait can transfer the tea estate which is a debutter Property with prior permission of the government for the interest of the Deity as alleged. The Shebait cannot do so in view of discussions made above. Even if it is assumed that the Shebait can transfer a portion of the estate for the welfare of the Deity, he cannot alienate the entire property of the Deity. A point may arise as to the status of the endowed tea estate after the acquisition of rent receiving interest. Section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act deals with khas land which a rent receiver is entitled to retain in his khas, after the acquisition of his rent receiving interests under Chapter V of the Act. This section puts the maximum area of lands retainable by such rent-receiver in his possession by sub-section (2). However, a person or persons can retain beyond the retainable land for the purposes of the cultivation and manufacture of tea or coffee or cultivation of rubber or company holding land for the cultivation of sugarcane for the purpose of manufacture of sugar provided that he obtains a certificate from the Revenue Authority. Sub-section (4A) of section 20 is relevant which is reproduced below:

"(4A) Notwithstanding anything contained in subsection (2), a person or persons holding land for the purposes of the cultivation and manufacture of tea or coffee or the cultivation of rubber or a company holding land for the cultivation of sugarcane for the purpose of manufacture of sugar by that company may, if he or it is no they are certified in that behalf by the prescribed Revenue Authority, retain possession of and hold such quantity of land in excess of the limit specified in the said subsection as may be specified in the certificate granted by such Revenue Authority:

33. Provided that such a certificate shall be subject to revisions by the said Revenue Authority at such intervals as may be fixed in this behalf by the Government:

34. Provided further that for the purpose of this sub-section a derelict tea garden shall not be deemed to be land held for the purpose of the cultivation and manufacture of tea."

35. In respect of lands held by debutter, waqf-alal-al-aulad or a trust which are exclusively dedicated to religious or charitable purposes without reservation of pecuniary benefit for any individual, the restriction imposed in sub-sections (1), (2), and (3) of section 20 shall not apply. Sub-section (5)(i)(c) provides:

"(5) (i) Nothing in sub-sections (i), (2) and (3) of the sections shall apply — (c) to so much of the lands held under Debutter, waqf, waqf-al-al-al-aulad or any other trust as is exclusively dedicated and the income from which is exclusively applied to religious or charitable purposes without reservation of pecuniary benefit for any individual.

(ii) Where, under any debutter, waqf, waqf-al-al-awlad or any other trust, the income from the lands covered by such trust is partly dedicated for religious or charitable purposes and partly reserved for the pecuniary benefit of any individual, only portion of the lands, as may be selected in accordance with the rules to be made in this behalf by the Government, shall come within the purview of sub-clause (c) of clause (i)."

36. Clause (c) of Sub-section (5)(i) is concerned with the question of lands held under debutter and irrespective of the area provided are excluded from acquisition by the government. The lands which were completely dedicated for religious purposes cannot be acquired by the government. If the dedication is partly for religious or charitable purposes and partly reserved for the pecuniary benefit of any individual, only portion of the lands as has been selected shall be governed in the manner provided in rule 37 of the State Acquisition Rules, 1951.

37. Under this rule the portion of the land be selected under clause (ii) of sub-section (5) of section 20 shall be such as would, in the opinion of the Revenue Officer, yield an annual net income equivalent to the amount exclusively applied annually to religious or charitable purposes without reservation of pecuniary benefit for any individual. Sub-Rule (3) provides that where the waqf waqf-alal-aulad, debutter or other trust exists for more than ten years, mean the annual average or the amounts exclusively applied to religious or charitable purposes during the last ten years, and in other cases, the annual average of the amounts so applied during the entire period elapsed since the creation of such trust; and include such remuneration of the Mutawalli, Shebait or trustee, as the case may be, as the Revenue Officer may, in consideration of the nature, extent and other circumstances of the trust determine as fair and reasonable. There is a proviso in this sub-rule which provides that in determining such annual average, the Revenue Officer shall not take into account any amount on account of remuneration of Mutawalli, Shebait or trustee, unless the deed of trust expressly provides for payment of remuneration to him.

38. So, under no stretch of imagination the Shebait can transfer the entire debuttor property with the permission of the government.

<u>39. Taking into consideration of the above position of law, let us consider the factual matrix of the case. In the impugned order the Divisional Commissioner upon a thorough inquiry noticed that the transfer of the tea estate was made by resorting forgery, inasmuch as the writ petitioners procured a forged permission. Secondly, it is reported that after taking possession, the writ petitioners set up a medical college and established a housing estate and a market. Naturally they demolished the tea plantations and used the land for commercial purpose which is not permissible under any law of the land. The property being a tea garden even if it is assumed that the Ministry of Land has accorded permission for transfer, the transferee cannot utilize the land of the tea estate for the purposes other than the purposes for which the tea garden has been dedicated. The said conversion is hit by section 20(4A), and 20(5) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The Deity is entitled to retain the property under subsection (5) of section 20. In no way the said property can be converted and used for other purposes.</u>

40. Mr. Prabir Neogi submitted that the deed of endowment permits the alienation of the property for the welfare of the Deity. He has produced a copy of the deed of endowment. In the cause title the founder Sree Baikuntha Chandra Gupta clearly stated the purpose of the creation of the deed of gift to the effect that “শ্রীহট" শহরের সন্নিকটবর্তী ষ্ঠার নামক চা বাগান শ্রী শ্রী রাধাকৃষ্ণ দারুমন মূত্তিদ্বয় স্হাপন করিয়াছি ৷ উক্ত বিগ্রহ দ্বয়ের নিত্য সেবা পূজা ভৈনমিত্তিক উৎসবাদি এবং বার্ষিক তেহরে পর্বাদি সুনিয়মে এবং সুচারু রুপে সম্পন্ন হ্ইবার উদ্দেশ্যে এবং তৎসম্পর্কীয় প্রয়োজনীয় ব্যয় ও কোন কোন থেকে হিতকর কার্যো আয় ব্যয় নির্ধারন। So, the object of the dedication was completely for religious and charitable purposes. There is no doubt about it. He then stated “লিখিত স্হাবর সম্পত্তি দেবাত্তর স্বরুপ বর্নিত বিগ্রহদ্বয়কে দান করতঃ দান বিয়াদি অধিকারে এবং অন্যান্য স্বার্থ ও সম্পর্ক ত্যাগ করিলাম অদ্যাবধি উল্লিখিত সম্পত্তিতে বিগ্রহ দ্বয়ের স্বতৃ ও অধিকার জন্মিল ৷ সেবাইত বা অধ্যক্ষগনকে ১ম তপসীলের প্রদত্ত অধিকার ভিন্ন দান বিক্রয়াদি কোন প্রকার হস্তান্তরের কি দায়াবদ্ধের অধিকার প্রদত্ত হইল না।” There is thus clear recital in the deed that after the dedication he has extinguished his right, title and interest in favour of the Deity and reserved limited power of the Shebait as mentioned in schedule one. No power has been given to the Shebait to alienate the property for any other purposes. In the first schedule, it is stated that the Shebait is entitled to bear the expenses of the sebapuja of the Deity out of the income; that he shall pay the salary to the guards, scholarship to students; that if any religious school for teaching Veda (ঢোল) is established, to pay the expenses; to pay rent and taxes; to teach or arrange for teaching of sanskrit to Brahmin's son and to pay scholarship of Tk.50/- to his daughters till their life time annually and to maintain the tea estate.

41. A question may arise, by reason of reserving a scholarship of Tk. 50/- annually for daughters of the founder can the endowment be treated as exclusively for religious and charitable purposes? There is no reason to infer as such, inasmuch as, the founder has donated the tea estate on 2nd July, 1915, reserving scholarship of Tk. 50/- only annually to his daughters without reserving any provision for their maintenance and also for the maintenance their heirs. So, the dedication is out and out for religious and charitable purposes. More so, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act operated at Sylhet on 1st August, 1963 when they were not alive.

42. Mr. Neogi refers to schedule 7 of the said deed wherein it was recited that “ন্যাস্ত সম্পত্তির হিতকল্পে বা উন্নতি সাধনোদ্দেশ্যে দেবালয়ের সেবাইত বা অধ্যক্ষগণের একযোগে ট্রাস্টি কোম্পানী কোন স্থাবর বা অস্থাবর সম্পত্তি ক্রয় করিতে কিংবা এরুপ সম্পত্তির চিরস্থায়ী বা স্থায়ী পাট্রা কিংবা পত্তনী দিতে বা গ্রহণ করিতে এবং প্রয়োজনীয় দলিল আদি আদান প্রদান এবং সম্পাদন করিতে পারিবেন ও তৎসম্বন্ধে মতভেদ হইলে সেবাইতদের মতানুসারে কার্য্য হইবে।” Schedule second to sixth, relates to the mode of maintenance of the Deity and the charitable works have been elaborately described. It has been revealed in the deed that the founder made a trust previously with a sum of Tk. 2,90,000/- and the amount was kept in government promissory notes. It is recited that as the annual interest accrued out of Tk. 2,90,000/- kept in the government promissory notes in the names of Deity's trustee M/S B.C. Gupta & Sons Ltd. was not sufficient to meet the expenses of the Deity and charitable works, he has dedicated the tea estate with for meeting the expenses. In the seventh schedule, it is provided that for the welfare and development of the endowed property, the Shebait and the trustee company conjointly may purchase or alienate any property. This clause does not relate to the alienation of the tea estate, rather it is for the maintenance of the Deity and the development of the tea estate. It relates to the purchase of property out of the income and in case of necessity, they can sell such acquired property for the welfare of the Deity.

43. Therefore, even if it is assumed that the Shebait has agreed to transfer the property in favour of the writ petitioner, it was beyond the powers given to him and therefore, the lease was without jurisdiction on the principle that a delegate cannot exercise more power than the delegator.

44. Writ petitioners have withdrawn Tk. 30,76,189.20/- which was given by the government as compensation for the purpose of acquisition of some lands of debutter property for the purpose of construction of a Divisional Stadium and establishment of the Sylhet University. The deed of endowment clearly provides that any income out of the money and the tea estate will be invested exclusively for religious and charitable purposes preserving the debuttor property intact. Ragib Ali cannot become the Shebait of the deity, and therefore, he cannot withdraw the said money. The writ petitioners claimed in paragraph 9 of the writ petition that after the execution of the lease deed 'the petitioner no.1 became absolute owner and possessor of the tea estate. They treated a religious property into a secular property. This statement nakedly focused the motive behind the creation of the lease deed. It is only the legal Shebait who can withdraw the compensation money from the government and the money can be spent only for the welfare of the Deity and also for charitable purposes as per deed of endowment. Annexure "Al" to the writ petition clearly reveals that no letter under memo dated 14th August, 2005 of the Ministry of Land has been issued. Writ petitioners have annexed this letter as annexure "C" to the writ petition. It is alleged that this letter was procured by resorting forgery. On the other hand, writ petitioners claimed that the Ministry issued this letter. This being a disputed question of fact cannot be decided in a summary manner in writ jurisdiction.

45. Therefore, the High Court Division acted access of jurisdiction in quashing the proceedings in Sylhet Kotwali P.S. Case Nos. 117, dated 22nd September, 2009 and 12 dated 2nd November, 2015 filed against the writ petitioners. We are shocked to note that though no prayer was made in the writ petition for quashing those proceedings, the High Court Division suo moto quashed those proceedings. The rule was issued on the terms as to why the letters under memos dated 12th September, 2005 and 31st October, 2005 directing the writ respondent No. 5 to take over possession; control and management of Tarapur Tea Estate and the order of recovery of Tk. 30,76,189.20/- from the writ petitioners to have been issued without lawful authority. The High Court has traveled beyond the rule issuing order.

<u>46. The High Court Division was of the view that since 32.91 acres of land of the tea estate belonging to the Deity has been acquired for construction of Sylhet Divisional Stadium and Shahajalal University of Science and Technology and since the compensation money of Tk. 30,76,189.20 assessed for the acquisition of the land has been given to the constituted attorney the writ petitioner No.2, the writ respondents are estopped on the principles of estoppel from questioning the transfer of the tea estate. How fallacy the opinion of the High Court Division is in making the rule absolute without at all looking at as to whether a property which has been exclusively dedicated for religious and charitable purposes can be transferred by the alleged Shebait who is none but the manager of the Deity and that's too, by resorting of forgery? There is no legal bar in the acquisition of any debutter property under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of the Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982. The bar is provided in the proviso to section 3 is that "no property used by the public for the purpose of religious worship, graveyard and cremation ground shall be acquired".</u>

<u>47. The idol of the Deity or the temple where the worship is being offered has not been acquired by the government. Admittedly, the Deity and the temple were in existence at the time of acquisition. Therefore, this is not a legal ground for justifying the alienation of the Deity's property. Estoppel is an ancient English word which originally bore precisely the same signification as the equally ancient English word 'stop' whereof it is merely a variant. An estoppel may be said to arise when a person executes some deed, or is concerned in or does some act, either of record or in pais, which will preclude him from averring anything to the contrary. 'Estoppel by matters in pais' is defined by Blackstone as 'an assurance transacted between two or more private persons in pais, in the country, that is, upon the very spot to be transferred. Coke defined it "It is called an estoppel or conclusions, because a man's own act or acceptance stoppeth or closeth up his mouth to allege or plead the truth". The rule is founded on the equitable doctrine that it would be most inequitable and unjust if a person, who by a representation made or by conduct amounting to a representation, has induced another to act as he would not otherwise have done, should be allowed to deny or repudiate the effect of his former statement to the loss and injury of the person who acted on it. This doctrine has no manner of application in this case.</u>

<u>48. The High Court Division was totally unmindful to the laws applicable in this case or in the alternative, it was totally confused as to the application of law in the matter and delivered a judgment which has no sanction of law. The judgment of the High Court Division is, therefore, liable to be interfered with and accordingly it is done. Accordingly, we sum up our opinion as under:</u>

<u>(a) a religious and charitable trust by way of debutter is created only when a property is dedicated for the worship or service of the idol;</u>

<u>(b) a Hindu idol is founded upon the religious customs of the Hindus;</u>

<u>(c) a Shebait, cannot delegate his duties to another, no matter whether such other is a stranger or a co-trustee on the principle of the maxim Delegatus non potest delegare';</u>

<u>(d) an idol is a juristic person in whom the title of the property of the endowment vests; but it is only in an ideal sense that the idol is the owner;</u>

<u>(e) the office of the Shebait being used for religious purposes under the Hindu Law, apostasy is a disqualification in the heir and execution of his inheritance as well as for holding the office of Shebaitship;</u>

<u>(f) when a pious Hindu establishes a Deity cannot conceive of its `seba' and `puja' being carried on under the supervision of a non-Hindu religion believer;</u>

<u>(g) the founder of an endowment can confer upon a Shebait appointed by him the right of nominating his successor subject to the limitation that the nominee cannot be a believer of any religion other than a Hindu religion;</u>

<u>(h) the deed of endowment does not permit the alienation of the debuttor property i.e. Tarapur Tea Estate by the Shebait or his nominee;</u>

<u>(i) the transfer of the Tarapur Tea Estate for 99 years by the alleged Shebait is void ab initio.</u>

<u>(j) the writ petitioners are directed to Shift Ragib Ali Medical College and Hospital at a suitable place within six months from the date of the judgment so that the academic education of the students is not hampered;</u>

<u>(k) The conversion of a portion of the tea estate into a medical college, a housing estate and use of the same for other purposes is totally illegal, and therefore, Tarapur Tea Estate should be restored to its original position;</u>

<u>(l) the Deity installed by the founder should be installed at its original place, if it is removed from its original site in the meantime;</u>

<u>(m) the withdrawal of Tk. 30,76,189.20 as compensation money from the government by Ragib Ali was illegal and without jurisdiction. Ragib Ali is directed to refund the said amount within 7(seven) days from the date of receipt of the judgment to the legal Shebait of the Deity and in the absence of the legal Shebait, in the account of the Deity;</u>

<u>(n) the writ petitioners Abdul Hai and Ragib Ali are directed to hand over vacant possession of Tarapur Tea Estate in favour of the Shebait of the Deity within 1(one) month from the date receipt of the judgment;</u>

<u>(o) the constructions made on a portion of the Tarapur Tea Estate should be dismantled within six months and the writ petitioners are directed to transplant tea plantations thereon. If they fail to dismantle them, the Shebait shall dismantle them with the help of police and the city corporation, and the costs be recovered from the writ petitioners by the Deputy Commissioner;</u>

<u>(p) In the absence of a legal Shebait of the Deity, the Deputy Commissioner is directed to appoint a Shebait of the Deity in consultation with the ten leading Shebaits or priests of the temples of Sylhet town;</u>

<u>(q) The writ petitioners are directed to refund Tk. 5,00,00,000/- (five crore) which they admittedly earned by exporting tea to the Shebait (Para 10 of the writ petition).</u>

49. The Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet shall monitor the implementation of the directions given above. If the writ petitioners fail to comply with the direction, he shall take legal action against them and shift the medical college to a suitable place by freezing the bank accounts of the writ petitioners and withdrawing money from those accounts for the purpose of taking temporary lease of a house suitable for the medical college.

<u>50. If the writ petitioners fail to make tea plantations, the Deputy Commissioner shall make plantations by constituting a committee at the cost of the writ petitioners and the amount be realized from their moveable and immovable properties. The Kotwali P.S. Case Nos. 117 dated 27.9.2005 and 12 dated 2.11.2005 shall proceed forthwith. The Chief Judicial Magistrate or the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, as the case may be, is directed to proceed with the cases expeditiously.</u>

<u>51. The appeal is allowed with cost of Tk. 5,00,000/- in the above terms.</u>

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 733 of 2010
lawyer:
Bishmodeb Chakrabortee, Deputy Attorney General instructed by B.Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners.
A.M. Aminuddin, Advocate instructed by Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Respondent.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh and Others -------- Petitioners
Vs.
Mrs. Daizy Hossain @ Rebeka Kanis -------- Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 03.11.2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 76 of 1989)
full_judgment:
Nazmun Ara Sultana, J. This Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal, at the instance of the government of Bangladesh and others, is directed against the Judgment and order dated 03.11.2009 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No. 76 of 1989 allowing the appeal filed by the plaintiff against the judgment and decree dated 29.04.1989 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Narayangonj in Title No. 637 of 1981 decreeing the suit partly.

<u>2. The respondent here in filed the above mentioned Title Suit No. 637 of 1981 for declaration of title to the suit property and also for a further declaration that the order dated 22.03.1978 passed by the defendant No. 2 (A.D.C. Revenue) treating the suit property as vested and non-resident property is illegal, void, malafide and not binding upon the plaintiff. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit property, as described in the schedule to the plaint, together with other properties originally belonged to Shashi Mohan Saha, Surendra Chandra Saha, Khetra Mohan Saha, Raj Mohan Saha, Rajendra Chandra Saha, Suresh Chandra Saha, Ranjit Kumar Saha, Brojendra Chandra saha, Gogan Chandra Saha and Bhagaban Chandra Saha. Those owners sold the suit property along with their other ejmali lands to Bhakta Das Saha, Ananta Kumar Saha, Sachinanandan Saha and Joshoda Lal Saha by two registered Kabalas dated 05.03.1935. Thereafter, Sachinanandan Saha and Joshoda Lal Saha surrendered their interest in the suit property along with other lands in favour of Bhakta Das Saha and Ananta Kumar Saha by a registered deed dated 26.07.1938. On the basis of Partition Suit No. 29 of 1938, the suit property together with other lands fell in the saham of Bhakta Das Saha alone. Bhakta Das Saha died leaving 5 sons, namely, Haripada Das Saha, Shaoni Manda Das Saha, Durga Sankar Das Saha, Gouri Sarkar Das Saha and Jogesh Chandra Saha, Subsequently there was an amicable partition of their paternal properties amongst 5 brothers and the suit property fell in the exclusive share of Haripada Das Saha along with some other properties. Thus Haripada Das Saha became owner and possessor of the disputed property and he got his name recorded in the S.A. Khatian vide order dated 02.01.1973 passed in Mutation Case No. 37/N of 1972-73. Municipal holding was also opened in his name and he had been possessing the suit property on payment of regular rents to the Government and also paid taxes to the Narayangonj Municipality. During R.S. operation, his name was also recorded and he was possessing the suit property by letting out the same to different monthly tenants. Thereafter, Haripada Das Saha transferred the suit property to the plaintiff by a registered Kabala dated 03.01.1976 for valuable consideration and delivered possession in her favour. Brother of the vendor, Namely, Durga Sankar Saha was also an attesting witness to the said transfer deed and thereby admitted exclusive ownership of Haripada Das Saha in the suit property so transferred. He also admitted exclusive ownership of his brother Haripada Das Saha by swearing affidavit before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka. After purchase of the suit property, the plaintiff got her name mutated in place of her vendor Haripada Das Saha on 12.01.1976 and she has been paying rents to the Government regularly. Her name was also recorded against the municipal holding of the suit property and she has been paying taxes. She has been possessing the suit property by letting out the same to different monthly tenants as before.</u>

3. The defendant No. 2 A.D.C. Revenue, at the instance of some persons inimical to the plaintiff, suddenly issued notice in the year 1977 by starting a vested property case. The plaintiff appeared and submitted objection in writing, but the defendant No. 2 arbitrarily passed an order 22.03.1978 declaring the suit property as vested and non-resident in the V.P. Miscellaneous Case Nos. 30-32 of 1977 and took steps to lease out the suit property to others. Thus the title of the plaintiff in suit property has become clouded and as such she filed the suit.

4. The defendant No. 2 A.D.C. Revenue, Narayangonj contested the suit by filling written statement denying the exclusive right and title of the plaintiff in the entire suit property. This defendant has contended, inter-alia, that the plaintiff might have, at best, acquired share in the suit property by purchasing from one of the 5 brothers who were owners of the suit property. According to the defendants case, the suit property ultimately belonged to Bhakta Das Saha who died leaving 5 sons including the plaintiffs vendor Haripada Das Saha. That the other four brother of Haripada Das Saha left this country for India in the year 1965 and there in the suit property vested in the Government and accordingly, the defendant No. 2 being competent authority, passed an order treating the same as vested property in accordance with law. That the story of the family arrangement and amicable partition amongst the 5 sons of Bhakta Das Saha is concocted and it has been fraudulently introduced for grabbing the vested property. That the plaintiff has not acquired any right, title and interest in the suit property except the share of Haripada das Saha and as such the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The trial Court, on consideration of the evidence adduced by both the parties though found plaintiff's possession in the entire suit property, but disbelieved her vendor's exclusive ownership in the suit property by way of amicable partition. Accordingly, the trial Court declaration plaintiffs title to the extent of 2/5 annas share in the suit property.

<u>6. The plaintiff preferred First Appeal No. 76 of 1989 against part decree passed by the trial court. The High Court Division, on consideration of the evidence and other facts and circumstances allowed the appeal and decreed the suit in full declaring the plaintiff's right, title and interest in the entire suit property and also declaring the order passed by the defendant No. 2 in V.P. Case Nos. 30-32 of 1977 treating the suit property as vested and non-resident property as illegal, malafide, void, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff. The High Court Division made observation to the effect that after repeal of the Vested and Non-resident Property ordinance by Ordinance No. 92 of 1976, there was no scope to start new V.P. Case under the provision of repealed laws in the year 1977 and in the circumstances the very initiation of the instant V.P. case in the year 1977 for treating the suit property as vested and non-resident property was illegal.</u>

7. Mr. Bishmodeb Chakrabortee, the learned Deputy Attorney General has frankly conceded that this observation of the High Court Division is correct and that the initiation of the V.P. case in question in the year 1977 for treating the suit property as vest property was illegal and the order dated 22.03.1978 passed by the defendant No. 2 (A.D.C. Revenue) in that V.P. case treating the suit property as vested and non-resident property has been illegal.

8. It appears that the High Court Division, on meticulous examination of the evidence, both oral and documentary adduced by the plaintiff and also the other facts and circumstances on record found that the plaintiff's case that Haripada Das Saha became the exclusive owner of the suit property by way of amicable partition among his 5 brother has been proved sufficiently. Undisputedly this Haripada Das Saha transferred the entire suit land to the plaintiff by a registered deed in the year 1976. The plaintiffs possession in the entire suit land has been admitted by the sole witness of the contesting defendants also.

9. In the circumstance we find no reason to interfere with the findings and decision arrived at by the High Court Division. In our opinion the High Court Division rightly found the plaintiff's right, title and possession in the entire suit land and, therefore, rightly declared her title in the suit land. The High Court Division rightly declared also that the treating of the suit property as vest property in the year 1977 has been illegal.

10. Evidently there is no merit in this civil petition for Leave to Appeal and hence it is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1032 of 2010
lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Senior Advocate (with Probir Neogi, Advocate), instructed by Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Petitioners
Sarder Rashed Zahangir, D.A.G instructed by B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For Respondent No.1
For Respondent No.2 ------ Not Represented.
parties:
Md. Firoz Miah and another ------- Petitioners
VS
Bangladesh represented by the Ministry Of Housing and works and another ------- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 29th day of October, 2010 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 4971 of 2001)
full_judgment:
Surendra Kumar Sinha J. Writ petitioners are the petitioners before us and they seek leave from this Division from a judgment of the High Court Division passed in a writ petition discharging the rule and maintaining a judgment of the Court of Settlement.

<u>2. The property in question was enlisted in the (b) list of the abandoned building published by the Government of exercise of powers under section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No.  LIV of 1984). According to the writ petitioner, the disputed property was leased out in favour of one Md. Habibullah. Subsequently, Habibullah transferred the said property in favour of Mr. Shamsun Nahar Rahman by a registered deed dated 28th February 1978, who in turn by-another deed dated 30th July, 1984, transferred the same in favour of the petitioners. After purchase, they renovated old structures and have been possessing the same peacefully and at that point of time, one Mrs. Sufia Begum claimed ownership by purchase of I the said property for valuable consideration through one Aslam, the constituted attorney of Md. Habibullah. The petitioners with a view to avoid complications purchased her Right as well by a deed dated 30th August 1982. Subsequently, they came to know that the property was included in the (b) list,("kha" list) of the abandoned buildings which was wrongly done since the property was not left abandoned or uncared for at any point of time of on the date of promulgation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 (P.O.16 of 1972) and therefore , the Gazette notification was illegal and void. They unsuccessfully   moved the Court of Settlement in Settlement Case No. 88 of 1996 and then the High Court Division in its writ Jurisdiction.</u>

<u>3. The High Court Division has held that it cannot interfere with the findings of the Court of settlement under its extra ordinary Jurisdiction unless it is shown that the said court has acted without jurisdiction and made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence causing prejudice to the petitioners or it has acted mollified or in violation of the principles of natural justice. The High Court Division then following the dictum in the cases of Bangladesh V. Md. Jalil, 15 BLD (AD) 175, Secretary, Ministry of works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh V. Rowshan Ara Begum, 59 DLR (AD) 167, Government of Bangladesh V. Asraf Ali, 2 MLR (AD) 96 and some other cases held that though there was service of notice, it was not in terms of section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance No.  LIV of 1984; that the petitioners failed to adduce evidenced in the Court of settlement that Md. Habibullah occupied, managed or supervised the property on 28th February, 1992 and that the property was legally enlisted in the (b) list.</u>

4. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner argues that the High Court Division having found that prior notice required under section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance No.  LIV of 1984 was not served in accordance with law, it erred in law in not holding that the inclusion of the disputed property, in the abandoned buildings list was not lawful or illegal. Learned Counsel next contends that in view of the decisions given by a five member Bench of this Division in Government of Bangladesh V. Syed Chand Sultana, 51 DLR (AD) 24, Bangladesh V. Amela Khatun 53 DLR (AD) 55 and Government of Bangladesh. V. Bibi Marium, 54 DLR (AD) 100 on the question of non service of notice in accordance with section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance the High Court Division acted illegally in relying upon decisions of three member Bench of this Division in Golam Rabbani V. Chairman, Court of Settlement, 13 MLR (AD) 345 and Rowshan Ara V. Secretary, Ministry of works. 59 DLR (AD) 165, It is finally contended that in view of the conflicting decisions of this Division on the question of service of notice, leave should be granted to settle the conflicting decisions on the question of service of notice.

5. "Abandoned property" within the meaning of clause (1) of Article 2 of P.0.16 of 1972 means "any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property including-

(i) Any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a state which at the time after 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operation against the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

(ii) Any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972

6. It is proved in Article 4 that on the commencement of P.O.16 of 1972 all abandoned properties in Bangladesh shall "vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of, by transfer or otherwise, in accordance with the provisions of this order. So, as soon as any property, covers the definition of abandoned property it automatically vests in the Government and it can deal with the property in accordance with law. There is restriction of transfer or creation of any encumbrance of abandoned property in any manner otherwise than in accordance with the provision of the said order. Any property which has been vested in the Government under Article 4 shall be exempted from all legal process, including seizure distress, ejectment attachment or sale by any officer of a court or any other authority, and the Civil courts are debarred from passing any interlocutory order of injunction restraining the Government of any of its officer from tacking possession of the said property and if after service of notice upon any person requiring or directing him to surrender possession of such property who fails to surrender possessions. The Officers designated in Article 7 May pass such order as they deem fit, that is to say, they have been given absolute discretionary power to take legal action against such person.

7. The Government then promulgated the Bangladesh Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance LIV of 1985). In this ordinance "building" defined under clause (a) of section 2 means "any residential or other building or structure of any kind in an urban area and includes the land adjunct, and the courtyard, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground appearing to such building". Section 5 of the ordinance empowers the Government to publish from time to time in the official Gazette two lists of buildings; namely (a) and (b). List (a) to contain buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property under the Order, and list (b) to contain buildings in respect of which notices for surrendering or taking possession as abandoned property under the Order, 1972 has been issued upon the persons concerned. No such lists shall include any buildings in respect of which any decree or order has been passed by any civil court declaring the building not to be an abandoned property or not be have been vested in the Government, and secondly, in respect of which a suit, appeal or application or other legal proceeding is pending before any court, immediately before the date of publication of the lists in the official Gazette in which the vesting in or possession of the Government of the building as abandoned   property under the said Order has been called in question.

8. It is provided in sub-section (2) of section 5 that the lists shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have been vested in the Government: Section 7 requires the claimant of the building to establish that the building is not an abandoned property and has not (been) vested in the Government ---'This Ordinance has been promulgated as a supplementary provision to P.O.16 of 1072 for the purpose of administration, control, management and disposal of abandoned property finally, so that nobody can claim ownership of the property after the expiry of prescribed period. So, a person can claim ownership of the property which has been declared as abandoned if he was present in Bangladesh on 28th February, 1972 of that he was not a citizen of a state which was at war in 1971 against Bangladesh and that he did not manage and supervise the property during the relevant time. That is why, there is reference of P.O.16 of 1972 in section 4, 5, 6, and 7. The lists of the buildings to be enlisted will be abandoned property within the meaning of P0.16 of 1972 as is evident from the language used in sections 5 and 7 of the Ordinance.

<u>9. There is presumption of abandoned character of the property if it attracts the definition of abandoned property and the onus to rebut the presumption in the person who claims otherwise, that is to say, the property is not an abandoned property. So also, the publication of the lists shall have legal presumption that the buildings have been legally enlisted as abandoned property and vested in the Government. After the publication of the lists, any person interested in the said property claiming any right or interest in any of the buildings, which is included in any lists before a court or settlement constituted in exercise of powers under section 9 of the Ordinance is required to prove that the building is not an abandoned property and has not been vested in the Government under PO.16 of 1972. The onus squarely lies on the person who claims the exclusion of the building from the lists. This presumption is closely allied to the subject of burden proof under the Evidence Act. When the burden of proof of a fact is on a party, it may be said that there is presumption as to non-existence of that fact, and where there is a presumption as to existence of a fact, the burden of proving the non-existence of that fact is on the party who asserts its non-existence. These are established principles of presumption of fact.</u>

10. A presumption is a rule of law that the courts shall draw a particular inference from a particular fact, unless and until the truth of such inference is disproved by the person who asserts its non-existence. A presumption of law is a rule of law that a particular inference shall be drawn by a court from a particular circumstance. Some of these presumptions are natural presumptions which the law simply recognizes and enforce. There presumptions of law are, however, rebuttable and these presumptions are intendments made by law, but, unlike them, they only hold good until disproved. In presumptions of law, the law peremptorily requires a certain inference to the made whenever the facts appear which it assumes as the basis of that inference. As presumptions of law are, in reality, rules of law, and part of the law itself, the court may draw inference whenever the requisite facts are before it. In case of presumption of law, the law declares a certain inference to be made whenever facts appear which it assumes on the basis of that inference. It is to be borne in mind that it is the established principles of law that the presumption is always in favour of the constitutionality of an enactment the reason is obvious. It is assumed that the legislature understands and correctly appreciates the needs of its own people that its laws are directed to problems made manifests by experience and its determinations are based on adequate grounds. It is presumed that the legislature does not make mistakes or omissions. In the words of lord Halsbury, A court of law is bound to proceed on the assumption that the legislature is an ideal person that does not make mistakes (Pemsel, 1891 AC 531 (549).

11. Keeping the above position of law on the subject, let us now consider the cases cited by Mr. Mahmudul Islam. In Syed Chand Sultana (Supra), one Syed Mozaffar Hossain of Jessore, a practicing Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh was the lessee of the disputed property who during his life time gifted the same orally followed by an affidavit as evidence of gift in favour of his heirs sometimes in June, 1974. The said gift was duly accepted by the then Dhaka Improvement Trust now Rajdhani Unnayan Katnpakha and then the heirs got a plan duly approved in their own names for construction of a building and pursuant thereto, they constructed a building between the period 1978 and 1980. Thereafter with a view to transfer the said property, they applied to RAJUK for permission when they were informed that the property was included in the '(b)' list of the abandoned buildings. As no notice was served upon them, they challenged the inclusion of the property in the list by a writ petition stating that they could not avail the opportunity provided in section 7. The High Court Division found that no copy of the notice was produced before it nor was it shown when and how it was issued and although the property is situated in Road No 138, in (b) list it was mentioned that the property is situated at Road No.  137. In the facts of the given case, this Division upheld the decision of the High Court Division on the reasoning that in the absence of any allegation that "the writ petitioners or their father are not Bangladeshi or that they were nationals of any country at any time after 25th March, 1971 was at war with Bangladesh" the inclusion of the property in the (b) list was totally illegal and also approved the High Court Division's finding that as no copy of the notice under section 7(sic) of the Ordinance was produced before it nor was it shown when and how it was issued upon the writ petitioners, the alternative remedy available under section 7 will not stand in the way of invoking writ jurisdiction since the very inclusion of the property in question in the (b) list was ex-facie void for want of jurisdiction and vocatives of article 42 of the Constitution. So this case is quite distinguishable and not applicable in this case.

12. In Amela Khatoon, the claimants produced original deeds relating to the disputed property before the Court of Settlement and the same were considered relevant fact that the owner Bibi Homaira was at Dhaka on the date of execution and registration of the deed on 30th April, 1973 and that these facts proved that the property was managed by the owner till that date. This Division maintained the judgment of the High Court Division observing that as the respondents were in possession in assertion of their right, title and interest, the enlistment of the property in the (b) list of the abandoned buildings without issuing any notice upon them was illegal.

13. In Bibi Marium, (54 DLR (AD) 100), this Division noticed that the Court of Settlement was not properly constituted when the writ petitioner moved the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.  701 of 1987 challenging the inclusion of the disputed  property in (b) list. The High Court Division found that the original lessee Ahmed Hossain was in possession till his death, who sold the property by a registered deed dated 8th February, 1973, in favour of Abul Hashem who continued his possession till his death on 13th June, 1085. This possession was not denied by the Government. In the facts of the given case,. it was observed that the High Court Division rightly found that "the judgment of the Court of Settlement is Coram non-judice, the illegal inclusion of the buildings  in the Kha; list of the abandoned buildings was unlawful. The ratio of these cases are that the owners of the disputed property were present in Bangladesh during the relevant time ,that they did not cease to occupy, supervise and manage of their property and that inclusion of the same in the (b) list without proper service of notice required by law was illegal.

14. In case of Roushan Ara, this Division noticed that the Court of Settlement on examination of the materials on record II held that Sahara Khatun, who has said to have alienated the disputed property in favour of her daughter Ansari Khatun was present in Bangladesh and her whereabouts were known on the date of promulgation of P.0.16 of 1972. On the question of non-service of notice this Division observed that the non-service of notice being a question of fact and the determination thereof is required to be determined upon consideration of the evidence by the parties and since Roushan Ara did not raise the issue before the Court of Settlement, the raising of the said point at a belated stage merited no consideration.

15. In Gulam Rabbani, as the daughter of the original lessee refused to execute the sale deed in pursuance of the agreement in respect of the property executed by her predecessor in January, 1971, the writ petitioner instituted a suit seeking for a declaration that the property was not an abandoned property and for specific performance of contract. The suit was decreed by the trial court and thereafter, the sale deed was executed through Court. However, as the property was enlisted in the (a) list, the Writ Petitioner moved a petition in the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the property from the list. One Mobina claiming the daughter of the original lessee Md. Muslim also filed a case in the Court of Settlement for release of the property. One Abdus Sattar also filed another case for release of the property on the plea that he took the property on lease from the Government. The case filed by the decree holder was dismissed by the Court of Settlement and its judgment was affirmed by the High Court Division. It was on record that Md. Muslim appeared in the Court of Settlement on 8th January 1992 and deposed stating that he never executed any agreement for sale in favour of the writ petitioner in January, 1971. The identify of Md. Muslim Mia, the original lessee, was not challenged by the writ petitioner. In view of that fact, the High Court Division came to a definite finding that as the identify of Md. Muslim Mia had not been challenged, the agreement in favour of the writ petitioner was a disputed question of fact and that he committed gigantic fraud upon the court in securing a collusive decree in the suit. In that case also writ petitioner failed to produce the original documents before the court of Settlement. In view of the above, this Division observed that the facts of the case in Amela Khatun were distinguishable. The question of service of notice was not an issue in that case.

16. In the case in hand, the petitioner filed photocopy of the power of attorney said to have been executed by Md. Habibullah in favour of Matiur Rahman, who on the strength of the said authority transferred the property in favour of Shamsun Nahar Begum but he did not file the original deed without giving any explanation. It was further held that though Shamsun Nahar said to have transferred the property in favour of the petitioner, the said deed had not been proved in evidence; that the petitioner also did not file the power of attorney of Md. Aslam executed by Md. Habibullah; that he filed the certified copy of the deed dated 13th August, 1982, executed by Sufia Khatun; that from the deeds it appeared to the court of settlement that from time to time the property was sold by the attorneys, but in order to avoid the future complications, he did not file the original deeds that the explanation given by the petitioner about non-filing of the original deeds was not acceptable that petitioner also failed to prove that Md. Habibullah was a citizen of Bangladesh after the liberation war and that he failed to prove that Md. Habibullah was in this country in 1973 or 1976.

17. The High Court Division on consideration of the said findings held that there was no explanation on the part of the petitioner why he did not adduce evidence in the Court of Settlement to the effect that Md. Habibullah managed and supervised the property in question on 28th February, 1972 and that the deeds of purchase adverted in the writ petition are nugatory so far as the abandoned character of the disputed property is concerned and that those deeds could not be called in aid to prop up the case of the petitioners.

<u>18. As to the question of non-service of notice, it is not the case that no notice was at all served upon the petitioners. A notice in fact was served upon them on 9th March, 1986, directing them to appear before the Ministry of works in support of their possession of the property with the documents pointing out that the property was enlisted as abandoned property. True, the notice was not issued in accordance with the requirements of law, but by the same time, it cannot be ignored that they were served a notice intimating about the enlistment of property as abandoned property. By operation of law, the disputed property became abandoned property. The petitioners failed to prove before the Court of Settlement that the original lessee Md. Habibullah was in this country on the date of promulgation of P.O.16 of 1972 of that he managed, supervised and controlled the property. Rather, according to petitioners case, two persons simultaneously claimed ownership of the property. They allegedly purchased from Shamsun Nahar Rahman as transferee from Md. Habibullah and another from Mrs. Sufia Begum, who had also claimed to have purchased the same property from Md. Habibullah through his attorney Aslam. Both transfers were made through their alleged attorneys. It Md. Habibullah was in Bangladesh, what prevented him to transfer the property through his attorneys is not clear to us. This fact sufficiently suggested that Md. Habibullah was not present when the property was declared as abandoned property and that Md. Habibullah did not occupy, manage or supervise the property.</u>

19. In Hazerullah V. Chairman, 1st Court, 3 BLC (AD) 42, a question arose about the legality of the enlistment of the property as the Government was not in possession of the property but the property was enlisted under section 5(1) (a) of the Ordinance. A five member Bench of this Division held that 'This contention will stand only when the claimant can prove that the disputed building was not an abandoned property.' Similar view was taken in Government of Bangladesh V. K.M. Zaker Hossain, 23 BLD (AD) 24. The principle is that if the property has declared as abandoned property and a Gazette notification has been passed, there is presumption that it has been legally declared as abandoned property and in such cases the enlistment of the building either in (a) or (b) list or that proper service of notice is immaterial unless the claimant can prove that the property is not abandoned property.

<u>20. The Court of settlement was, therefore, perfectly justified in holding that the petitioners failed to prove that the property was legally enlisted in the abandoned (b) list and that the petitioners right or interest had not been affected by P.O. 16 of 1972. This technical defect of the service of notice would confer not legal right upon the petitioners to retain possession of the abandoned property once it was legally declared as abandoned property. Nor would the abandoned character of the property be changed. This improper service of notice does not shift the onus upon the Government to prove that the property is legally declared as abandoned property. The rebuttal onus will shift only when the claimant of the property proves that the owners was in this country on 28th February, 1972 and that the property was not left abandoned or uncared for on the date of promulgation of P.O. 16 of 1972.</u>

21. We find no merit in the contention that the High Court Division acted illegally in relying upon the cases of Golam Rabbani and Rawshan Ara which are said to have been inconsistent with the views taken by five member Bench in Syed Chand Sultana and Bibi Marium on the question of the effect of service of notice under section 5(1) (b) of the Ordinance or that the decisions given in Golam Rabbani and Rawshan Ara are per incurium constituting on binding effect. We hold that those decisions still hold the field in the facts of the given case. A decision is binding not because of its conclusions but in regard to its ratio and the principle laid down therein. (Shama Rao V. Union Territory of Pondicherry, (1967) 2 SCR 650). In extracting a ratio decidendi of a case, Goodheart in his Essays in Jurisprudence and Common Law, (1931) 1 suggests a 'material fact' test and defines the ratio decidendi as the material facts of the case plus the decision therein. In the words of Jessel, MR. The only thing in a Judges decision binding as an authority upon a Surendra Kumar subsequent Judge is the principle upon which the case was decided: (Osborne to Rowlett, (1880) 13Ch.D. 774(785). It is to be noted that no case can be an authority on facts. So the cases cited by Mr. Mahmudul Islam are quite distinguishable. The High Court Division, in the premises, has committed no legality in not interfering with the judgment of the Court of Settlement relying upon the cases of Golam Rabbani and Rawshan Ara.

22. The petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No.3220 of 2011
lawyer:
Mr. Md. Noor Hossain Chowdhury, Advocate with Mr. Md. Abdul Halim Mandal, Advocate  ----- For the Petitioner 
Mr. Ataul Gani, Advocate ----- For the Opposite party No.1
parties:
Md. Bahauddin ----- Petitioner
Versus
Joynab Bibi and others ----- Opposite parties
full_judgment:
Mr. Sharif Uddin Chaklader, J :- This rule calls in question the order passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka on 16.6.2011 in Civil Revision No.30 of 2011 affirming the order dated 10.1.2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka allowing opposite party No.1 to be added as defendant in Title Suit No.377 of 2009. 
2. Plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit on 11.6.2009 challenging the Memo No.Jagrik (BhuSob)/A,L154/90/224/1 (5) dated 1 3. 1 .2009 issued by defendant No.3 as illegal and null and void. Shortly, plaintiff's case is that, plaintiff got registered lease deed being No.4278 dated 7.12.1998 registered at Sub-registry office at Mohammadpur. While the suit was in progress, opposite party No.1 filed application for addition of party on the ground that defendant Joynab Bibi, mentioned in the plaint, is a fictitious person and present opposite party No.1, Joynab Bibi is real person and disputed property was originally belonged to father of opposite party No.1, which was acquired by the government and as affected persons, the heirs of late Noya Mia was given compensation as such, she is necessary party in the suit. Trial Court by a non speaking order and revisional Court by also called reasoned order allowed the application. 
3. Mr. Md. Noor Hossain Chowdhury, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, submits that, registered deed cannot be cancelled by administrative order. Learned Advocate elaborately submits that registered deed has sanctity and if there 100's of frauds be committed in getting the registered deed the proper course open is to file suit for its cancellation not by administrative order. If this type of administrative order be passed then nobodies’ registered deed would be safe. Learned Advocate relied on the case of Jobeda Bewa and others Vs. Md. Abdur Razzaque reported in 26 BLD (AD)-271 wherein it is held that "it is settled principle of law that nothing short of a decree of a competent civil Court can undo a registered document. If such type of cancellation of a registered instrument is allowed to continue, there will be no sanctity of any registered instrument." 
4. Mr. Ataul Gani, learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party, submits that, Joynab Bibi as described in the plaint is fictitious person, and plaintiff by purchase acquired no title from such fictitious Joynab Bibi and as soon as opposite party No.1 came to know of the aforesaid deed, he moved before the authority and authority on proper inquiry cancelled the registered deed as per provision of Clause 29 of Lease Deed. 
5. The facts disclosed in the application for addition of party suggest that opposite party No.1, Joynab bibi is real person and on her initiate everything relating canceling the deed has been done as such, she is necessary and proper party. 
6. We have gone through the papers and impugned orders. It is a fact that plaintiff challenged the Memo relating to cancel the registered deed which was registered on 7.12.1998. It also appears from the papers and from the application filed by opposite party No.1 that she came to know on 5.2.2003 about the registered deed, as such, by this time much water has flows in the river Buriganga. The facts disclosed by Joynab Bibi suggest that she can file a suit challenging the registered deed but the suit which has been file by plaintiff, it is our consider view that facts are not so much important, wherein it is to be decided whether law permits for cancellation of registered deed by administrative order. It may refer that case relating to Begum Khaleda Zia's house where her registered deed was cancelled by administrative order and as we see, said order was affirmed by the High Court Division as well as by the Appellate Division. This decision is the only decision of this subcontinent which was passed, not on law but on some other "better law". As such that judgment as passed is per-inqurium and that decision cannot be applied universally. We are of the view that plaintiff challenge the Memo canceling the registered deed of the plaintiff by administrative order by principal defendant, in such a situation, applicant opposite party No.1 is neither a proper party nor a necessary party. Applicant- can file separate suit if so advise, challenging the registered deed. If she file separate suit immediately, we are of the view that both the suits should be heard simultaneously.
7. We find merit in this rule. 8. In the result, this rule is made absolute with this observation. No costs. 

9. Judgment and order are complained are set aside. 

10. Communicate this order at once. 

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 27 of 1980
lawyer:
Mr. Marfat Ali---For the Appellant. 
Mr. Moazzem Hossain, D.A.G---For the respondent.
parties:
Fazlur Rahman ------ Appellant.
Versus
People's Republic of Bangladesh ------Respondent.
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Abdul Karim, J: This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 31.5.79 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Dinajpur, in O.C. Suit No. 436 of 1977 dismissing the suit for declaration of plaintiff’s tenancy right in the land of schedule A to the plaint. 

2. Plaintiff Fazlur Rahman filed the suit for declaration on his tenancy right under the government in respect of the land measuring 20.41 acres described in schedule A to the plaint with the averment, inter alia. that his father took settlement of the land described in schedule B to the plaint measuring 0.83 acres at a rental of Tk. 1-1-0 on the basis of a chit, Ext. 1 dated 12 Falgoon. 1350 B.S. and that he (plaintiff) got settlement from the ex-land-lords Ranjit Singh Nahar and others of the land described in schedule A to the plaint measuring 20.41 acres at a rental of Tk. 14/0 on the basis of a chit. Ext. 1 (a) dated 15 Chaitra, 1352 B.S. The two jamas were subsequently amalgamated and the plaintiff paid rent to the government on the basis of the amalgamated jama of Tk. 5/1/1. Plaintiff claims to have made the land fit for cultivation by removing bushes at a cost ranging between Tk. 15,000/-and 20.000/- and the P.R.R. and S.A. Khatians were duly prepared in his name. The plaintiff has been in peaceful enjoyment and possession of the land on payment of rent to the government. Curiously the plaintiff received a notice from the Government Tahasildar to appear before him with papers relating to the suit land. Accordingly he appeared before the Tahasildar and showed Government Dakhilas and Khatians but the Tahasildar asked the plaintiff to come again with papers of the sheriata of the ex-landlords. This time the plaintiff did not go to the Tahasildar who reported the matter to the C.O. (Rev). The plaintiff was directed to appear before the C.O. (Rev) with relevant papers. The plaintiff did not go to the C.O. (Rev) and the matter was subsequently reported to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), who asked the plaintiff to appear with necessary papers in respect of the suit property. The plaintiff appeared with all necessary papers before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) who gave the finding that the alleged pattan of the plaintiff from the ex-landlords was concocted and that all his papers relating to the settlement are fabricated and forged. though the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) accepted the pattan of plaintiff's father as genuine, he found over writing the Resister-II and other papers of the Revenue Office with the observation that these were concocted and forged showing false amalgamation of plaintiffs father's pattan with his alleged pattan relating to the land of schedule A. This finding of the A.D.C. (Rev) has cast a cloud upon the title of the plaintiff to the suit land. The plaintiff has, therefore, filed the suit for declaration of his tenancy right under the government in respect of the land of schedule A measuring 20. 41 acres. 

3. Defendant No. 1, People's Republic of Bangladesh and defendant No. 2, A.D.C. (Rev), contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. Their case, in brief, is that an area of 80.86 acres of land including the suit land belonged to Zaminders Ranjit Singh Nahar and others and the said lands were recorded in khatian No. 3 in mouza Nafanagar within P.S. Bochegeni in District Dinajpur. The said lands were sold in auction No. 26.4.63 in Certificate Case No. 22 of 1962-63 and was purchased by the Government, who got possession of the same. It is seated by the defendants that plain-tiffs father had a jama for 0.83 acre (schedule B land) at a rental of Tk.1/1-and the land was recorded in the name of the plaintiffs father in khatian No. 11. Plaintiffs father paid rent up to 1369 B.S. Subsequently in collusion with some employees of the Tahasil Office plaintiff caused overwriting in Karcha Book, changed the page of R.O.R. and Register-11 showing amalgamation of the jama of Tk. 1 /1- of Khatian No. 11 and made an amalgamated jama of Tk. 15/1/- in respect of the said land. The plaintiff has illegally tampered with P.R.R., R.O.R. and Karcha Book and other Registers and papers of the settlement offices and he did so in collusion with the employees of the Revenue Department. The defendants categorically assert that plaintiffs papers in respect of the land of schedule A to the plaint are forged concocted and vogue without creating any right, title and interest in his favour. The matter having been reported to the A.D.C. (Rev), he sent a notice to the plaintiff. Thereafter he perused the plaintiffs papers. examined Register-II and other relevant documents and registers of the Revenue Office and being satisfied about the forgery committed by the plaintiff in respect of the said amalgamated jama, under his order dated 8.9.77 restored plot Nos. 554, 694, 682, 500, 501. 474, 473, 472 and 544 to khatian No. 3 of the landlord by excluding the same from R.S. khatian No. 11 where these were entered through forgery and manipulation and maintained 0.83 in R. S. Khatian No. 11 in the name of the plaintiff. 

4. At the trial court plaintiff examined six witnesses as against one by the defendants. Both sides have filed a number of documents in support of their respective cases. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record and 'examination of all papers filed by both sides came to the finding that the plaintiff failed to prove the settlement of the land of schedule A from the landlord, that P.W.4 Serajul Haque and other witnesses of the plaintiff could not be relied on and that the papers filed by the plaintiff were of recent origin created with an eye to the suit. With this finding the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit.

5. Aggrieved by the judgment and decree the plaintiff has preferred this appeal. Mr. Marfat Ali, learned Advocate for the appellant has taken us through the pleadings the impugned judgment and decree and the evidence on record contending that the plaintiff has proved the document of pattan Ext. 1 (a), which is a chit dated 15 Chaitra. 1352 B.S. granted by the landlords Ran Singh Nahar and others to prove his settlement of the land of schedule A and that this pattani paper. Ext. 1 (a). is supported by dakhilas Ext. 2 and Ext. 2(b). granted by the Tahasildars of the land-lords. Mr. Marfat Ali has contended that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error in failing to hold that the plaintiffs chit and dakhilas are genuine documents in support of his title to the suit property. The learned Advocate for the appellant has further submitted that plaintiffs dakhilas, Ext 2(c) dated 11.3.75 granted by the Government Tahashil and the P.R.R. and S.A. khatian in the name of the plaintiff should have been relied on by the trial court for decreasing the suit for declaration of tenancy right of the plaintiff under the government. 

6. Mr Moazzem Hossain learned Deputy Attorney General has supported the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge as being properly based on evidence and in accordance with law. 

7. It is not disputed that plaintiffs father Mashiruddin took settlement from the ex-Land-lords Ranjit Singh Nahar and others the land of schedule B measuring 0.83 acre at a rental of Tk. 1/1 /- recorded in R.S. khatian No. 11. The dispute centers round the alleged story of pattan by the plaintiff in respect of the land of schedule A measuring 20.41 acres on the basis of a chit. Ext. 1(a). bearing the date 15 Chaitra, 1352 B.S. Plaintiff has examined some witnesses in order to prove the story of settlement of the land of schedule A to the plaint. In his evidence as P.W.1 plaintiff Fazlur Rahman states that his father took pattan of 0.83 acre (schedule B) at a rental of Tk. 1/1/- on the basis of a chit and that he himself got settlement of 20.41 acres (schedule A) at a jama of Tk. 14/- and he has filed two chits said to have been granted by Narendra Chatarjee, Naib of the ex-landlord. Plaintiff himself was present when the said chit, Ext. 1 (a). was granted and he got settlement of the land of schedule A on the basis of this pattan. This witness has also filed 3 dakhilas and claims to have made the land fit for cultivation. P.W. 4 Serajul Haque states that he was a Tahasildar of the Zaminder and he states that Narendra Chatarjee, Nail) of the Zaminder, wrote the chit, dated 12 Falgoon, 1350 B.S. (Ext. l) in respect of 0.83 acre of land in the name of plaintiffs father and that the said Naib also wrote a chit. Ext. 1 (a), in respect of 20.41 acres at a jama of Tk. 14/-. P.W.4 Serajul Haque, wrote dakhila, Ext. 2(a), in respect of 0.83 acre of land in the name of plaintiffs father and also granted dakhila Ext. 2 in respect of 20.41 acres in the name of the plaintiff. P.W.4 further states that the dakhila, Ext. 2(b) in respect of 20.41 acres in the name of the plaintiff is in the handwriting of Bhupati Chowdhury, who was the Zamindar's Taltasildar before him. In cross-examination the defendants challenged that P.W.4 Serajul Haque was in the employment of the Jamindar as a Tahasildar or that Bhupati Chowdhury was ever employed by the Zamindar as a Tahasildar. It was further challenged in the cross-examination of this witness that Narendra Chataijee was employed as Naib. P.W.4 has, in fact, failed to show any paper or document showing that he was the landlord's Tahasildar at any time or that Bhupati or Narendra Chatarjee were ever employed by the landlords as a Tahasildar or Naib. The other witnesses supporting the plaintiffs story of settlement is P.W.5 Kalu Mohammad who claims to have been present at the time of taking of pattan by the plaintiff. In his cross-examination, P.W.5 Kalu Mohammad states that he cannot say the plot number or area of the suit land. He claims that he went to the landlord's Sheresta in the morning by train but he can-not say the time of the train. The learned Deputy Attorney General has challenged the veracity of these two witnesses to supporting plaintiffs story of pattan from the Zamindar. There is no doubt that these two witnesses, P.W.4 and P.W.5. have not been able to prove plaintiffs story of pattan satisfactorily.

8. Mr. Moazzem Hossain, learned Deputy Attorney General, has attacked the disputed chit. Ext. 1 (a) bearing the date 15 Chaitra, 1352 B.S. as a forged paper on the ground that the writings thereon are fresh. An examination with nacket eyes demonstrates the freshness of the writings in spite of an attempt at turning it into an old document and, in fact, the learned Subordinate Judge has found it difficult to believe the genuineness of the so called pattani chit, Ext. 1(a) bearing the date 15 Chaitra, 1352 B.S. Mr. Moazzem Hossain has assailed dakhilas. Ext. 2 and 2(b), as spurious, Dakhila, Ex. 2, for 20.41 acres was granted by P.W.4 Serajul Haque and dakhila. Ext. 2 (b), for 20.41 acres is according to P.W.4, in the handwriting of Bhupati Chowdhury, Tahasildar of ex-land-lord. In cross-examination of P.W.4 it has been challenged that this witness or Bhupati Chowdhury was never employed by the ex-landlords as a Tahasildar and, in fact, no paper has been tiled to show that they had ever been employed by the ex-landlords as Tahasildars. The learned Subordinate Judge has accordingly refused to accept the genuineness of the dakhilas. Ext 2 and Ext. 2(b). 

9. Before the trial court the defendants filed a number of documents. These are Ext. E an order sheet of certificate Case No. 22/62-63, Ext. F certificate of public demand. Exts. G and G(1). notices of the certificate case, Ext. H sale proclamation. Ext I certificate of sale, Ext J order of delivery of possession and other papers in support of the defendant's story about an auction sale of the suit land for default in payment of rent in Certificate Case No 22 of 1962-63. It is the case of the defendants that the auction' sale took place on 26.4.63 followed by delivery of possession in favour of the auction purchaser, namely, the government and subsequent settlement in favor of a number of borga tenants, namely Kafiluddin Abdul Matin and Kudratullah. The sole witness of the defendant, D.W.1 Government Tahasildar Abdul Latif Sarker has spoken about borga settlement to different persons. Unfortunately the exhibits filed on behalf of the defendants before the trial court were not filed before us for consideration and the list of documents shows that the Government pleader received back those documents on 26.7.79 on condition of filing the same, if necessary. Though the appeal was filed on 22.8.79, long after 13 years these exhibited documents, taken back on condition of refiling, have not been filed before this court. The learned Deputy Attorney General has found it to difficult to say as to why these documents have not been filed before this court. The learned Subordinate Judge has rightly observed that a plaintiff does not succeed on the weakness of the case of the defendant but he must succeed on the merit of his own case. 

10. The learned Deputy Attorney General has contended that if the story of plaintiffs pattan had been true, there would have been payment of rent from 1956 to 1975. In fact, no evidence of payment of rent is coining before us during this long span of 18 years in support of plaintiffs story of settlement in respect of the land of schedule A to the plaint. 

11. Ext. 4(a) is certified copy of an order dated 8.9.77 passed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev), Dinajpur, in case No. 71/27 of 1976-77 under rule 23(4) of the Tenancy Rules made under section 152 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950. The present plaintiff was opposite party in this proceeding and he filed his pattani papers including dakhilas alleged to have been granted by the ex-landlords. In his order the A.D.C. (Rev) mentions that the first set of dakhilas showing settlement of 0.83 acres at a rental of Tk.1.06 by the ex-landlord appears to be genuine, but the second set of dakhilas showing settlement of 20.14 acres at a rental of Tk.14/- appears to be forged and produced recently. On examination the A.D.C. (Rev) found that S.A. Khatian No. 11 in respect of 0.83 acre of land was rightly recorded in favour of the opposite party but subsequently through manipulation 20.14 acres of land of different plots were brought into that khatian by increasing the rent to Tk. 15/-. On examination by the A.D.C (Rev). Registrar-II showed signs of manipulation by overwriting. The P.R.R. and Tahasil the copy of S.A. Khatian were examined and it was found that nine plots of khas land were included in Khatian No. 11 with different ink. It was further noted that though the opposite party (present plaintiff) paid rent for the khatian at the rate of Tk. 1.06 up to 1369 B.S. yet after this manipulation rent was again realised from him for the same holding from 1367 B.S. to 1370 B.S. On examination of the Office copy of the S.A. khatian of the C.O. (Rev) it was found that vanishing ink was used to erase those plots from the khas khatian and that handwriting of khatian No. 11 (disputed khatian) was entirely different from the handwriting of khatian Nos. 10 and 12. The A.D.C. (Rev) found Khatian No. 11 in the name of the opposite party (present plaintiff) which contains 0.83 acre at a rental of 11.1.06 but subsequently through fraud khas land measuring 20.14 acres of 9 plots were brought in Khatian No. 11 and accordingly plot Nos. 554, 694. 682. 500, 501, 474, 473, 472 and 554 fraudulently entered into khatian No. 11 were restored to Khatian No. 3 maintaining 0.83 acre of land in the name of the plaintiff in khatian No. 11 under rule 23 (4) the State Acquisition Rule. Under rule 23(4) the Revenue Officer is empowered to direct excision of fraudulent entry from the record of rights after final publication there of after consulting the previous settlement records, preliminary rent-rolls, draft record-of-rights. tahasil copies of records and Register-II. 

12. Ext. 4 is certified copy of an order dated 9.4.79 of the court of a Magistrate, First Class in T.R. Case no. 1269 of 1977 under section 379 of the Penal Code against the plaintiff for cutting of paddy from the suit land. The learned Magistrate acquitted plaintiff Fazlur Rahman of the charge under Section 379 of the Penal Code with the finding of possession in his favour. Mr. Marfat Ali, learned Advocate for the appellant, has submitted that the two chits namely, Ext.1 and 1(a) being similar there is no reason to make discrimination. In other wards he has contended that the trial court having relied on the chit Ext, 1, committed an error in not accepting the other chit, namely, Ext. 1 (a) as being genuine. We find no substance in this contention as we have discussed of the evidence coming before us in respect of the chit, Ext. 1 (a), on merit and also there being no dispute about the settlement of the land of schedule B in the name of plaintiffs 
father. It is clear from the evidence on record that the chit Ext. 1 (a) bearing the date 15 Chaitra, 1352 B.S. and dakhilas, Ext, 2 and 2(b). are forged and fabricated papers. In fact, we find no basis for the alleged story of pattan in respect of the land of schedule A to the plaint. Plaintiff has, however, managed to secure a dakhilas Ext. 2 (c) from the Government Tahasil Office. But this paper as well as the P.R.R. and S.A.
