Khatian in respect of the suit land are of no consequence as those have been secured by the plaintiff in collusion with the employees of the Revenue Department. 

13. Plaintiff has examined a number of witnesses to show his possession in the suit land. The plaintiff as P.W.1 states that after taking settlement he invested a lot of money running between Tk. 15,000/- to 20,000/- for removing bushes and making the land fit for cultivation. P.W.2 Haji Salah Mohammad supporting plaintiffs possession for 30 years in his relation. P.W.3 Kashiruddin has supported plaintiffs possession in the suit land for a period of 30/35 years. In cross-examination he can neither say about the area of the suit plots nor about their location from nearby the river. P.W.5 Kalu Mohammad speaks about plaintiffs possession for 30/35 years without any knowledge about the plot Nos. or area of the suit land. The other witness supporting the plaintiffs possession is P.W.6 Sakibuddin. He says that the plaintiff has been in possession for a long time. In cross-examination he states that there is a case against him in the Court of A.D.C. in respect of Government land and that an eviction case is pending against him. Evidently this witness is not a disinterested witness. In fact, no impartial or reliable evidence has come to support plaintiffs possession. P.W. 1 examined on behalf of the Government is a Tahasildar of Local Tahasil Office and he states that he served a notice upon the plaintiff to produce necessary papers, but the plaintiff did not appear before him. Thereafter he reported the matter to C.O. (Rev) and from there the matter was reported to A.D.C. (Rev) and, after getting notice, the plaintiff produced his papers. The A.D.C. examined all relevant papers and dakhilas and passed an order dated 8.9.77 restoring plot Nos. 554, 694, 682, 500, 501, 474, 473, 472 and 544 to khatian No. 3 of the landlord by excluding the same from R. S. Khatian No. 11 where these were entered through forgery and manipulation and maintaining 0.83 acre in R.S. khatian No. 11 in the name of the plaintiff. D.W. 1 states about auction-sale of the suit property on 26.4.63 in Certificate Case No. 22 of 1962-63. This witness states that the Government took delivery of possession and thereafter the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) under his order dated 8.9.77 set aside the fraudulent pattan of the plaintiff in respect of the land of schedule A and the Government took delivery of possession on 2.12.77 by beat of drum in the locality. Thereafter the Government gave settlement to different persons including Kafiluddin, Abdul Matin and Kudratullah. The learned Advocate for the appellant has relied on the judgment passed in the criminal case being T.R. Case No. 1269 of 1977 under section 379 of Penal Code in support of plaintiffs possession in the suit land. The learned Deputy Attorney General has, on the other hand, sub-mitted that this being a government khas land limitation of 60 years will apply to this case and the story of plaintiffs pattan cannot stretch beyond 1352 B.S. We find enough substance in the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General. 

14. The learned Subordinate Judge has found substance in the story of pattan setup by the plaintiff and has rightly found the papers submitted by the plaintiff including the chit Ext. 1(a) bearing the date 15th Chaitra, 1352 B.S. and the dakhilas as fabricated papers created with an eye to litigation in order to create title in the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge accordingly dismissed the suit. We find no ground to interfere with the judgment and decree passed by him and the appeal should be dismissed.

In the result, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is affirmed. 

Md. Mozammel Haque. J: I agree. 

End.

full_judgment:
MD. MOZAMMEL HOQUE, J:  This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff-appellants is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 24. 11. 87 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 21 of 1984 dismissing the suit. 

2. The appellants being plaintiffs instituted the aforesaid suit for a declaration of title and also for a declaration that the suit property cannot be treated as vested and non-resident property (enemy property) alleging, inter-alia, that the Jagat Chandra Karmaker was the C. S. recorded owner of the suit property. After his death his son Gopal Karmaker inherited the said property. This Gopal Karmaker transferred the suit property to one Harendra Lal Saha and Jagannath Saha 71 2 decimals each. After the death of Harendra his property was inherited by his two sons Chandi Gopal Saha and Ashutosh Saha. Jagannath Saha had purchased 7/ 2 decimals of land from Gopal Karmaker. Thereafter, one Parveen Akhter purchased the suit land by the registered deeds of sale from Chandi Gopal Saha and Ashutosh Saha and also from Jagannath Saha. After purchase, this Parveen Akhtar mutated her name in S. A records of right and in Govt. Tahsil Office and paid rents to the Government. From this Parveen Akhtar the present plaintiff-appellants had purchased the suit property by three deeds of sale each measuring 5 decimals. After purchase they also mutated their names in Government Tahsil office and also recorded their names in S. A. khatian.. While the plaintiffs were possessing the suit land, they came to know on 15. 1. 84 that the property in question was declared as vested and non-resident property. This fact has created some cloud over the right title of the plaintiffs and as a result the plaintiffs were compelled to file the present suit. 

3. Defendant No. 2, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) appeared and filed a written statement contending, inter-alia, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form as the plaintiffs had no right and title over the same It is the case of the defendants No. 2 that the owners of this land left this country for India long ago and according to Defence of Pakistan Rules this property was treated as enemy property, no vested and nonresident property in pursuance of V. P. Case No. 45 of 1977. In that V. P. Case No. 45 of 1977 the suit property was leased out to the Bishu Mia and Abdul Jabbar. The plaintiffs had forged and fabricated documents and thereby they are illegally claiming the suit property. 

On the aforesaid pleadings of the parties the following issues were framed by the learned Subordinate Judge: I) Is the suit maintainable in its present form? 

2) Whether the plaintiffs hare got any right and title over the suit proper' y; and 

3) Whether the plaintiff entitled to have a decree in pursuance of their prayer as made in the plaint.

 All the issues were taken up together and heard by the learned Subordinate Judge. In this case the plaintiffs examined as many as seven witnesses and the defendant examined one witness only. The plaintiffs filed papers and documentsl6 in number which have been made exhibits No. 1 to 4. The defendant also filed two copies of the lease deed vide Exts. A and A (1), After hearing the parties and perusing the materials evidence on record the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved by the Judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge, the plaintiffs preferred this First Appeal. 

4. Amjad Hossain is P. W. I. He is also plaintiff No 1. He stated in his deposition that the total area is 15 decimals of land in plot No. 515. He in fact, re-iterated the plaint case stating that the original owner of the suit property was Jagat Chandra Karmaker and his name appeared in the Khatian Jagat Chandra Karmaicer died leavin behind one son, namely, Oval Karmaker. This Copal Karmaker was owning and possessing the suit land and he sold 7/-2 decimals of land to Harendra Saha and 7/2 decimals of land to Jagannath Saha. In this way Harendra Lal and Jagannath became the owners of the suit property and their names had been recorded in the S. A Khatian. Harendra Lal died leaving behind two sons, namely, Chandi Gopal Saha and Ashutosh Saha. These Chandi Gopal Saha and Ashutosh Saha sold their 7 /2 decimals of land to Parveen Akhtar on 29. 7. 81 by a registered sale deed. Jagannath Saha also sold his 7 /2 decimals of land to this Parveen Akhter by a registered sale deed on 7. 8. 81. After purchasing the suit land this Parveen Akhtar recorded her name in the record of rights and mutated her name in the Tahsil Office and while she was owning and possessing the suit land, she sold it to the present plaintiff-appellants by three registered sale deeds dated 2. 1. 85. After purchasing the suit property the plaintiffs have separately mutated their names in the record of rights and also in the Tahsil Office. He further stated that the suit land in question is not an enemy property in view of the facts that this Parveen Akhtar purchased the property from the S. A. recorded owners of the suit property who sold it to the plaintiffs in 1985. He further stated that an inquiry was made in the office of the S.D.O who gave a clearance to the effect that it was not an enemy property. The plaintiff Nos. 2 and 3 have been residing in a pucca house on the suit property with their family members. He denied the suggestion that this Harendra Lal Saha another owner long ago left this country for India and this suit property had been treated as enemy property. 

5. One Md. Fafiquddin is P. W.2. He is a deed writer in the Sub-registrar Office at Savar. He simply proved the three deeds by which the plaintiffs purchased the suit property from Parveen Akhtar. 
6. One Raba Kumar Saha was examined as P. W. 3. He stated that he is a resident of Sava Madhya Para and the suit property was situated at about 100 cubits away from his house. He knew the plaintiffs of the suit. He stated that in the suit, property the plaintiffs were residing and before them Parveen Akhtar lived there. He stated that neither Bishu Miah nor Abdul Jabbar live in the suit property. He knew Chandi Gopal, Ashutosh and Jagannath. About 4/5 years back they left the suit property and Parveen Akhtar left the house about 2/3 years before. He denied the suggestion that before 1965 these Chandi Gopal Saha and. Ashutosh Saha left this country for India. 

7. P. W. 4 is one Md. Jasimuddin who stateel that he knew the plaintiffs and the suit property. Before it was purchased by the plaintiffs one Parveen Akhtar was the owner of the suit property. This Parveen Akhtar by three registered sale deeds transferred the suit property to the plaintiffs. He is an attesting witness in all the three deeds. He proved the documents as well as passing of the consideration money to Parveen Akhtar from the plaintiffs. He stated that this Parveen Akhtar purchased it from Chandi Gopa. Saha, Ashutosh Saha and Jagannath Saha denied the suggestion that these Harendra Nath and Asutosh, the owners of the house left this country for India during liberation war. He stated that this property in question is not an enemy property. 

8. P.W. 5 is Ashutosh Saha, son of Harendra Kumar Saha. He stated that he and his brother got half of the suit property by way of inheritance. His other brother is Chandi Gopal Saha. He stated that in the middle of 1981 they sold 7 a decimals of land to Parveen Akhtar by registered sale deed. Both these Ashutosh and his brother Chandi Gopal Saha executed the deed of sale art handed over possession of the suit property to Parveen Akhtar. He denied the suggestion that Harendranath and Jagannath left this country foi India before 1965 India Pakistan war and that they never came back to this country. He stated that according to law this property cannot be treated as an enemy property They have every legal right to transfer the suit property. 

9. PAV 6, Chandi Gopal Saha, son of late Harendra Kumar Saha. He stated that they both the two brothers, got 7 /2 decimals of land by way of inheritance and they sold to Parveen Akhtar by registered sale deed which was executed by both the brothers. They also handed over possession of the portion of the suit property to Parveen Akhtar. In cross-examination he -denied that the owners of the suit property left this country for India long ago and that the suit property is an enemy property. He further denied the suggestion that at the relevant time they had no right and title over the property to sell the same to others.

10. P. W. 7 is one Kanai Lal Paul. He is an attesting witness of the deed of sale. He proved the execution and registration of the three sale deeds in favour of the plaintiffs. 

11. The defendant No. 2 examined one witness named Serajul Karim. This D. W. 1 stated that he is an .Assistant in the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Dhaka. He further stated that one Harendra Lal Saha and hers were the owners of this suit property an all left this country in the year 1965 and Government treated this suit property as vested and nonresident property by Govt. V. P Case No. 45 of 1977. In 1977 one Shafiqul Islam and tWo others were given lease of this property. In 1987 also Bishu Miah and Abdul Jabbar were given lease of the suit property. After taking lease the lessees arc in possession. He stated that he did not know anything about this sale and purchase of the suit property. In cross-examination he stated that on 18. 10. 84 he joined the present post. He could not say the name of mouja, the area of the land and the Khatian number. He did not even see the suit property. He further stated that as the owners of the suit property left for India, the property was treated as vested and non-resident property. But in support of the statement he did not file any Government record before the Court. 

12. The plaintiffs in support of their claim filed several documents which have been marked as exhibits. Ext.-1 is the copy of C. S. Parcha which was published in the name of Jagat Chandra Karmaker which shows that plot No. 515 is homestead. Ext.-1 (A) is S. A. Parcha of Mouja Savar, District Dhaka which shows that Harcndra Lal Saha and Jagannath Saha, sons of Hira Lal Saha, were the owners of the suit property. Ext.-1 (B) is S. A. Mutation Parcha prepared in the name of Md. Amjad Hossain Molla. Ext.-1 (EC) is S. A Mutation Parcha prepared in the name of Mrs. Parveen Akhtar in respect of the suit property. Ext. 1 (D) is S. A Mutation Parcha prepared in the name of Mohammad Ali, one of the plaintiffs, Ext-1(E) is S. A. Mutation Parcha prepared in the name of Md. Shamsul Alam who is also a plaintiff in the suit Ext- 1 (F) is the copy of the duplicate carbon receipt book issued in the name of Md. Amjad Hossain Molla. Ext.-1 (G) is a rent receipt issued in favour of Md. Amjad Hossain Molla. 

Ext-2 is the registered sale deed executed by Jagannath Saha in favour of Parveen Akhtar in respect of 7 /2 decimals of land. Ext-2 (A) is the registered sale deed executed by Chandi Gopal Saha and Ashutosh Saha, sons of late Herendra Lal Saha, in favour of Parveen Akhtar with regard to 7 /2 decimals of land Ext. 2(B), 2 (C) and 2 (D) are the three separate registered sale deeds executed by Mrs. Parveen Akhtar in favour of the present plaintiff-appellants. Ext.-3 is the duplicate carbon receipt book issued in favour of Parveen Akhtar. Ext.-3 (A') is the rent receipt given to Mrs. Parveen Akhtar, Ext. 3 (B) and 3(C) are also rent receipts issued in favour of Parveen Akhtar, Ext.-4 is a copy of the letter issued from the office of the S. D. O Dhaka Sadar, showing that.the suit property had not been enlisted as vested and non-resident property. Ext-A is a document filed on behalf of the defendant No, 2 who contested the suit. This is a copy of the lease order treating the suit property as enemy property issued in favour of one Shafiqul Islam Bhuiyan and others. It is dated 8.2. 77 Ext- A CI) is another letter showing lease of the suit property in favour of Bishu Miah and Abdul jabbar vide vested and Non-Resident property case No. 45 of 1977. It is dated 11. 8. 78. These are more or less the oral as well as documentary evidence filed on behalf of the parks. 

13.1n the back ground of the aforesaid evidence the learned Advocate Mr. Abu Baker, appearing for the plaintiff-appellants submits that the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are absolutely illegal in view of the fact that the same are contrary to the evidence on record. He submits that the learned Subordinate. Judge failed to consider the material evidence on record properly and on presumption and hypothesis he treated the suit property as vested and non-resident property, although the defendant failed to produce any document whatsoever claiming the same as vested property. He further submits that in the year 1977 no property of this country can be treated as vested and non-resident property in view of the fact that the law on vested and non-resident property was repealed in the year 1976 vide Ordinance No-92 of 1976. 

14. We have perused the Judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge. From the Judgment it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge had disbelieved the story of transfer of the suit property from Copal Karmaker to Harendra Lal Saha and. Jagannath Saha holding that the plaintiffs failed to produce any document to show the transfer in between Gopal Karmaker and Harendra Lal Saha and others. 

15. The suit property measuring 15 decimals of land is covered by plot No. 515. From the plaint it appears that there was averment to the effect that original C. S. recorded owner was Jagat Chandra Karmaker and after his death it was inherited by his only son Gopal Chandra Karmaker P.W . 1 in his evidence clearly stated that original C. S. recorded owner was Jagat Chandra Karmaker and after his death it was inherited by his son Gopal Chandra Karmaker who sold the suit property to Harendra Lal Saha and two others. In this connection we may refer to the deposition of D.W.1 as well as the written statement filed on behalf of the defendant No.2. In the written statement the defendant No. 2 clearly stated that the suit holding previously belonged to Harendra Lal Saha and others who left this country for India and thereby the suit property became the enemy property, now vested and non-resident property. D. w. 1 stated that one Harendra Math Saha and others were the owners of the suit property. We will see later on whether they had gone to India or lived in this court. But the fact remains that in the written statement this defendant No. 2 himself admitted that the suit property belonged to Harendra Lal Saha and others which clearly shows that the Harendra Lal Saha and others became owners of the suit property and this is supported by the evidence of the P. W. I as well Evidence of D. W. I show that Harendra Lal Saha and others were the owners of the suit property. Above facts show that Harendra Lal Saha and others got right and vide over the suit property from the heirs of Jagat Chandra Karmakar. 

16, Further, it appears that after purchase this Harendra Lai Saha and Jagannath Saha recorded their names in the S. A. record of rights. Further, P. W. 5 Ashutosh Saha who is the son of late Harendra Kumar Saha stated that he and his brother Chandi Gopal Saha got the suit property by inheritance. P. W. 6 is Chandi Gopal Saha. He also stated that they two brothers inherited 7 /2 decimals of land from their father and they sold the same to Parveen Akhtar. It further appears from the evidence of D. W.1 that Harendra Lal Saha and others were the owners of the suit property. This is a clear admission by the defendant No. 2 that the suit property belonged to Harendra Lal Saha and two others which in fact, supports the case made out by the plaintiffs in the plaint as well as in his evidence. If we consider the averments made in the plaint and the evidence of P.W.1 together with the written statements of defendant No. 2 and the evidence of D. W. 1 it clearly appears to us that Harendra Lal Saha and others became the owners of the suit property and they possessed the same and sold the same to Mrs. Parveen Akhtar by registered sale deeds in 1981. 

17. Records show that several copies of C. S and S. A Khatians along with several Rent receipts were submitted by the plaintiffs and the same were marked as exhibits. These exhibits were not properly considered by the Court below. In the case of Erfan All Vs. Joynal Abedin Mia, 35 D. L. R. (AD) 216, it was held by our Appellate Division that the Rent receipts are important evidence of possession and the same may be used as collateral evidence of title. Relying upon the above principle settled by the Appellate Division in the above case we hold that the Rent receipts together with the continuous records of right vide exhibits 1 series may be treated as collateral evidence of title in favour of the plaintiffs. Nov, if we consider the oral as well as documentary evidence as stated above, we find that this Harendra Lal Saha and other acquired right and title over the suit property. The documents by which the heirs Harendra Lal and Jagannath transferred the suit land to Parveen Akhtar and the registered document by which Parveen Akhtar transferred the suit land to the present plaintiffs are not disputed at all. So it is held that the learned Subordinate Judge failed to consider the material evidence on record as stated above and he has arrived at a wrong finding stating that there is no evidence to show that Gopal Karmaker transferred the land to Harendra Lal Saha and others. It appears from the Judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge that he did not, in fact, disbelieve the documents as produced by the plaintiffs in the suit. But only because there was absence of any evidence regarding transfer of the suit property from Gopal Karmaker to Harendra Lal Saha and others, he found that in the suit property the plaintiffs did not acquire any right and title. The finding is absolutely incorrect and contrary to the evidence on record and as such it cannot be sustained.

18. The learned Subordinate Judge further made certain statements in his Judgment regarding suit property which is claimed to be vested and non-resident property. He stated that by Ext. A and A (1) this suit property was treated as vested and non-resident property and it was stated by the defendant in the written statement that the owners of the suit property, namely, Harendra Lal Saha and others left this country long ago. In this connection we may refer to the deposition of P.W. 5 Ashutosh Saha. This Ashutosh Saha is the son of late Harendra Lal Saha who according to the defendant, was the owner of the suit property. P.W. 6 Chandi Gopal Saha is also son of late Harendra Lal Saha. Both these brothers sold their 7 /2 decimals of land to Mrs. Parveen Akhtar as they inherited the same from their father. From these two evidences together with the Exts.-2 and 2 (A) it appears that the heirs of Harendra Lal Saha and Jagannath Saha have been living in this country and they sold their property vide these two exhibits to this Parveen Akhtar on 29. 7. 81 and 7. 8. 81. Since the heirs of Harendra Lai Saha and Jagannath Saha were living in this country and they executed and registered two deeds of sale in the year 1981, the suit property by no stretch of imagination, can be treated as any enemy property, namely, vested and non-resident property. 

19. Further it appears from the written statements as well as from the documents of the defendant No. 2, namely, Ext’s- A and A (1) that in the pursuance of V. P. Case No, 45 of 1977 this property was treated as vested and non-resident property and the same was leased out with one Shafiqul Islam Bhuiyan and others. These two exhibits show granting of leases dated 8. 2. 87 and dated 11. 8. 78. In this connection we may refer to the Ordinance No. 92 of 1976 by which this Vested and Non-resident Property Act was totally repealed and even there is no saving clause. If in the year 1976 the Vested and Non-resident Property Act was repealed, how a property could be treated as vested and non-resident property in the year 1977? Though there was no saving clause in the Ordinance, yet the provision of General Clauses Act will be applicable. Section 6 of the General Clauses Act provides that if any proceeding was started or any action was taken in a repealed law, even after repeal of the law the proceedings will continue under the repealed law as if law is not repealed. In this case the defendant No. 2 appeared before the learned Subordinate Judge and also appeared before this Court. But unfortunately, the defendant No. 2 failed to produce any papers whatsoever before the Court showing that before 1976 this property was treated as enemy property or enlisted as enemy property or any inquiry proceeding was started as to whether this Property was enemy property or not. In fact, no scrap of paper nor any evidence whatsoever was produced before this Court in support of the contention. Only in the written statement and in the deposition of D. W. 1 it is stated that the owners of the property left this country for India long ago and as such it was treated as vested and non-resident property. But in support of such averment no documentary evidence could be produced before the court showing that before repealing of Vested and Non- resident Property Act in 1976, any proceeding was started in respect of this property. In this view of the matter, the claim of the defendant No. 2 that the suit property was treated as vested and non-resident property cannot be at all sustained. 

20. We have heard the learned Advocates, perused the material evidence on record as well as the Judgment of the Trial Court. The findings arrived by the learned Trial Court are contrary to the evidence on record and as such the same cannot be sustained. As a result we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge has illegally passed the judgment dismissing the suit. So, the Judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are liable to be set aside. 

21. In the result, this appeal is allowed without any order as to costs and the Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are hereby set-aside and the suit of the plaintiffs is hereby decreed. 

22. Send down the L. C records immediately to the Trial Court. 

End.

full_judgment:
Muhammad Abdul Mannan, J : This Civil revision is directed against the judgment and decree dated 19.3.1990 passed by the District Judge, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 119 of 1987 affirming those dated 24.12.1986 by the subordinate Judge, Chandpur in Title suit. No. 136 of 1982 decreeing the suit. 

2. The predecessor-in-interest of opposite party No. 1 Kali Das Singha instituted Title Suit No. 136 of 1982 against the present petitioner and others for declaration of his title in respect of 'Kha' schedule property and recovery of Khas possession in respect of 'G' schedule property during the pendency of the suit kali Das Singha died and the opposite party No. 1 Dipak Boron Singha was substituted as his heir. 

3. There is a long genealogy of possession and ownership of the suit land which has been discussed at length by the learned trial court and the lower appellate court, and so this court need not repeat the same. The only point before me is that the plaintiff is a owner of 2/3rd share which was owned by Arun and Barun in equal shares, who left the country for India in 1947. Since then the plaintiff is in possession on payment of rent of the entire suit land. Now whether the joint property without partition left by owner of 2/3rd share in the property should be declared as enemy property by virtue of Enemy property law and vested in the Govt. Who allegedly leased out the same to others without gazette Notification and any notice to the plaintiff. 

4. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that be along with two sons of Nagendra Nath Singha namely Arun Chandra Singha and Barun Chandra Singha leaving in a joint family and the plaintiff having 1/3rd share in the paternal property and the rest 2/3 share belonged to Arun Chandra Singha and Barun Chandra Singha who left the country in 1947 leaving the joint property in possession of Taini Kumar Singha and he enjoyed the property on payment of rent to the Government, The plaintiff was possessing the entire undivided property of the Hindu Joint family together with 1/3rd share as his own and adversely 2/3rd share of the plaintiff acquired possessor title in the suit land in plot No. 446 comprising 7.25 acres of the homestead land of the plaintiff, while plot No. 401 measuring 8.89 acres of their paternal pond and dighi. The defendants created some fraudulent deeds of gift and gifted the land to Khajuria High school without any lawful basis. 

5. The defendant Nos. 3.4.13/9 and 43 field separate written statements but only the defendant Nos. 3/4 and 43 contested the suit. The defendants could not prove their case by adducing the evidence before the trial Court and also the suit was decreed against them but later on the defendant nos. 3,4 filed Title suit No. 32 of 1987 against the judgment and decree but subsequently he compromised with the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 by filing a solenama on 16.7.1987. Accordingly the impugned judgment and decree was passed in Title Appeal No. 32/87. 

6. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the Government claimed the 2/3rd share of the joint family property as enemy property which was left by Arun Kumar Singha and Barun Singha who left the country for India in 1947'and the Government took up the property as such so there is no illegality in declaring the property as vested property vide Enemy property case No. 157/68-69. V.P. Case No. 2/68-69 and V.P. Case No. 147/68-69 and the same was leased out to different persons. He submits that the courts below failed to consider the papers and document relating to the suit property and so the decree should be set aside. 

7. The learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that all the relevant facts and the genealogy of the inheritance and the ultimate co-sharers of the property was considered by the courts below and the plaintiff opposite party predecessor of opposite party No. 1 and Arun Kumar Singha and Barun Kumar Singha who left the county who upon the plaintiff opposite party possessed and enjoyed the same on payment of rent. He submits that there being no partition of the property of the family and the property being the homestead land and the pond and (light possessed jointly the same cannot be taken without partition and the declaration of the same as enemy property' was illegal. He also submits that no notice was give to the plaintiff. There is no Gazette Notification and the Government illegally leased out the undivided share of the property to the different defendants. He submits that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is in possession of the suit land by virtue of his inheritance and also of adverse possession and more over as the property is a joint property and it was not partitioned the possession was intact in the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. 

8. Heard the learned Advocate perused the petition and the judgment of the lower appellate court and the points raised before me by the defendants and the plaintiff were settled by concurrent finding of facts. Therefore, the same cannot be raised before this court for decision' in revision. It has been settled that 1/3rd share of the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 and 2/3rd share of co-sharers on left the country and their property was possessed and enjoyed by the plaintiff opposite party as the property was joint having no partition. In the circumstance the Government by declaring the property as Enemy property or vested property could not take possession of the same and unless the share of the parties is determined by partition suit the undivided property cannot be declared as Enemy property. It is holding the reported case in one B.C.R. 1981 AD, 109 that appellant in undisputed possession of the entire property and claimed Title the custodian of enemy property cannot take over possession without effecting partition and the order of lease is illegal, because the undivided share in a joint family property cannot be possessed by the Government. In this case the nature and character of the suit property is homestead land, pond and Dighi of the family and therefore, it is not so easy to effect partition and lease out to others. The property is a Hindu joint family property and the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 is living in the house and so the same cannot be leased out to any other persons of other religion. The trial Court as well as the lower appellate court found that the plaintiff opposite party has got adverse possession of the property left by his co-sharer and this being the concurrent findings of fact the same cannot be questioned before this court. 

9. In view of the contention raised by the learned Advocate and my discussion made above I am of the view that there is nothing to interfere in the concurrent judgment and decree passed by lower appellate court. 

10. In the result I discharge the Rule without any order as to costs and uphold the judgment and decree passed by the courts below. Let the record be send down atonce. 

11. The connected Civil Rule No. 249 (R)/92 1597(R)92 and 1981(R)/92 are accordingly disposed of with the discharge of the Rule in revision and this judgment covers them. 

End.

caseno: Writ Petition No. 5029 of 2000
lawyer:
Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Hoq with Mr. A. F. Hasan Arif ------ for the petitioner

Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud with Ms. Mubma Asif Rahman ------ for the respondents 1 & 3
parties:
Islamic Trade & Commerce Ltd. ------ Petitioner
-Versus-
Bangladesh Bank and others ------ respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. Abu Sayeed Ahammed, J: This petitioner in this case is Islamic Trade & Commerce Limited (hereinafter he called 'ITCL'). The Rule Nisi has been issued calling upon the respondents, the Bangladesh Bank and others to show cause as to why the memo No. BRP 1760/29(2)/2000-3602 dated 22.11.2000 (Annexure-G) issued by the respondent No. 1 (Bangladesh Bank) stopping the operations and transactions of the petitioner company purportedly under Section-52(1) of the. Banking Companies Act, 1991 for; Alleged violation of Section-31(1) of the said Act on the plea that the activities of the petitioner company come within the purview of Banking business, as defined in Section-5IP) of the said  Ac and the proceeding taken under the memo No. BRP /760/29(2)/2000-3045 dated 21.9.2000 (Annexure-D) by the respondent No. 3 General Manager (Banking regulation and policy Division Bangladesh Bank) shall not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

	2. The petitioner ITCL is said to be a private limited trading company incorporated in Bangladesh registered with the Registrar of the Joint Stock Companies on 20.1.1997 and since then it is running different kinds of business having a memorandum of Articles of Association along with the certificate of incorporation (Annexure-A). The petitioner ITCL says that it is a pure and simple business company and not a Banking Company as is alleged by the Bangladesh Bank in the impugned notifications and the ITCL never indulges in any Banking activity or business, as stated in para 3 of the writ petition and it rum its business according to the Islamic method. According to the Bangladesh Bank, the respondent No. 1, the petitioner is not a simple business company it is rather a banking company and it does carry on with banking business and activities without the permission of the Bangladesh Bank as required under Section-31(1) of the Banking Companies Act. 1991 and without taking a license, there upon as required under Section-31(1)(2)(3) of that act which read as follows :- 

	"31(1)- License of banking companies :- (1) Except as hereinafter provided, no Banking company shall early on banking business in Bangladesh without banking license issued in that behalf by the Bangladesh Bank.

	(2) While issuing a license under subsection-(1) the Bangladesh Bank may impose any condition as it may think tit and proper. 

	(3) Every banking company already existing n:t the commencement of this act prior to the expiry of six months from such commencement and every other banking company prior to commencing banking business in Bangladesh shall apply in -writing to the Bangladesh Bank for a license under this section."

	Since according to the Bangladesh Bank without fulfilling the legal requirement of Section-31(1) of the Banking Companies Act, the petitioner is carrying on its Banking Business and transaction. the Bangladesh Bank exercising its power and authority under Section-51 of the Banking Companies Act, 1991 has informed the petitioner by its letter dated 17.9.2000 that one Mesba-Ul-Hoq, a Deputy Director of Bangladesh Bank was appointed to seize some relevant papers and documents of the petitioner as mentioned in that letter and on the following day (on 18.9.2000) said Deputy Director seized these papers and documents and kept them in the Zimma of one Biplab Kumar Sadhu. D.G.M. (Accounts) of the petitioner's company as per the seizer list and Zimma Nama. Thereafter, the respondent No. 1 by a notice dated 21.9.2000 (Annexure-D) asked the petitioner to show cause as to legal why action should not be taken against the petitioner as provided under Section-52 of the Banking Companies Act for violation of Section-31(1) of the said Act as the Transactions were carried on by the petitioner without the permission of Bangladesh Bank. The petitioner gave a reply on 2799.2000 through its Lawyer Mr. Md. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury. On 26.9.2000 and on 28.9.2000 the respondent No. 6 MC Bank dishonored two cheques of the petitioner for considerable amount and so also the National Bank and Uttara Bank and as both the petitioner ITCL has been constrained to file this present writ petition and obtained the Rule.

	3. The case of the petitioner in a nut shell is that it is a business company and under going simple business on dividend and profit basis and it receives money from different persons and invest the same Or different products as detailed in paragraph 3 of the writ petition which are of several and various in kinds and nature and it never indulges in any banking business and as such the impugned notice the proceedings and the action taken against the petitioner have curtained the fundamental and constitutional right of the petitioner. The petitioner also alleged that natural justice has been denied to the petitioner, alleging that the inquiry was held behind the back of the petitioner. 

	4. On the allegations that ITCL in disguise of trading in Islamic method, was carrying on banking business like other banks and is under going activities of similar nature and kind like other Banks, and therefore, under Section-52(1) of the Banking Companies Act, legally the Bangladesh Bank took up the matter for enquiry and necessary action and on 9.7.2000 the Bangladesh Bank ordered an investigation upon the affairs of ITCL and in course of investigation which was done by a competent Investigating Officer of Bangladesh Bank, the real picture of the activates of ITCL came out, inter alia, as to receiving deposits from the public and also payment of interests, On demand and by order like other banks to its customers. 

	5. Bangladesh Bank also has stated in the affidavit in opposition that it collected legal and correct. materials from different customers and avenues of the ITCL and being satisfied that the ITCL was going on with the banking business in violation of the provision of Section-31(1) of the said Act which Bangladesh Bank could find from the documents seized by its Investigating Officer from the different officer of the ITCL and then the Bangladesh Bank by a letter dated 21.9.2000 asked the ITCL to show cause as to why it should not be declared under Section-52(1) of the Banking Companies Act it is a Banking company has been illegally carrying on the banking business in violation of the Section-3 I (I) of the said Act. ITCL replied to the aforesaid show cause notice on 27.9.2000 stating inter alia that their business was not illegal and it was not banking business, but at the same time in the same written reply the ITCL admitted the transactions it has made with its customers who can be said depositors. 

	6. The Bangladesh Bank upon considering the reply of ITCL found the same as unsatisfactory and not correct and thereafter formed an opinion that the ITCL was carrying on banking business by receiving the deposits from the public and paying the interest on their deposits at the proportionate rate in observance of other formalities like other Banks in their so called business including issuance of pass books and keeping accounts of the business, maintaining ledger and account books etc. 

	7. Mr. Rafique-Ul-Hoq, the learned Counsel along with Mr. A.F. Hasan Arif, appearing for the petitioner ITCL submits that ITCL is never a banking company and it is a business company and its activities do not bring the same within the purview of Banking business, and the papers and documents such as passbooks etc are kept for the purpose of correct accounting only of the deposits made by it's customers and further he submits that the ITCL although pays some amount of money upon the deposits as profits and benefits but it is not interest in any way, it is rather, part of the financial profits made by the ITCL, by investing the deposits of the customers of the ITCL in the manufacturing fields and purposes.

	8. Another argument has been advanced by Mr. Raliq-111-Hoq for the petitioner ITCL before as against the Bangladesh Bank that the purported materials were collected by the Bangladesh Bank. against the ITCL behind the bock and without the knowledge of the ITCL and as such the opinion allegedly by formed by the Bangladesh Bank under Section-51 of the said Act cannot be called a legal and correct opinion and as such natural justice also has been device to the ITCL and as such the whole impugned proceedings according to Mr. Hoq against the petitioner is illegal and ultravires of the Constitution and it has infringed the fundamental right of the petitioner. 

	9. The materials collected by the Bangladesh Bank are all based on documentary evidence which have been annexed to this writ petition and these are the documents of ITCL itself and sonic others have produced by the respondents to it can be said that the opinion has been formed on admitted documents of the ITCL. 

	10. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Counsel for the respondent Bangladesh Bank submits that the show cause notice which is annexure-'D' to this writ petition arid Annexure-6 to the affidavit in opposition of the respondent No. 1 which has been challenged in this petition was served upon the petitioner to show cause and he further submits that by the method of collecting the materials the petitioner has not been prejudiced in any manner as it has been done upon the investigation which was very much impartial and was made after compliance of the legal formalities of the said relevant law. This submission of Mr. Mahmood bears strong substance in this legal conflict, for the respondent No. 1 Bangladesh Bank. 

	11. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud further submits that other requirements of law also have been complied with before issuing of the impugned name and notice by the Bangladesh Bank which in our view also cannot be divide by the petitioner. We hold that any company which is engaged in the manufacture of goods or carries on any trade or business and which accepts the deposits of money from the public more by for the purpose of financing its business such as manufacturing or trading shall not be deemed or called to transact the business of banking within the meaning of Section-5 of the Banking Companies Act, 1991 but-

	In Section-5(p) of the said Act the 'banking has been defined as follows:- 

	"banning means the accepting for the purpose of lending or investment of deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise, and with-drawable by draft, order or otherwise." 

	The Bengali version of sub-section 'গ' of Section-5 of that Act reads as follows:-

	“ব্যাংক কোম্পানী অর্থ বাংলাদেশ ব্যাংকের কার্যাবলী পরিচালনাকারী কোন কোম্পানী এবং যে কোন নতুন ব্যাংক ও বিশিষ্ট ব্যাংক কোম্পানীর অন্তর্ভুক্ত হইবে।

	ব্যাখ্যাঃ-
	যে কোম্পানী মূলত পণ্য উৎপাদন বা বাণিজ্য পরিচালনা করে এবং শুধুমাত্র উক্ত উৎপাদন বা বাণিজ্যের অর্থ সংস্থানের জন্য জনগণের নিকট হইতে ঢাকার আমানত গ্রহণ করে, সেই কোম্পানী এই দফার অধীন ব্যাংক ব্যবসা করিতেছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে না।”

	Bengali version of sub-section of Section-5 is as follows:- 

	“ব্যাংক ব্যবসা অর্থ কর্জ প্রদান বা বিনিয়োগের উদ্দেশ্যে জনসাধারণের নিকট হইতে টাকার এই রূপ আমানত গ্রহণ করা। যাহা চাহিবামাত্র বা অন্য কোনভাবে পরিশোধযোগ্য এবং চেক, ড্রাফট, আদেশ বা অন্য কোন পদ্ধতিতে প্রত্যাহারযোগ্য।”

	It is further submitted on behalf the Petitioner that the terms and condition of their business is that of Mudaraba and Musharika as defined in Section-5 of the Banking Companies Act, 1991. Mudaraba and Musharika have been defined in four clauses in Section-5 of that Act and those are as follows:- 

(i)	Mudaraba certificate means a certificate issued or the basis of mudaraba: 
(ii)	Mudaraba means such an agreement in terms of which a bank conducted in accordance with the Islami Shariah provides capital for anything and the customer employs his efficiency, efforts, labour and intelligence. 

(iii)	Musharika certificate means a certificate issued on the basis of Musharika, 

(iv)	Musharika means such an agreement under which a portion of capital of anything is provided by a bank conducted in accordance with the Islami Sharias and the other portion is given by the customer and in which profit in distributed in such proportion as mentioned in the agreement and loss is distributed in proportion to the capital." 

	It is also submitted for the petitioner that the activities and transactions of the ITCL do not invite payment of any interest which is prohibited by Islamic Principle and method of business. 

	From our above discussions it is clear that the activities of the ITCL do not come either within the ambit of Mudaraba or Musharik Method of business. 

	12. Section-31 of the Banking Companies Act reads as follows:-

	"31 Licensing of banking companies. (1) save as hereinafter provided, no company shall carry on banking business in Bangladesh unless it holds a license issued in that behalf by the Bangladesh Bank. 

	(2) At the time of issuing license under sub-section-(1), the Bangladesh Bank may impose such conditions as it may think fit to impose. 

	(3) Every banking company in existence on the commencement of the Act before the expiry of six months from such commencement and every other company before commencing banking business in Bangladesh shall apply in writing to the Bangladesh Bank for a license under this section." 

	The allegation of the Bangladesh Bank is that although it is mandatory and compulsory that without license and permission of the Bangladesh Bank no banking business can be carried on but the ITCL are under going banking business in contravention of the said mandatory provision of law. 

	Section-51 of the Banking Companies Act, 1991 reads as follows:-

	"51. power to call for certain information, etc. 

	Wherefore it appears to the Bangladesh Bank that a company or any other person is transacting the business of banking in contravention of Section-31(1) the Bangladesh Bank may-

	(a) direct the company or such other person or any person who is or has, an any time, been dealing, doing business or associate in any manner with the company of such 'other person, to give or furnish to the Bangladesh Bank within the specified period such information, documents or records respiration any business carried on by the company or such other person as may be within its or his knowledge or in or under its or his possession, custody or control: 

	(b) authorise any person to enter and search any premises any seize book accounts or other documents or records respecting any business carried on the company or such other person as may be in or under the possession, custody or control of the company or such other person or a person who is, or has at any time been, dealing, doing business or associated in any manner with the company or of such other person or any officer or employee of the company of such other person of the person dealing, doing business or associated with the company or such other person. 

	(c) inspect on examine any of its books, accounts or other documents to records referred to in clause (b) and question any person, officer or employee. 

	(d) exercise as far as may be applicable to the company or such other person. or any person who is, or has at any time been dealing doing business or associated with it or him as aforesaid. the power conferred on the Bangladesh Bank by Sub-sections-(1). (2), (4) and (5) of Section-14." 

	Section-52 of the said Act provides the power or Bangladesh Bank to make the declaration or order as follows:-

	"52. Power I o make declaration (1) Where the Bangladesh Bank, after making such enquires as it may deem fit. is of opinion that a company or Person referred to in Section-51 is transaction in any manner or from whatsoever the business of banking in contravention of Section-31(1), the Bangladesh Bank may after giving the company or such person an opportunity of showing causes against the proposed action being taken, make a declaration to that effect. 

	(2) The Bangladesh Bank shall publish, or cause to be published a declaration, made under sub-section-(1) in the newspaper and, upon such publication the company or such other person or the Chief executive by whatever name called, officers, employees or agents of the company or such person, or any other persons referred to in sub-section-(1),(2),(3)(4) of Section-54 or Section-55 shall not be allowed to plead ignorance of the making of such declaration. 

	(3) A declaration under sub-section-(1) shall, for the purpose of this part, be conclusive proof of the fact stated the rein.' Section-53 of the said Act reads as follows:-

	"53. Consequences of a declaration under Section-52, A company or other person in respect of which or whom a declaration has been made under Section-52(1) shall, on the publication of such declaration, cease function or to transact business and any transaction with such company or person, or with any person acting or purporting to act for and on behalf of such company or person, on or after the publication of the declaration as aforesaid, shall be void." 

	13. it is also noticed that the law makers were very much careful and aware of the consequence of violation of the provision, which is relevant, as to any banking business without a license or permission from the Bangladesh Bank and for that reason they have enacted Section-109 as penal provision to prohibit Banking business without the license of Bangladesh Bank and to control and stop illegal banking business, which is as under: - 

	"Penalties-(1 ) Whoever deals in banking business without having been licensed to do so or whoever deals in banking business after the license therefore is cancelled, he shall be published with imprisonment not exceeding seven years and shall also to liable to fine." 

	14. Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the learned Counsel on behalf of the respondent Bangladesh Bank has produced some papers of the ITCL before us and specially he draws our attention to the agreements which are annexure-10 series which were effected in between the customers/depositors of the ITCL and the ITCL itself containing the Methods of receiving the money and the money receipts the pass books, depositors ledgers etc. As in (Annexure-10 series) including the application forms of the customers of the ITCL and the rate of interest against which the money is received of the deposited discloses the method of repayment of the deposited money. 

	15. Part of the Contents of one of the deeds of agreements effected between the. ITCL and Khalilur Rahman, who made some deposit (part of Annexure-10) are quoted below which are in Bengali and read as follows:-

চুক্তিপত্র
(বাইরে মুদারাবা ব্যবসা বা স্বনিয়োজিত উদ্যোক্তার মাধ্যমে ব্যবসা পদ্ধতি)
	(পণপ্ৰজাতস্তী বাংলাদেশ সরকার কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত ইসলামিক ট্রেড এন্ড কমার্স লিঃ- এর মেমোরেন্ডাম অব এসোসিয়েশনের ধারা (ঘ) এর ১১, ১৬, ২১ ও ২৪ এবং আটিকেলসৃ…এর ধারা ২৫ ও ৪৫…এর (ক) মোতাবেক)

প্রথম পক্ষ : মুদারিব/ইসলামিক ট্রেড এন্ড কমার্স লিমিটেড
	পক্ষে : জেনারেল ম্যানেজার
	বরণ ভবন, ১৫ কামাল আতাতৃর্ক এ্যাভিনিউ
	গুলশান…২, ঢাকা-১২১২ ৷

দ্বিতীয় পক্ষ : সাহেবে মাল/নাম : মোঃ খলিলুর রহমান
	পিতার নাম : ধৃত লালু মিয়া সরকার
	গ্রাম : দাড়িগাঁও, ডাকঘর : ৰিজয়নগর

	18. Therefore the question of depriving the petitioner from natural justice does not arise at all.

Mr. Rafique-Ul-Hoq, the learned Counsel for the petitioner also refers to L.L.R 1946 KB. p. 221, and Section-44 of the Banking Companies Act and he submits that Section-44 should be read with Section-51(D) of the said act to determine whether ITCL is really doing banking business or not our meticulous study and consideration of those decision and the provision of Section-44 of the Banking Company's Act law, reveal that those are not helpful or applicable to decide the instant legal conflict Mr. Hoq, also cites the decisions in the case reported in 49 DLR. 127 1961 cal, 666. AIR 1961 Mad. p. 8, AIR 1945 FC.P.2. 

	20. In our view those are not applicable in the present case and for the present purpose, as we have already found above that natural justice has been met in this case legally and correctly. 

	21. It is further submitted by Mr. Hoq, that personal hearing was not given to the petitioner as to the allegations and as such, the ITCL has been seriously prejudiced. 

	But it is very much there in the reply of the show cause notice (Annexure-5) that ITCL did not pray for personal hearing or appearance before the Enquiry Committee. So the submission of Mr. Hog does not bear any substance.

	22. Mr.Rafique-U1-Hoq cites the decision in the case of Stafford Vs. Minister of Health reported in L.R. 1946, 1 Kings Bench Division, P. 621. Which case is distinguishable in facts and circumstance with the instant one, So it is not applicable there in this conflict. It is 
found and held that although, it is said that the ITCL, is carrying on business according to Islamic method, but in fact they pay interest against the deposits like other Banks and the manner of business is quite against the Islamic Principle and method although said by ITCL interest is called.

	Riha (সুদ) in Arabic which is totally prohibited by the Islamic principles as it is in the Holy Quoran. 

	In Sura Bakara (Ayat No. 274) it has been said as follows:- 

	Allah has permitted sale and purchase but prohibited interest (Riha) In Bengali it is said:-

	“আল্লাহ ক্রয় বিক্রয়কে হালাল করিয়াছেন কিন্তু হারাম করিয়াছেন সুদকে।”

	Mr. Rais Uddin Ahmed Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 5, National Bank Ltd. has adopted the submission of Mr. Rokanuddin Mahmud, the Counsel for the respondent Nos. 1 to 3. 

	On our very anxious scrutiny of all the documents of the parties and after hearing the Counsel's of both parties at length, we are satisfied and convinced that the ITCL has been carrying on Banking business, whatsoever be its now and the Bangladesh Bank after examining the necessary documents legally, holding the enquiry after observing all the necessary legal formalities formed its legal opinion that ITCL is a Banking Company, based on which it can be called sufficient materials and it has been made on the basis of records of ITCL itself. 

	23. Therefore, for the reasons and discussions made above the rule does not interference and it is dicharged. No order as to costs.

End.
