lawyer: For the Petitioner: Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali. Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. A.K.M. Shahidul Huq. Advocate-on-Record. Respondents: Not Represented.
parties:
Md. Esher Ali Sheikh ------ Petitioner
Versus
Md. Mokarram Ali & others ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Ruhul Amin, J: This petition for leave to appeal by the defendant is against the judgment dated May 15, 2001 of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2088 of 1996 discharging the rule and consequent thereupon has affirmed the judgment and decree dated November 25, 1995 of the Court of Additional District Judge, Kushtia in Title Appeal No. 262 of 1990. The appellate court decreed the suit in full upon reversing the judgment and decree dated November 13, 1990 of the Court of. Subordinate Judge. Kushtia passed in Title Suit No. 35 of 1985 which was tiled seeking specific performance of contract as regard .2631 acre of land. 

2. It is the case of the plaintiff- respondent No. I that 41 decimals of land belonged to Tushtu Pramanik who died leaving wife Sarijan Nessa and his sister by name Sonabi Nessa. Sonabi Nessa transferred her share to Sarijan Nessa by a registered deed of sale on February 3. 1959, that 14 decimals of land out of the total 41 decimals of land were recorded in Plot No. 2650 and the rest 27 decimals were recorded in plot No. 2632, that land measuring .0069 out of 27 decimals of land was acquired by the Kushtia Municipality and the remaining .2631 acre was owned by Sarijan Nessa who entered into an agreement with him to sell the same for a consideration of Tk. 60,000/- and executed an agreement for sale on October 5,1979 upon receiving Tk. 37,000/- out of the total consideration money and that put him into possession of the land so agreed to sell and that on two other subsequent occasions Sarijan Nessa received the balance of the consideration money in presence of witnesses. Sarijan Nessa died 
before executing and registering the kabala in respect of the land she agreed to sell to him. Sarijan Nessa died leaving two sons and that they having had declined to execute and register the kabala, he was constrained to file the suit. 

3. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 i.e. sons' of Sarijan Nessa and the added defendant Nos. 3-10 as well as by defendant No. 11 by filling two separate sets of written statements denying the case of the plaintiffs. It was the case of the defendant Nos. 3-10 that Tushta Pramanik's wife Sarijan Nessa inherited 1/4 of the property left by him and the rest 3/4 was inherited by the son of Tushta Pramanik's cousin brother Janik Pramanik and that Soanbi Nessa died before Tushta Pramanik and as such there was no question of her inheriting the property of Tushta Pramanik. 

4. It was the case of the added defendant No. 11 that Tusta Pramanik died leaving wife Sarijan Nessa and sister Sonabi Nessa as his legal heirs and representatives and that Sarijan Nessa inherited '/4th of the land left by Tushta Pramanik and the rest 3/4th was inherited by his sister sonabi Nessa and that on her death he being the son of Sonabi Nessa has inherited the share of his mother. It is also the case of the defendant No. 11 that his mother and he did not transfer any land by the sale deed dated February 3, 1979 and the said deed is collusive, fraudulent and without consideration. The further case of defendant No. 11 is that he does not know how to read and write, but in the deed of February 3,1959 there are signatures alleged to be his. 
5. The trial court on the evidence on record held the agreement for sale dated October 5. 1979 as genuine but held that the deed of sale dated February 3,1979 was forged and as such Sarijan Nessa could not acquire more that '/4 of the land out of 417decimals and thereupon decreed the suit to the extent of the share of Sarijan Nessa. 

6. As against the judgment and decree of the court of first instance plaintiff went on appeal before the Court of District Judge, Kushtia and the said appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge who upon modification of the judgment and decree of the Court of first instance decreed the suit in respect of entire land as regard to which specific performance of contract was sought. Thereupon defendant No. II moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule, Civil Revision No. 2088 of 1996. The High Court Division discharged the Rule on the finding that kabala dated February 3. 1979 is genuine and that also on consideration of' the evidence on record held that plaintiff is in possession of the land in suit. 

7. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel appearing for the defendant No. 11-petitioner submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract, Government being a necessary party as per Provision of Article 6 of Bangladesh Transfer of Immovable Property (Temporary Provisions) Order, 1972 (P.O. 142 of 1972) and that inspite of raising the question of non-impleading Government as party in suit in the written statement and that government having not been made party in view of the mandatory provision of Article 6 of P.O. 142 of 1972 and consequently suit being bad for defect of party but this very vital aspect was not at all considered by the courts below as well as by the High Court Division and as such the same has caused miscarriage of justice. The learned Counsel further submits as it appears that undisputed fact being that in the agreement for sale, (Ext. 3) plaintiff was not a party but inspite thereof the courts below as well as the High Court Division had decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff which was totally illegal and thus has caused failure of justice. 

8. The second contention, of the two aforesaid contentions of the learned Counsel for the petitioner is that plaintiffs name does not appear in the Binapatra and as such courts below as well as the High Court Division were in error in decreeing the suit. It has been held in the background of the evidence on record and that also in the facts and circumstance of the 
case by the High Court Division that Sarijan Nessa agreed to sell the land to the plaintiff who paid the entire consideration money to her. The learned Counsel for the petitioner failed to point out any infirmity in the discussion and consideration of the evidence as regard the fact that plaintiff in fact paid the money through his father for the purchase of' the land in suit and that the scribe of the agreement at the time of writing the agreement for sale drew up the same in the name of plaintiffs lather as an intending buyer of the land and that the fact of writing the name of plaintiffs father wrongly by the scribe in the agreement was admitted by plaintiff's father upon executing an ekrurnama stating the fact that plaintiff actually made advance of the amount for the purpose of purchasing the land in suit and that seller agreed to sell the land in suit to him and that balance of' the consideration money subsequently received by the seller from the plaintiff and that in pursuant to the agreement for sale possession was made over to the plaintiff The other contention is that the suit was had for non-impleading the necessary parties i.e. Government as per provision of Article 6(a) of P.O. No. 142 of 1972. 

9. Article 6(a) of P.O. 142 of 1972 provides that without impleading the Government, being the necessary party no suit for specific performance of any contract relating to the transfer of any immovable property or for declaration of title to, or assertion of ownership of any such property shall be filed or proceeded with. P.O. No. 142 of 1972 as seen form the title of the said order that the law therein has been enacted as a temporary measure in the context of the situation prevalent immediately after the liberation of Bangladesh. As it appears the said law was enacted to prevent at the said relevant time obtaining of' the decree of the nature mentioned in Article 6(a) of P.O. No. 142 of 1972. The said P.O. was enacted to safeguard the interest of the Government as regard the property that has vested in the Government being the abandoned property or because of the absence of the rightful owner so that Government is not deprive of such kind of property by the decree of the kind as mentioned in Article 6(a) of P.O. No. 142 of 1972. As appears to us the said P.O. has been enacted to prevent certain kind of transfer of immovable property in derogation of some legislative enactments and the prohibition therein and that keeping in view the said dominant purpose of, the enactment it in no way can be said that the contract for the enforcement of which the instant suit was filed the same was bad for non-impleading the Government as a party. Since no question is involved in the instant suit that transfer of the property in question or in other words property which is the subject matter of the instant suit is barred by law or prohibited by law or that is of a kind of property that has vested in, the Government because of the absence of the rightful owner or that because of the operation of the provision of any law vesting property of particular kind of person in the Government. In the suit i.e. Title Suit No. 33 of 1985, plaintiff has prayed for a decree of specific performance of contract for sale of land on the basis of the agreement for sale of October 5, 1979 against the defendants who were not of' the category of person whose land because of the provision of any law enacted at any time could vest in the Government and that the land in respect whereof specific performance of contract for sale has been sought is also of not the kind of or class of land to which the Government could lay any claim under any law. It was never the case of the defendants either in the courts below or before the I high Court Division that the suit was not maintainable as the property was of kind that vested in the Government rather it is seen from the materials on record the defendants who are Bangladeshi nationals, are claiming the property in suit as of their ancestral property. The contention as regard non- impleading Government as being the necessary party is being pleaded for the first time in connection with the hearing of the petition for leave to appeal. In the background of the facts of the instant suit the question as to whether Government is a necessary party in the suit is a question of fact and further more no fact has been brought on record to substantiate the contention that Government was a necessary party for the adjudication of the subject matter of the suit. In the context of the aforesaid facts and circumstance we are of the view that contention of the learned Counsel for the petitioner that because of non-impleading of the Government necessary party as per provision of Article 6(a) of P.O. No. 142 of 1972, the suit was bad in law is of no merit. 

10. In the light of the discussion made herein above the petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Appeal No. 85 of 1997
lawyer:
For the Appellant: Mr. Salah Uddin Ahmed, Advocate, instructed by Mr. Md. Nawab Ali, Advocate-on-Record. 
For Respondent Nos.1 and 2: Mr. Fida M. Kamal, Additional Attorney General, instructed by Mr. Mvi. Md. Wahidullah, Advocate-on-Record. 
For Respondent Nos. 3 and 4: Mr. A.F. Hasan Ariff, Senior Advocate, instructed by Mr. Ahsanullah Patwary, Advocate-on-Record. 
Respondent Nos.5 and 6: Not represented
parties:
Pubali Bank Limited ------ Appellant
Versus
Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce, and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mr. Md. Ruhul Amin, J: This appeal, by leave, is by the writ-petitioner against the judgment dated April 10, 1997 of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.3396 of 1991 discharging the Rule obtained impugning Memo. No. 1221(5)J,M,60 dated 14.12.1991 of the Office of District Magistrate, Chittagong issued under the signature of Mr. Azim Uddin Ahmed Chowdhury, Magistrate, 1st Class, Sadar, Chittagong addressed to the Deputy Police Commissioner, Sadar Head Quarter, CMP Chittagong requesting him for placing police personnel at 10 hours on December 19, 1991 for eviction of the appellant from the property of M/s. Lazaf Commercial Corporation Ltd. at 40, Shaheed Saifuddin Khaled Road, Chittagong.

 2. Facts, in short, are that the property as stated hereinbefore belongs to the Respondent No.3, M/s. Lazaf Commercial Corporation Ltd. (hereinafter in short the Corporation), that the said Corporation is a Company registered in the then East Pakistan, that in 1972 when the share-holders of the Corporation stranded in Pakistan the property in question and the other properties of the Corporation were declared abandoned property as per provision of P.0.16 of 1972, that while the share-holders of the Corporation returned to Bangladesh and found the property to have been treated as abandoned property and has been leased out to the appellant, the Corporation and another filed Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 seeking declaration that the properties of the Corporation including the one which is the subject matter of the present appeal are not abandoned property' and for release from the list of abandoned property and a further prayer for restoration of possession of the properties to the writ-petitioners, that the High Court Division made the Rule obtained in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 absolute declaring that the properties of the Corporation are  not abandoned property and made direction for release of the properties of the Corporation from the list of abandoned property. The High Court Division in the aforesaid writ petition, as seen from the judgment passed thereof instead of making direction for handing over possession of the property to the Corporation rather directed the Respondent No.1 i.e. Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce to hand over possession of the property which was previously declared as abandoned property to the Respondent No.3, i.e. appellant herein, as "mortgagee of the said properties". After the judgment in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 negotiations were held over the mortgage matter between the Respondent Nos.3 and 4 and the appellant but ultimately the same were not successful. That the abandoned property authority leased out the property in question to the appellant and that while Government took step for sale of the property the appellant accepted the offer of sale and in connection therewith deposited Tk.39 lacs and odd in favour of the Abandoned Property Authority but the sale could not be materialized since Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 was filed challenging the action of the Abandoned Property Authority treating the Corporation's property in question and other properties as abandoned property and in that state of the matter the appellant prayed for return of the money but the same was not returned to the appellant. The appellant as allottee having had not paid rent a certificate case was initiated against it. The appellant challenged legality of the certificate proceeding by filing a suit but ultimately the appellant was not successful upto this Division. While appellant's suit filed challenging legality of the certificate issued for realization of the arrear rents, yet to reach finality at that stage from the office of the District Magistrate a Memo was addressed to the Deputy Police Commissioner, Head Quarter, Chittagong with the request for making available police force for eviction of the appellant. The appellant filed writ petition challenging legality of the said Memo. 

3. The Rule was opposed by the Respondent No.2, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Chittagong and the Respondent No.3 and 4 i.e. the Corporation and its one of share-holders by filing separate sets of affidavits-in-opposition. 

4. It was the case of the Respondent No.2 that the property in question was mortgaged to the appellant. It may be mentioned that the nature and character of the mortgage was equitable mortgage. That during the war of liberation in 1971 while the miscreants tried to occupy the mortgaged property the appellant as mortgagee took control of the property in question, that the Respondent Nos.3 and 4 mortgaged the property on December 8, 1971 to the appellant and that by 1974 debt was liquidated, that the Respondent No.3 filed writ petition and the High Court Division declared that the property in question is not abandoned property and as such Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 are required to hand over possession of the property to the Respondent No.3. that the appellant owe to the Respondent No.3 an amount of Tk.12,70,00,000/-, that when the property in question was taken over as abandoned property the same on the asking of the appellant was leased out to it and though the Bank possessing the property but did not pay rent, that in spite of declaration by the High Court division that the property in question is not an abandoned property the appellant is not paying rent to the Respondent No.3 and that without any rent the appellant .is occupying the property in question illegally, that in spite of the property being not an abandoned property the appellant is illegally withholding possession thereof and that as the property is not an abandoned property the Respondent Nos.1 and 2 is required to hand over possession thereof to the authoritatively declared owner of the property and as such the Memo impugned in the writ petition is quite legal since the abandoned property authority is required to hand over possession of the property to the claimant, the Respondent No.3, upon evicting its allottee. 

5. It may be mentioned that ownership of the property by the Respondent No.3 is undisputed one. It is the case of the appellant that since he is mortgagee in respect of the property iii question and as the mortgagor, the Respondent No.3; did not discharge its obligation by paying back the amount due the mortgagee is legally competent to retain possession of the property till payment of the dues by the mortgagor i.e. Respondent No.3. It is also the contention of the appellant that the process resorted to by the Respondent Nos.1 and 2 for eviction of the appellant from the property in question is not legal and that the reason mentioned in the Memo impugned in the writ petition cannot be the ground for eviction of the appellant since it is a mortgagee of the property in question and is possessing the same as mortgagee. It has already been mentioned that the mortgage in question is an equitable mortgage. Lastly it has been contended by the appellant that in the judgment passed in the earlier writ petition i.e. in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 the High Court Division instead of making direction to hand over possession of the property to the Corporation directed the Government to hand over possession of the rest of the properties of the Corporation to the appellant as mortgagee of the said properties so that "the entire question of claims by the bank and possession of the petitioners may be settled as a package between them either by negotiation or by litigation". As stated hereinbefore that in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 the relief was sought by the Corporation seeking declaration that the property in question and the other properties of the Corporation are not abandoned properties and for release of the property in question and other properties of the Corporation from the list of abandoned buildings as well as for the possession those of. The High Court Division granted first part of the relief i.e. declared that the properties of the Corporation are not abandoned properties and made direction to release the properties of the Corporation from the list of abandoned properties and instead of granting the second part of the relief, i.e. handing over possession of properties to Respondent No.3, made direction to the Government for handing over possession of the rest of the properties of the Corporation to the Bank as mortgagee. 

6. From the materials on record it is seen that the appellant accepting the property in question as abandoned property prayed to the authority for leasing out the same to it and thereupon the property was leased out to the Bank and the Bank was possessing the property as allottee on payment of rent fixed by the Abandoned Property Authority but at one stage stopped payment of rent since the appellant deposited an amount of Tk.39 lacs and odd when the property offered for sale but ultimately when the sale could not be materialized the appellant asked for return of money but the Government did not return the said money. 

7. The Respondent No.3 approached the Government for restoration of possession of the property in question and the other properties of the Corporation since the same have been declared not abandoned property and thereupon the abandoned property authority is legally required to restore possession of the property to the rightful claimant i.e. Respondent No.3. The Government having had found justification in the claim of the Respondent No.3 for restoration of possession of the property which was taken over as abandoned property and leased out to the Bank, the Government issued the Memo impugned in the writ petition for eviction of the appellant since it did not surrender possession amicably/voluntarily, rather retaining possession upon referring to the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985.

8. As stated hereinbefore that the issue in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 whether the properties of the Respondent No.3 were abandoned properties and that if the properties of the Respondent No.3 are not abandoned properties, whether the Respondent No.3 is entitled to get possession thereof or in other words Abandoned Property Authority is required to handover possession of the property of the Respondent No.3 treated abandoned property and possession taken over. The High Court Division in the said writ petition 4- declared that the listing of the properties of the Respondent No.3 as abandoned property is not legal but made no direction for handing over of possessing to the Respondent No.3 rather made direction to handover possession of the same and other properties, which have been allotted to some other lessees, to the appellant, who was Respondent No.3 in the said writ petition as mortgagee, to enable the mortgagee to realize its claim either through negotiation between the mortgagor i.e. Respondent No.3 and the mortgagee i.e. the appellant herein or by litigation. 

9. The Respondent No.3 for the reason best known to it did not go on appeal against the judgment of the High Court Division in refusing to Made direction for handing over possession of its property and that making direction to handover possession of its property to the Respondent No.3 (in the previous writ petition) i.e. appellant herein, as mortgagee. 

10. The direction of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 to handover possession of the properties of the Respondent No.3 to the Respondent No.3 of the said writ petition i.e. the appellant to enable it to realize its claim against the Respondent No.3 i.e. Corporation was beyond the scope of the writ petition as well as beyond the issue involved in the said writ petition. 

11. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that there had been negotiations between the Corporation and the appellant but the same were not fruitful. 

12. The High Court Division upon making observation that whatever the direction given by the High Court Division in the previous writ petition relating to the property of the Corporation "were incidental to the main issue" and as such in the background of the said direction the Bank as lessee of the abandoned property is not entitled to retain " possession since the property has been declared by the High Court Division in the previous writ petition is not an abandoned property and that the property being not an abandoned property the Government as well as the Abandoned Property Authority are duty bound to restore possession of the property of the Corporation which was not legally taken over as abandoned property, that the appellant on the basis of incidental direction of this Court made in the judgment of the earlier writ petition this petitioner Pubali Bank is not entitled to hold and keep illegal possession of the property till eternity. In the changed circumstances this Pubali Bank is bound to handover possession to M/s. Lazaf Corporation immediately", that the Abandoned Property Authority leased out the property of the Lazaf Corporation to the Bank and two others and as the property is not an abandoned property the Pubali Bank is not entitled to retain possession and is not legally competent to take exception to the action of the authority when the authority in discharge of his legal obligation taken step for restoration of possession to its rightful owner, that the Bank is not entitled to retain possession on the plea of adjustment of claim between it and the Government. The High Court Division in the background of the materials on record as well as in the background of the submissions made by the learned Counsel of the Bank arrived at the finding that M/s. Lazaf Corporation "had already satisfied the dues of the Pubali Bank", that Pubali Bank owes huge amount as rent. On the aforesaid findings and observations the High Court Division discharged the Rule. 

13. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division misdirected itself in discharging the Rule in that it was nowhere found that the impugned order dated 14.12.199.1 (Annexure-D to the writ petition) was lawfully passed under proper lawful authority, that the High Court Division not only misread the operative part of the order passed in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 but also acted contrary thereto in giving the direction for restoration of possession of the disputed property to the Respondent No.3 (M/s. Lazaf Commercial Company Limited) which, in any case, was an illegal and improper order in the facts and circumstances of the case, that the High Court Division was wrong in giving the direction to the writ-petitioner and the writ Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 to give possession of the property in question to the writ Respondent No.3 irrespective of any suit or case or any order of any kind of any Court relating to the property in suit and that in making direction to the writ-petitioner Pubali Bank to deliver possession to the writ Respondent Nos.3 and 4 (Latif D. Fancy, Director of Writ Respondent No.3) within the time fixed by the High Court Division from the date of receipt of the copy of the judgment in the writ petition and that in of writ-petitioner's failure to deliver possession the writ Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 i.e. Government and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) Chittagong would be competent to proceed in the light of Annexure-D to the writ petition and upon evicting the write petitioner from the property in question would deliver possession thereof to the writ Respondent Nos.3 and 4 without considering at all the point at issue, i.e. whether the impugned order was passed with any lawful authority or not. 

14. It was the case of the appellant that it went into possession of the property in question on the verge of emergence of Bangladesh when the law and order situation was quite unstable to save the same from being damaged by the miscreants since it was mortgaged to the appellant. Me: contention so made may be correct in the context of the point of time and situation in which the appellant claimed to have went into possession of the property for saving the same from being damaged but he was not competent to go into possession of the property as mortgagee since the mortgage as claimed by the appellant was an equitable mortgage. The property in question was treated as abandoned property and was taken over by the Ministry of Commerce for management. While the property was taken over as the abandoned property by dal! Ministry of Commerce, the appellant represented to the Abandoned Property Authority for allotment of some of the properties of M/s. Lazaf Commercial Corporation Ltd. (Respondent No.3) to it. Accordingly allotment was made upon fixing the rent. It is seen from the materials on record that the appellant defaulted in the payment of rent and in the said premise the Government initiated certificate case. The appellant challenged legality of the proceedings of the certificate case but failed at all stages. The Abandoned Property one time took decision to sell the property of Respondent No.3 which was earlier taken over by the Abandoned Property Authority and the appellant came forward to purchase the portion of the property allotted to it and in connection therewith deposited Tk.39 lacs and odd in the account of the Abandoned Property Authority but ultimately the sale could not be finalized since the Respondent No.3 and others challenged legality of the action of the Abandoned Property Authority in treating their property as abandoned property and was successful in obtaining declaration from the High Court Division to the effect that the property of the Respondent No.3 herein is not an abandoned property and also obtain a direction to the Abandoned Property Authority for de-listing the properties of the Respondent No.3 from the list of abandoned properties. The Respondent No.3 in its earlier writ petition i.e. Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 prayed for a direction to the Abandoned Property Authority to handover possession of the property but instead of allowing the same the High Court Division made direction to place some other properties of the Respondent No.3 herein also in the possession of the Bank who was Respondent No.3 therein, to secure the claim of the Bank being mortgagee. 

15. Facts as transpire from the records that the property of the Respondent No.3 was taken over by the Abandoned Property Authority and was managed by the said authority upon allotting the same to the different organizations. It also transpires that the appellant although initially of its own volition entered upon the property in question but later on the appellant stayed in the property as allottee of the Abandoned Property Authority. So the contention that as mortgagee the appellant is quite competent to retain possession is factually not correct and that also the appellant was not competent to enter upon the property as mortgagee since the mortgage claimed by the Bank was an equitable mortgage wherein physical possession of the property is not parted with by the mortgagor to the mortgagee. Since the property was declared as not abandoned property it became obligatory on the part of the Abandoned Property Authority to release the property from the list of abandoned properties and to restore possession of the property to the accepted claimant of -the same free from encumbrance created by the Abandoned Property Authority and for performance thereof the Abandoned Property Authority took step for eviction of the tenant inducted by it since the tenant so inducted was not vacating the property allotted to it after repeated requests. As it is seen from the materials on record that on different occasions the appellant was asked to vacate the property in question but he having had not vacated the premises the Abandoned Property Authority took steps for obtaining the possession of the property in question in the manner as in Annexure-D to the writ petition i.e. for the eviction of the appellant and for that asking the law enforcing agency to make available police personnel on the date of eviction of the appellant from the property in question, so that law and order situation is not disturbed. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that it was the contention of the appellant that in the light of the judgment passed in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 the Bank is quite competent to retain possession of the property in question as well as other properties placed in its possession in the light of the judgment of the High Court Division and as such action proposed to be taken in the light of the Annexure-D to the writ petition is illegal. As has already been observed that after the property being declared not abandoned property, the Abandoned Property Authority that took over possession of the property of the Respondent No.3 as abandoned property and managed the same for some time by inducting different agencies as allottees was legally duty bound to restore possession of the property of the Respondent No.3. We have already mentioned that the appellant is in the property as allottee of the abandoned property authority and not as mortgagee. It may be mentioned in the earlier writ petition i.e. Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 the issue was whether the property of the writ-petitioner was abandoned property. In the said writ petition it was held that the property of the writ petitioner .is not an abandoned property. In the Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 the write petitioner's prayed for restoration of possession was not granted but there was a direction for handing over the other properties of the writ-petitioner to the appellant, who was Respondent No.3 therein, as mortgagee of the said properties. It may be mentioned the aforesaid direction was given on the view that thereby the claim of the bank against the Respondent No.3 and the claim of possession of the property by the Respondent No.3 would be settled "as a package between them either by negotiation or by litigation". In the Writ Petition out of which the appeal has risen it has been asserted that there had been negotiations between the bank and the Respondent No.3 but those were fruitless and in that context the Respondent No.3 approached the abandoned property authority to deliver possession of the property in question which was taken over as abandoned property and thereupon abandoned property authority took step as in Annexure-D to the writ petition impugning which the writ petition was filed. It has been contended on behalf of the appellant that the action proposed for eviction of the appellant was without jurisdiction since process of eviction of the appellant from the property in question should have not the one as initiated but should have been different kind and that while the High Court Division discharging the Rule it was not held that the action so proposed was legal. The appellant is an allottee of the abandoned property authority in respect of the property in question but the moment the property has been declared not an abandoned property and the abandoned property authority directed the allottee to vacate the property for handing over possession of the property to the claimant but the allottee having had not heeded to the request of the abandoned property authority and consequent thereupon appellant's stay in the property being of an unauthorised person the abandoned property authority has quite legally initiated the action for getting the property clear from the possession of the unauthorised occupant. The other contention is that in view of the judgment in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 and the direction therein to retain the property by the appellant for facilitating settlement of the claims of the bank by negotiation or by litigation is also not legally well founded since it has been specifically asserted by the Respondent No.3 that negotiations failed. So one aspect of settlement of claim of the Bank stood fruitless and the other process although initiated but the plaint of the said proceeding has been rejected. It may be mentioned that the mortgage as claimed by the bank was an equitable mortgage as regard the property in question and other properties of Respondent No.3 and as such there is no occasion for the bank to be in possession of the land as security of the mortgage in question. The above being the factual position the High Court Division was not in error in making direction to the appellant to handover possession of the property in question and other properties, if any, in the possession of the Bank to the said Respondent. It has also been contended on behalf of the appellant that the reason given in support of the proposed action for eviction of the appellant from the property in question cannot be considered as legal ground. As to the appropriateness of the action of the Respondent No.2 it may be mentioned that the appellant accepted the property as an abandoned property by approaching the abandoned property authority for allotment thereof to it and thereupon the abandoned property authority allotted the property in question to the appellant and that while the property of the Respondent No.3 was declared not an abandoned property and a direction was made to release the properties of the Respondent No.3 from the list of the abandoned properties it was the legal duty of the Respondent Nos.1 and 2 to restore possession of the properties of the Respondent No.3 to it, hence the step taken by the Respondent Nos.1 and 2 towards the discharge of its afore stated legal duty the action proposed in Annexure-D cannot be considered unlawful and unauthorised or that there is no sanction therefor. The Respondent No.1 in support of the proposed action as in Annexure-D has submitted that High Court Division in the background of the facts and circumstances of the case had quite legally held that the Memo. impugned in the writ petition valid since the bank had accepted the fact that the property at the time when it was allotted to it was abandoned property and that when the action of the abandoned property authority was challenged it was held that the property was not an abandoned property and a direction was made to release the property of the Respondent No.3 from the list of the abandoned property. The learned Additional Attorney General has also referred to the observation of the High Court Division about the order passed in the previous writ petition i.e. Writ Petition No.35 of 1985, that "Other order or directions given in the judgment were incidental to the main issue" and that the observation so made by the High Court Division was quite correct since the main issue in the earlier writ petition was whether the property is abandoned property or not and that in the said writ petition in has been held that the properties of the Respondent No.3 including the property in question as being possessed by the appellant are not abandoned properties. It has been also submitted by the learned Additional Attorney General that High Court Division was quite correct in holding that the notice impugned in the writ petition is valid since the properties of the Respondent No.3 part of which is in the possession of the appellant are not abandoned properties. 

16. The learned Counsel appearing for the Respondent Nos.3 and 4, i.e. M/s. Lazaf Commercial Corporation Ltd. and its Director respectively, submitted that in the earlier writ petition i.e. Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 the primary issue was whether the properties of the Respondent No.3 are abandoned property or not and that it has been held that the properties of the Respondent No.3 are not abandoned properties and a direction was made to release the property of the Respondent No.3 from the list of abandoned properties. The learned Counsel has also submitted that the claim as made by the appellant as mortgagee could not be the subject matter for consideration in the context, facts and circumstances in which the previous writ petition was filed and the relief sought and as such incidental order made relating to the claim of the appellant as mortgagee against the property of the Respondent No.3 in no way be considered as a bar to consider the prayer of the Respondent No.3 by the abandoned property authority for restoration of the property which was earlier taken over as abandoned property and managed by the said authority through the allottee and by itself. The learned Counsel has also submitted that the moment the property was declared as not an abandoned property it became a legal obligation and duty of the abandoned property authority to restore possession thereof to the claimant i.e. Respondent No.3 and as the abandoned property authority has taken step for the discharge of the said obligation and duty it cannot be said by the appellant that the same was unauthorised and there is no sanction therefor. Lastly it has been submitted by the learned Counsel that the observation relating to retaining of possession by the appellant and further to handover possession of the properties in the possession of the Respondent No.1 which were once treated as abandoned property but ultimately held by High Court Division not abandoned property to the appellant was beyond the scope of the writ petition filed seeking declaration that the property was not an abandoned property and the honorable Court declared that the property is not an abandoned property and as such the moment it was declared as not abandoned property it became obligatory for the abandoned property authority to return the property to the claimant upon removing the encumbrance created by the abandoned property authority and that for the discharge of the said obligation the abandoned property authority having had taken step as in Annexure-D to the writ petition the same has rightly been held by the High Court Division valid.

17. The learned Counsel for the appellant at the last stage of the hearing submitted that an observation may be made by this Division to the effect that whatever observation(s) has been made by the High Court Division in its judgment regarding the claim of the appellant against the Respondent No.3 and its share-holders shall have no bearing on the proceeding(s), if any, initiated or would be initiated by the appellant against the Respondent Nos.3 and its share-holders relating to the claim of the appellant as mortgagee as regard the property of the Respondent No.3. The submission so made appears to be of merit since the scope of the writ petition was limited to the legality of the proceeding initiated or the steps taken in the light of the Memo of the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong dated 14.12.1991 i.e. Annexure-D to the writ petition. In that state of the matter we like to observe that whatever observation(s) has been made by the High Court Division in its judgment dated April 10, 1997 in Writ Petition No.3396 of 1991 relating to the dues, if any, of the Respondent No.3 to the appellant and the proceeding(s), if any, initiated or would be initiated in connection with the said dues, as contended by the bank and denied by the Respondent No.1, against the Respondent No.3 and others by the appellant the same shall have no bearing on the proceeding(s). 

18. In the background of the materials on record the undented position is that the property in question i.e. the property possessed by the appellant and the other properties of the Respondent No.3 at one point of time although was taken over as abandoned property and managed by the abandoned property authority by allotting the same to the different organizations and person(s) including the appellant but the action of the abandoned property authority having been challenged by the Respondent No.3 and another it has been declared that the properties of the Respondent No.3 are not abandoned property and thereupon direction was made to release the property from the list of abandoned property. As such the moment it was held that the properties of the Respondent No.3 are not abandoned property, the abandoned property authority under the law is duty bound to return the property to the claimant upon removing the encumbrance created by it i.e. upon taking over possession from the person to whom the abandoned property authority allotted the property of the Respondent No.3 while managing the same as abandoned property and that in performance of the said legal duty the step taken by the abandoned property authority reflected in Annexure-D to the writ petition i.e. Memo of the office of the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong dated 14.12.1991 has quite correctly been held legal by the High Court Division. 

19. The appellant's claim to retain possession as mortgagee is not legally sustainable since the mortgage as claimed by the appellant is an equitable mortgage. 
20. It may be mentioned in Writ Petition No.35 of 1985 issue as to retention of possession of the property allotted to the Bank, the appellant, by abandoned property authority as mortgagee was not an issue for decision and as such the observation made by the High Court Division as to retention of possession of allotted property was an incidental one. The admitted position is that at one time the Bank, as claimed by it went into possession of the property in question, of which it was not in possession as mortgagee, to save the same from being damaged keeping in view its interest therein as mortgagee. In the background of the nature of the mortgage, i.e. equitable mortgage, when the property was taken over by the abandoned property authority the appellant stepped down from its previous position and approached the abandoned property authority to allot the property in question to it and on the basis of such allotment the appellant was possessing the property in question, but the moment the property has been declared as not abandoned property and thereupon while it became legal obligation and duty on the part of the abandoned property authority to restore possession of the property to the claimant of the property and that steps having been taken as in Annexure-D for discharging the said obligation and duty, the same cannot be considered to have been taken without jurisdiction or that the steps taken should not have been the one but there should have been different one because of the fact stated hereinbefore. The action as has been initiated by the abandoned property authority being for restoration of possession of the property which was taken over as abandoned property but later on declared by the Court not abandoned property to the authoritatively declared claimant/owner the action of the Respondent Nos.1 and 2 is quite legal and lawful. The contention of the appellant that the Respondent No.3 owes huge dues to the bank is not material in the context of the matter involved in the case brought by the appellant before the court and that the question of taking loan by the Respondent No.3 and the liability thereof, if . any, to the Bank are extraneous matter in the context of the subject matter of the writ petition out of which the appeal has arisen and as such is not an issue for determination in the writ petition. The only issue before the Court is whether the step taken for restoration of possession, as in Annexure-D to the writ petition, i.e. the impugned annexure, is legal or not. As regard the liability, if any, in connection with the mortgage, claimed by the appellant the same would be matter for decision in some other forum but not in writ jurisdiction. As such bank is not legally entitled to retain possession of the property of the Respondent No.3 on the said ground i.e. Respondent No.3 owes to the Bank in connection with the mortgage since in the case of the kind of mortgage as claimed by the appellant the mortgagee is not supposed to be in occupation of the mortgagor's property. It may be mentioned in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1820 of 2001 Bank's contention to retain possession of the property of the mortgagor i.e. Respondent No.3 was held not legal. The hard fact is that Bank was a aliottee of the abandoned property in question and as such taking a different stand the Bank i.e. the appellant is not legally entitled to retain possession of the property of the Respondent No.3 when its property has been declared not abandoned property Since in the background of .the authoritative pronouncement of the Court as to that the properties of the Respondent No.3 are not abandoned properties and thereupon abandoned property authority having had taken step to restore possession of the property which once taken over as abandoned property to the claimant the allottee i.e. the appellant cannot question the action of the abandoned property authority, i.e. challenged in the writ petition since the allottee did not voluntarily deliver the possession to the abandoned property authority for the purpose of handing over the property free from all encumbrances to the claimant of the property whose property was taken over as abandoned property but declared by the Court as not abandoned property. 

21. In the background of the discussions made hereinabove we find no merit in the appeal. 

22. Accordingly the appeal is dismissed with costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J.: This appeal by leave at the instance of the defendant-appellants is directed against the judgment and order dated 26.7.2000 passed the High Court Division discharging the rule against judgment and decree passed by the Additional District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No.136 of 1997 reversing those dated 29.5.1997 of the Assistant Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No.68 of 1985.

2. The predecessors of the respondents as the plaintiff filed the suit for decree, inter alia, that the defendants were legally bound to execute necessary documents relating to the suit property in favour of the plaintiff after accepting the price fixed by the Government for the property and also for a decree that sale of the suit property by auction to other than the plaintiff was illegal and also for a further decree that the auction schedule to be held on 31 July 1985 or thereafter was illegal. The case or deceased plaintiff, inter alia, is that he took rent of the suit property from one Md. Amin from January 1968 and had been in occupation of the suit property and carrying on business in the name and style M/s. General Exporters and also had been using the suit property for residential purpose. He continued to pay rent at the rate of Tk.90/- per month till February 1972. He failed to trace out the landlord after February 1972 and therefore applied to the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar Dhaka for declaring the suit property as abandoned property under President Order No. 16 of 1972. The Ministry of Works declared the suit property as the abandoned property on 20.3.1975 and the plaintiff paid rent of Tk.11,932/- at the rate of Tk.314/- per month. The Ministry of Works by letter dated 30.12.1975 informed the plaintiff that the Government had decided to hold the suit property and requested the plaintiff to hand over possession of the same to the Executive Engineer, City Building Division P.W.D. within 30 days of the receipt of the letter. The plaintiff requested the Government to reconsider its decision which was allowed by the Government by letter dated 9.9.1976 and plaintiff continued his business. The plaintiff continuing to reside and doing his business on the suit property paid enhanced rent of Tk.1645/- per month from 4.9.1983. The Government on 4.9.1983 decided to sell the abandoned house to the lawful allottees. The decision was published in the national newspapers and the Government constituted a Valuation Committee. The Valuation Committee valued the suit premises after enquiry and recommended transfer of the suit property to the plaintiff at a price determined by the Committee. The Sub-Divisional Engineer, defendant No.6, by his letter dated 6.8.1984 informed defendant No.5, Executive Engineer, P.W.D., that the Valuation Committee had determined the value of the suit property and the plaintiff as per Government policy expressed his willingness to pay/deposit money as per valuation determined by the Valuation Committee. The plaintiff was advised by the defendant No.3, Section Officer, Ministry of Works, to keep fund available for depositing the money when called upon but in spite of repeated requests by the plaintiff, the defendants did not allow the plaintiff to deposit the money. The plaintiff then received a letter dated 13.7.1985 from the defendant No.3 informing that the Government had taken a decision to sell the suit premises within 10(ten) days. It was submitted by the plaintiff that since he remained in possession and occupation of the suit premises for more than 18 years and since he accepted the offer to purchase the suit property as per valuation determined by abandoned property authority a right had been created in his favour which could not be taken away by the defendants. It was further submitted that if the suit property was sold in auction, the loss and damage to be suffered by the plaintiff case could not be compassed. 

3. The appellant as the defendant contested the suit denying the material contentions of the plaintiff-respondent stating, inter alia, that the suit property is an abandoned one within the meaning of President Order No.16 of 1972 and has been under the control, management and supervision of the defendants. The suit property is a commercial unit and the plaintiff-respondent had no legal right to proceed with the suit against the Government. The defendants rightly decided to sell the suit property by auction in accordance with the law. The defendant reserved the right to dispose of the suit property and the plaintiff had the right to participate in the auction to purchase the suit property through tender. That the learned Assistant Judge, lst Court, Dhaka dismissed the suit and thereafter the plaintiff took an appeal before the learned District Judge. The Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, who heard the appeal, allowed the appeal setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and directed the defendant-petitioner Government to register a document on acceptance of valuation fixed by Government and also declared the sale by auction of the suit property to any stranger to be illegal. The learned Appellate Judge also found that the valuation committee had fixed Tk.7,27,410/- as the valuation of the suit property- and recommended to sell the same to the plaintiff at that price. 

4. The appellants unsuccessfully moved the High Court Division. Thereafter the appellants moved this Court and leave was granted to consider the submission that the plaintiff not having instituted any suit for specific performance of contract the suit is not maintainable and the High Court Division erred in law is not setting aside the decree passed by the Court of apeal below. Further, the Government being the lawful owner having right to sell the property in auction and the plaintiff having right to participate in the said auction, he is not in a position to compel the Government to sell the property in his favour and the High Court Division erred in law in discharging the rule. It was further submitted that having regard to Rule 8(2) of Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Land, Building and other Properties) Rules 1972 providing clearly that abandoned buildings, not required for public purpose or in public interest, shall be sold to the highest bidder in open auction, the High Court Division erred in holding : "It is not understood why the plaintiff would go for participating in auction to purchase suit property in view of the promise given by Government to the plaintiff to sell the property on the valuation fixed by valuation committee constituted by Government" inasmuch as any offer by any official, if at all, is unauthorized and cannot operate as an estoppel on the Government. 

5. Mr. A.J. Mohammad Ali, the learned Additional Attorney general appearing for the appellants has submitted with reference to Rule 6(3) of the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order 1972 that the property being a commercial undertaking did vest in the Ministry of Commerce and as such the purported actions of the Ministry of Works in the matter of allotting the property to the plaintiff was unauthorised and accordingly his subsequent action both in the matter of alleged valuation and purported action to lease out the same permanently was unauthorised. The learned Additional Attorney General has further submitted with reference to rule 10 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Building in Urban Areas) Rules 1972 that the authority concerned was not competent to take the alleged action in the matter of sale to the plaintiff while disposing of the building other than the manner prescribed therein namely, (a) lease on monthly rental basis; (b) disposal on hire-purchase system, and (c) disposal by outright auction and in the manner provided therein and as such the alleged acceptance of offer of the plaintiff to purchase the property on the valuation determined by the Abandoned Property authority, no right has been created in favour of the plaintiff for enforcement in the Court of law inasmuch as if the property is sold in auction the loss or damage that would be suffered by the plaintiff could be compensated. The learned Additional Attorney General has further submitted that having regard to rule 8(2) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Land, Building and other property) Rules, 1972 providing that the abandoned building not required for any public purpose or in public interest, shall be sold to the highest bidder in open auction, the impugned judgment of the High Court Division affirming those of the Court of appeal below enforcing alleged promise given to the plaintiff to sale the property on the valuation fixed by valuation committee being unauthorized one, which the offer concerned cannot be legally give would not operate as a estoppel against the appellant for a decree in the suit as prayed for. 

6. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the plaintiff-respondents has however submitted that the Court of appeal below on discussion and consideration of the evidence on record both oral and documentary decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff-respondent was entitled to a decree for getting a deed executed in his favour on the principle of the promissory estoppel inasmuch as the plaintiff could reasonably expect that all other formalities accepting the execution of the deed in question in favour of the plaintiff on acceptance of the consideration amount was only left to be performed between the parties instead the defendant-appellant resorted to the illegal step of holding auction contrary to the process undertaken so far for conveying the property in favour of the plaintiff-respondent and as such the resort to hold auction for disposal of the property admittedly in possession of the plaintiff since 1968 was illegal. 

7. Admittedly the plaintiff has been residing in the said building and carrying some business taking lease from his owner one Md. Amin at the rate of Tk.90/- per month and paid rent to the said owner till February 1972. Since the said owner could not be traced out the plaintiff approached the then Sub-Division Engineer (South), Dhaka for enlistment in the list of abandoned property and the letter accordingly enlisted the property as such treating the plaintiff as an allottee and received Tk.11,932/- as arrear rent upto 1979 when the property was declared as abandoned property fixing the rent initially at Tk.314/- and subsequently enhancing the same to Tk.1645/- per month. The plaintiff as well has been regularly paying the rent. Following the rules the Government by notification in the daily newspapers dated 4.9.1983 published a list of abandoned properties to be sold upon determining valuation through valuation committee. The committee authorised for disposal of the property also recommended the sale of the property in favour of the plaintiff at the assessed value at Tk.7,27,410/-, issued on a letter dated 3.6.1984 that the property would be sold to the plaintiff on the valuation determined by the Government. But subsequently to the utter surprise of the respondent it was notified for the auction sale on 13.7.1985 giving rise to the cause of action of the suit. It is not disputed that the plaintiff has been residing in the suit building since 1968 and at his instance the property was declared abandoned in 1975 upon his approached to the concerned authority in 1972 when the owner of the land one Md. Amin whose where about were not known or could not be traced out. The Ministry of Works accordingly has accepted the plaintiff as an allottee at the rate of rent fixed by the Government since 1972. The plaintiff has produced the letter Ext.1 dated 20.3.1975 issued by the Ministry of Works, Urban Development, P.W.D. directing the plaintiff to pay arrear rent at Tk.340/- from 1.1.1972 to 28.2.1973 amount to Tk.11,972/-. The plaintiff has also produced duplicate challahs showing payment of rent for the building in question till February 1980. The plaintiff has also produced Ext.4 the valuation statement of 5 member committee appointed by the Ministry of Works fixing Tk.7,27,410/-. The plaintiff also produced Ext.5 series, challan showing payment of monthly rent from 30th January 1975 to 30th May 1983. The plaintiff also produced Ext.7 issued by the Ministry of Works dated 3rd of June 1984 that the Government has decided to sale the property in favour of the plaintiff at the valuation determined by the Government. 

8. From all these, it reveals the plaintiff though was initially tenant in a portion of the premises for commercial use he used the premises mainly for residential purpose and under the provision of the Bangladesh Abandoned- Property (Taking over possession) Rules, 1972 residential and other building in urban areas is required to made over to the Ministry of Works and not under the Ministry of Commerce as the plaintiff though carried on some business but the premises was predominately being used as residential one and but upon declaration as an abandoned property was inducted as an allottee by the Ministry of Works and pursuant to rules i.e., the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Buildings in Urban Areas) Rules 1972 in exercise of its management decided to dispose of the property to the occupier and accordingly assessed the valuation of the building through as authorized Valuation Committee on the basis of the costs of the building at the prevailing market rate, other then the modes of disposal being on a monthly rental basis and disposal by outright action. 

9. The procedure has been laid down in rule 10(b) thereof for disposal on higher purchase system and under rule 10(3) thereof the price of the building for disposal on higher purchase system shall be the value of the property including the cost of the site assessed of the rule 8 plus at the interest of 8% that would accrue over a period of 10 years on 2/3 rds of assessed value and at least 1/3 rd of the amount shall he payable of the first installment and the balance would be paid in equal amount installments over a period of 10 years. 
10. It is nobody's case that so far in the trial Court or before the Courts below or before the High Court Division that the disposal was not under hire purchase system or that the valuation not been done in accordance with law or the authority was no authorized to dispose of the property in the manner they sought to take steps for disposal or that the disposal was not unconformity with the law or rules. But while the process was on for disposal of the property in favour of the plaintiff-respondent, all on a sudden step for disposal by outright auction was taken and auction was fixed to be held on 3rd of July 1985, which has led to the cause of action of the suit. 

11. The word "hire-purchase" is synonymous to sale by way of hire-purchase agreement. A hire-purchase agreement, as its very name implies, has two aspects. There is first an aspect of bailment of the goods subjected to the hire-purchase agreement and there is next an element of sale which fructifies when the option to purchase, which is usually a term of hire-purchase agreements, is exercised by the intending purchaser. The distinguishing feature of a hire purchase agreement is that the property does not pass when the agreement is made but only passes when the option is finally exercised after complying with all the terms of the agreement. 

12. The learned Additional Attorney General though challenged that the transaction but has not challenged that this proposal to transfer the property to the plaintiff-respondent is not by way of higher purchaser as contemplated under Rule 10(1) (b) or that the transaction with the plaintiffs was not within the scope of the power of disposal by the said authority. 

13. The High Court Division has elaborately dealt with the proposition of law involved in the facts and circumstances of the case i.e., the promissory estoppel and since the Government has taken a decision that the suit land would be sold to the plaintiff on a price fixed by it, equity and natural justice, as well demands that the plaintiff is not deprived of the suit property and that the Government is very much bound by its promise to sell the property in favour of the plaintiff and it cannot full back and also cannot say that the suit property would be put to auction. 

14. "Estoppel" in Black's Law Dictionary is indicated to mean that a party is prevented by his own acts from claiming a right to the detriment of other party who was entitled to rely on such conduct and has acted accordingly. Section 115 of the Evidence Act is also more or less couched in a language which conveys the same expression. "Promissory Estoppel" is defined as an Black's Law Dictionary as "that which arises when there is a promise which promise should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character on the part of promise and which does induce such action for balance and such promise is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement of promise." Lord Denning in Central London Property Trust Ltd Vs. High Trees House Ltd, reported in 1974 QB 130 stated as under : 

"A promise intended to be binding, intended to be acted upon, and in fact acted upon is binding". 

Admittedly the property has been dealt with by the Ministry of Works which according to the rule quoted above has been the appropriate authority to deal with the abandoned building and has in fact dealt with the same since the declaration as abandoned building without any objection from any quarter including the Ministry of Commerce and in that view of the matter it is too late in the in the day to accept the submission of the learned Additional Attorney General that some other Ministry i.e., Ministry of Commerce responsible for management, control and supervision of the building in question treating the same as commercial establishment. Furthermore, the presumption of regularity is attached to the official work as the said Ministry of Works has been dealing with the property since 1972 and has also challenging before us the propriety of the impugned judgment of the Courts below. 

Rule 8(2) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Land, Building and other Property) Rules, 1972 though provides for sale of the property to the highest bidder in the open market but the said provision is only applicable in case of rejection under Article 15 of P.O. No.16 of 1972. 

15. The High Court Division has also affirmed and found that the suit is also maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as the plaintiff admittedly has been in possession of the suit building. 

16. In view of the above we do not find any substance in the submission of fie learned Counsel for the appellants. 

The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

End.
