Manir, C.J. delivering the judgment observed that;

"Where a statute is not ex facie discriminatory but is capable of being administered in a discriminatory manner, the party challenging its constitutionality has to show that it has actually been administered to the detriment of a particular class or in a partial, unjust and oppressive manner."

He further observed;

"I have no doubt that the High Court by issuing an appropriate writ would have controlled such improper exercise of that discretion because there can be little dispute about the proposition that where a statutory functionary acts mala fide or in a partial, unjust and oppressive manner, the High Court in the exercise of its writ jurisdiction has ample power to grant relief to the aggrieved party, and it seems to me to be equally clear that if the allegation be that a statute is being administered by a functionary in a discriminatory manner, his action can be successfully called in question on that ground that it offends against Article 5 of the Constitution."

The Act was held to be not ex-facie discriminatory and there was absence of any allegation by the appellant of any discrimination in practice.

38. While referring to the reliance of the learned Judges of the High Court Division on the observations made in the case of Matajoy Dobey vs. H.C. Share, AIR 1956 (SC) 44 at p. 48 that "a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory power and that abuse of power is not to be easily assumed where the discretion is vested in Government and not in a minor official", the learned Counsel submitted that the action taken against the appellant was obviously discriminatory, no reason has been offered and no fact has been stated by the Government from which the basis of the action could be discerned. The learned Counsel cited the case of Padfield vs. Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, ALL. E.R. 1968 694, in which the House of Lords had the occasion to consider the limits of the exercise of the discretionary statutory powers by a Minister and the extent of the judicial control over such exercise.

39. Facts of this case were that the appellants who were the members of a regional committee of the Milk Marketing Board made a complaint to the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food under section 19 (3) (b) of the Agricultural Marketing Act, 1958, requesting him to refer the complaint to the Committee of Investigation set up under the Act. In declining to refer the matter to the Committee the Minister gave reasons which included that the complaint raised wide issues which he did not consider suitable for investigation and that he had unfettered discretion and that if such complaint was upheld by the committee, a statutory order would have to be given by him to give effect to its recommendations. It was held that where a statute conferred discretion on a Minister to exercise a power but did not expressly limit or define the extent of his discretion, his discretion was nevertheless limited to the extent that it must not be so used as to frustrate the objects of the statute. Further, though the Minister had full or unfettered discretion he should not in exercising it, misdirect himself in law, or take into account irrelevant matters, or omit relevant matters from consideration. As to the extent of judicial control over the exercise of discretionary statutory powers, the Court observed that though the Minister gave no reasons for his decision, whether or not to exercise a discretionary power conferred on him by statute, it would not prevent the Court from reaching a conclusion in a proper case that prerogative order should issue.

40. The learned Counsel referred to a few observations of the noble law Lords which, I think, are relevant to the points raised before us for our decision. One of them shows whether a Minister who is not required by law to state reasons for his decision can avoid to do so where public interest demands that he should give such reasons for the protection of persons "treated contrary to the public interest." As Lord Hodson observed:

"It has been suggested that reason given by the Minister need not and should not be examined closely, for he need give no reason at all in the exercise of his discretion. True it is that the Minister is not bound to give his reasons for refusing to exercise his discretion in a particular manner, but when, as here, the circumstances indicate genuine complaint for which the appropriate remedy is provided if the Minister in the case in question so directs, he would not escape from the possibility of control by mandamus through adopting a negative attitude without explanation. As the guardian of the public interest he has duty to protect the interest of those who claim to have been treated contrary to the public interest." (p. 712).

41. If the Minister does not, or refuses to give any reason for his decision what would be the consequence of his failure or refusal, or what was the duty of the Court? This would be to allow him to defeat the purposes of the Act. In such cases; the Court would intervene so as not to silently thwart the intention of Parliament. In stating these principles Lord Pearce observed:

"It is quite clear from the Act of 1958 in question that the Minister is intended to have some duty in the matter. It is conceded that he must properly consider the complaint. He cannot throw it unread into the waste paper basket, He cannot simply say (albeit honestly) "I think that in general the investigation of complaints has a disruptive effect on the scheme and leads to more trouble than (on balance) it is worth: I shall therefore never refer anything to the Committee of investigation." To allow him to do so would be to give him power to set aside for his period at Minister the obvious intention of Parliament, namely, that an independent committee set up for the purpose should be available to Parliament. This was clearly never intended by the Act of 1958. Nor was it intended that he could silently thwart its intention by failing to carry out its purposes. I do not regard a Minister's failure or refusal to give any reasons as a sufficient exclusion of the Court's surveillance. If all the prima facie reasons seem to point in favour of his taking a certain course to carry out the intentions of Parliament in respect of a power which it has given him in that regard, and he gives no reason whatever for taking a contrary course, the court may infer that he has no good reason and that he is not using the power given by Parliament to carry out its intentions." (p. 714)

42. For proper carrying out of the purposes of an Act, discretion is sometimes conferred on the Government or the named Authority, but such discretion is not boundless or without its limits, though they may not appear from the provisions conferring the discretion. Where such limits do not appear from the language employed in the Act, it is claimed that the discretion is unfettered. In answering whether the discretion conferred on the Minister was unrestricted or "unfettered" as was claimed by him, Lord Upjohn observed as follows:

"My Lords, I believe that the introduction of the adjective 'unfettered' and its reliance thereon as an answer to the appellants' claim is one of the fundamental matters confounding the Minister's attitude, bonafide though it be. First, the adjective nowhere appears in s. 19, it is an unauthorized gloss by the Minister. Secondly, even if the section did contain that adjective, I doubt if it would make any difference in law to his power, save to emphasize what he has already, namely, that acting lawfully he has a power of decision which cannot be controlled by the courts; it is unfettered. But the use of that adjective, even in an Act of Parliament, can do nothing to unfetter the control which the judiciary have over the executive, namely, that in exercising their powers the latter must act lawfully and that is a matter to be determined by looking at the Act and its scope and object in conferring a discretion on the Minister rather than by the use of adjectives" (p. 718)

It was further observed:

"My Lords. I would add only this: that without throwing any doubt on that are well known as the club expulsion cases, where the absence of reasons has not proved fatal to the decision of expulsion by a club committee, a decision of the Minister stands on quite a different basis, he is officer charged by Parliament with the discharge of a public discretion affecting Her Majesty's subjects. if he does not give any reason for his decision it may be, if circumstances warrant it, that a court may be at liberty to come to the conclusion that he had no good reason for reaching that conclusion and directing a prerogative order to issue accordingly. The Minister, in my opinion, has not given a single valid reason for refusing to order an inquiry into the legitimate complaint (be it well founded or not) of the south-east region; all his disclosed reasons for refusing to do so are bad in law." (p. 718)

43. Referring to the observations of the learned Judges of the High Court Division that the superior Courts of this sub-continent found similar provisions of law empowering the Government to retire a public servant prematurely after attainment of certain age or completion of certain years of qualifying service valid and not violative of the equality clauses in their respective Constitutions and also that they upheld the discretion of the Government in retiring a government servant under such provisions of law, Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed submitted that a proper analysis of the decisions of these Courts would reveal that in most of these cases infringement of equality clause was not urged and, secondly, where such infringement had been urged, it was found that there was no such infringement, because, either the expressions "public interest" occurred in the Act itself or similar expressions or grounds existed in the rules made under the relevant laws providing for exercising discretion in prematurely retiring a government servant. If the laws did not provide any principle or guideline for regulating the exercise of discretion by the Government in so retiring a government servant, rules made thereunder provided such a principle or guideline.

44. Of the cases relied on by the learned Judges of the High Court Division first comes the case of Shyamlal vs. State of Uttar Prodesh, AIR 1954 SC 369, wherein challenge was made by the appellant against his compulsory retirement on completion of 25 years of service. Here, no ground was taken on infringement of Articles 14 and 16 of the Indian Constitution which contained the equality provisions. The service rules provided that a public servant can (on completion of 25 years of service only) be compulsorily, retired in the public interest and without assigning any reason. The background against which the appellant was compulsorily retired showed that there were allegations against him and out of several charges brought against him five were established in an informal inquiry which was held after giving him the opportunity to show cause. It was held that the order of compulsory retirement was not equivalent to removal within the meaning of Article 311 of the Constitution Reasons for the decision appear in the following observations:

"There can be no doubt that removal —I am using the term synonymously with dismissal—generally implies that the officer is regarded as in some manner blameworthy or deficient, that is to say, that he has been guilty of some misconduct or is lacking in ability or capacity or the will to discharge his duties as he should do. The action of removal taken against him in such circumstances is thus founded and justified on some ground personal to the officer. Such grounds, therefore, involve the leveling of some imputation or charge against the officer which may conceivably be controverted or explained by the officer. There is no such element of charge or imputation in the case of compulsory retirement... It is true that this power of compulsory retirement may be used when the authority exercising this power cannot substantiate the misconduct which may be the real- cause for taking the action but what is important to note is that the directions in the last sentence in Note I to article 465-A make it abundantly clear that an imputation or charge is not in terms made a condition for the exercise of the power In other words, a compulsory retirement has no stigma or implication of misbehavior or incapacity." (p. 894)

45. In the State of Bombay vs. Saubhagachand M Doshi, AIR 1957 SC 892, the Government was empowered under Service Rules to retire any Government servant on completion of 25 years of service or 50 years of age without giving any reason. The right to compulsorily retire was, however, not to be exercised except when it is in the public interest necessary to dispense with the further services of a government servant such as on account of inefficiency or dishonesty. In cases in which it was seen that the efficiency of the government servant had suffered and it was not desirable to make formal charges against him on such ground and cases were also there where corruption was being indulged in by a government servant but no specific charges were likely to be proved against him. The power of compulsory retirement could be used. No ground was urged on the violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The order of compulsory retirement was not viewed as removal within the meaning of Article 311 of the Indian Constitution.

46. In Shiva Charana vs. State of Mysore. AIR 1965 SC 280, Government was empowered under rule 285 of the Mysore Civil Service Rules to retire compulsorily a government servant in public interest after he completed 25 years of service or attained 50 years of age, though the age of normal superannuation was fixed at 55 years. This power could be exercised if retirement was considered necessary in the public interest, provided also notice was given to the government servant concerned at least 3 months before he was required to retire. Notice, in fact, was issued to the appellant. It was held that the compulsory retirement was not removal under Article 311 and the Service Rules empowering the government to compulsorily retire a government servant did not contravene the equality provisions of the Indian Constitution.

47. In Tara Singh vs. the State of Rajas than, AIR 1975 SC 1487, the appellant was retired on completion of 25 years of qualifying service and notice requiring the appellant to retire with effect from the date of the expiry of 3 months from the date of the notice was served upon the appellant. In the notice mention was made that the Government was satisfied that it is in the public interest to dispense with further service of the appellant. It was contended that there was violation of Article 14 because there was no guidance as to who would be selected or on what basis the selection would be made for compulsory retirement Though rule 244(2) of the Service Rules did not specifically mention that an order was to be passed in the public interest. Notes appended to the Rules gave indication as to how the order of compulsory retirement was to be exercised.

48 In stating that the Notes were promulgated in exercise of legislative power and that they were contemporaneously made the Court observed that the functions of the Notes were to provide procedure and to control discretion. Ray, who delivered the judgment of the Court, observed as follows:

"In the present case the notes are part of the rules because they are for the guidance of the authorities. They are not inconsistent with the rules but are intended to fill up gaps where the rules are silent. The only question here that formerly the rules said that compulsory retirement would be made in public interest but the present rule does not contain that part of the old rule. The deletion of that part of the rule does not mean that the orders of compulsory retirement are not made in public interest. The notes to the rule make explicit what is implicit in the rules."

It was further observed:

"The right to be in public employment is a right to hold according to rules. The right to hold is defeasible according to rules. The rules speak of compulsory retirement. There is guidance in the rules as to where such compulsory retirement is made. When persons complete 25 years of service and efficiency of such persons is impaired and yet it is desirable not to bring any charge of inefficiency or incompetency, the Government passes orders of such compulsory retirement. The Government servant in such a case does not lose the benefits which a Government servant has already earned. These orders of compulsory retirement are made in public interest. This is the safety valve of making such orders so that no arbitrariness or bad faith creeps in."

49. It may be mentioned that in arriving at the above conclusion the Supreme Court reviewed a number of its decisions on the question whether the order of compulsory retirement and the service rules under which they were made were valid or not. I have already referred to some of these cases above.

Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the appellant, referred also to other cases amongst which one has been decided by the Allahabad High Court, namely Krepa Ram Gupta vs. R.K. Talwar, AIR 1970 Allahabad 296, and the other by the Mysore High Court, Arlsrikar vs. The Union of India, AIR 1971-74. In these decisions it is held that the service rules concerned providing for retirement of a Government servant on completion of 25 years of service without assigning any reason were violative of Article 14 of the Indian Constitution, the reason being the absence of any principle or guideline for the exercise of the power of compulsory retirement. There was no reference to "public interest" in the rules under challenge. Such omission left ample scope for the authority to retire a perfectly fit and competent officer, thus causing detriment to public service.

50. In the Allahabad case the assertion was made that in paragraph (2) of the proviso to Fundamental Rule 56 there was nothing to indicate what is the group of persons sought to be isolated within the ambit of that paragraph. In stating why some guiding consideration should be provided in the Service Rules the Court observed as follows:

"It is not usual in measures of this nature to find a carte blanche given to executive authority. In the case-law cited before us, almost all the systems codifying the rights and obligations between the State and its servants invariably contain the controlling consideration that the power to retire a Government servant prematurely must be exercised only in the public interest or on account of inefficiency or dishonesty or some similar consideration. It is difficult to appreciate why such a factor of control was not included in the constitution of the impugned provision when it was framed."

51. The only limitation imposed upon the government's discretion to select an officer for retirement before the normal age of superannuation, that is, 57 years, is the completion by him of 25 years of service. This requirement, the learned Counsel submitted, was not sufficient to prevent discrimination, and the completion of a specified number of years being the only rule of selection under the, Mysore Service Rules, the Court held that for the rest, there is no guidance whatever. Elaborating the difficulty of selection in the absence of any other principle or guidance in the Rules and its possible consequence on the maintenance of efficiency in service, the Court made observations as follows:

There is nothing to show how and on what principle one out of the two or more persons who had completed 30 years of service can properly or validly be selected for retirement.

In the absence of any reference to public interest being the guiding factor, it is conceivable that perfectly fit and very competent and efficient officials may be retired to grave detriment to public service.

Apart from such possibility the necessity for indicating public interest as the real guiding, factor for compulsory retirement of this nature is regarded by the law as quite essential in all rules dealing with compulsory retirement." 52. Some cases relied on in support of the contention that there has been no impropriety in the conferment of discretion upon the government are seen not to deal with matter relating to the constitutionality of any legislative provision as section 9(2). For example, in A. M. Khan Leghery vs. Government of Pakistan, PLD 1967 Lahore 227, the scope and applicability of the provisions of Article 178 of the Constitution of Pakistan, 1962 (as amended in 1966) providing for retirement of Government servants in the public interest was involved. The Court, while rejecting the ground of malafide, because no particulars of malafide were given in the pleading, held that there was presumption of bonafide of Government action. It, therefore, expressed inability to go into the question whether the retirement was in the public interest. In another case cited before us, the question of compulsory retirement was not involved, as, for instance, in Pakistan vs. Daquat Ali Khan (1959) 11 DLR (SC) 73 ; PLD 1959 SC 37, the decision related to Fundamental Rules 56(b) which concerns superannuation. Here, the equality clause of the Constitution being not available was not urged. Both clauses (a) and (b) of Fundamental Rules 56 mention that if a government servant was to be retained after he attains the age of compulsory retirement, that is, 55 years, the decision of the Government must be on public grounds which must be recorded in writing. The case of Zaibtun Textile vs. Central Board of Revenue, PLD 1971 Karachi 333, which was cited in support of the principle that delegated legislation would not be hit for lack of standard unless the legislature abdicated its functions, did not deal with compulsory retirement, but related to fiscal legislation.

<u>53. As to the contention regarding the nature of and the reason behind the impugned order, Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel, emphatically asserted that though personal malafide was urged in the previous Petition, namely, Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979, which the learned Judges of the High Court Division rejected, the appellant did not consider it necessary to urge personal malafide in the present case because here malice in law had been fully established. Excepting claiming the power to make an order of compulsory retirement under section 9(2) of the Act, no other fact had been stated by the Government by way of justifying the impugned action, nor had the facts stated by the appellant been controverted by or on behalf of the Government. The Government chose to remain silent as to what was claimed to be the real reason for making the impugned order of retirement. It was stated to be to circumvent the judgment of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 which had declared the notification of November 22, 1978 purporting to relieve the appellant of the duties and designation of Professor of Medicine as having been made without any lawful authority.</u>

<u>54. What is malice in law and how it can vitiate an action as discriminatory was considered by the Indian Supreme Court in the case of The Regional Manager vs. Pawan Kumar Dubey, AIR 1976 SC 1966. In stating what would constitute '`malice in law" M.H. Beg, J., who delivered the judgment of the Court observed that "if an authority acts on what are, justly and logically viewed, extraneous grounds, it would be such a case." He further observed:</u>

<u>"We would, however, like to emphasize that before Article 16 is held to have been violated by some action there must be a clear demonstration of discrimination on a Government servant and reasonably explained except on an assumption or demonstration of "malice in law" or malice in fact. As we have explained, acting on a legally extraneous or obviously misconceived ground of action would be a case of "malice in law". Orders of reversion passed as a result of administrative exigencies, without any suggestion of malice in law or in fact, are unaffected by Sughar Singh's case (supra). They are not vitiated merely because some other Government servants, Juniors in the substantive rank, have not been reverted."</u>

55. In the present case the appellant has, instead of alleging malice in fact which might have raised disputed questions of fact, asserted that Government bad as mentioned above, no other reason to retire him from service than to frustrate or circumvent the effect of judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. Failing to deprive the appellant of his right to hold the rank and designation of Professor of Medicine, resort was taken to the provisions of section 92) of the Act, thereby to get rid of the appellant. It was also asserted that impugned action was not taken as soon as he completed 25 years of service, this having taken place one year before the order whose validity had been challenged in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. This, according to the appellant's counsel, constituted what is known as "malice in law". The contention has substance thus leading to the conclusion that the impugned order of retirement is not justified.

56. In reply to the main contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the provisions of section 9(2) are ex facie discriminatory and, therefore, violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, Mr. K.A. Bakr, Attorney-General, submitted that it would not be correct to say that the exercise of discretion conferred by section 9(2) has not been done in conformity with the object and policy of the Act. He read out all the provisions of the Act beginning with its preamble and submitted that section 9(2) enables the Government or the Authority concerned to exercise discretion in the matter of retiring government servants only in cases permitted by the Act In answering the query as to what was such object or policy the learned Attorney-General mentioned that the Act, though fixed the age of superannuation at 57 years, it gave power to retire a government servant after completion of 25 years of service. Unless and until, therefore, a government servant has completed 25 years of service he cannot be retired under section 9(2) of the Act which applies equally to all government servants. He submitted that since this discretionary power could be exercised only in fulfilment of the aforesaid object and policy of the Act, no guideline was necessary in exercising it. He could not, however, give any satisfactory answer to the question how the Government could select a particular officer from a group of officers similarly situated on completion of 25 years of service. According to him, provision laying down some guideline was necessary only in cases of abdication or excessive delegation, but where the legislature did not abdicate or delegate its authority, there was no necessity for providing any principle for regulating the exercise of discretion conferred by the section.

57. Referring to the provisions of Article 150 and paragraph 10(2) of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution, the learned Attorney-General contended that, in view of the aforesaid constitutional provisions, the legislature was competent to enact the present law regulating the terms and conditions of service of government servants. Further, such law enjoys protection from challenge regarding its constitutionality.

58. The learned Attorney-general submitted that since Act XII of 1974 had been made in terms of Paragraph 10(2) of the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution, it would prevail in spite of any inconsistency, if them be with the other provisions of the Constitution. Paragraph 10 is quoted below in full

"10. (1) Subject to this Constitution and to any other law —

(a) any person who immediately before the commencement of this Constitution was in the service of the Republic shall continue in that service on the same terms and conditions as were applicable to him immediately before such commencement ;

(b) all authorities and all officers, judicial, executive and ministerial throughout Bangladesh exercising functions immediately before the commence neat, continue to exercise their respective functions.

(2) Nothing in sub-paragraph (1) of this paragraph shall,

(a) derogate from the continued operation of the Government of Bangladesh (Services) Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 9 of 1972), or the Government of Bangladesh (Service Screening) Order, 1972 (P 0 No. 67 of 1972), Or

(b) Prevent the making of any law varying or revoking the conditions of service (including) remuneration, leave, pension rights and rights relating to disciplinary matters of persons employed at any time before the commencement of this Constitution or of persons continuing in the service of the Republic under the provisions of this paragraph.

59. This paragraph, besides being transitional and temporary, does not in our view protect Act XII of 1974 from any challenge to its constitutionality. What Article 150 of the Constitution has protected are the provisions contained in the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution. Article 150 reads as follows;

"The transitional and temporary provisions set out in the Fourth Schedule shall have affect notwithstanding any other provisions of this Constitution."

60. This Article does not protect any piece of legislation enacted under Paragraph 10 (2) (b) from challenge regarding its constitutionality. It, therefore, an Act is passed under this paragraph which is seen to have violated any provisions of the Constitution, as, for example, Articles 27 and 29, such law cannot be declared to be in conformity with the Constitution, and to have effect in spite of its infringement of such constitutional provisions. What Article 150 protects are the provisions contained in Fourth Schedule, even if they are contrary to any provisions of the Constitution.

61. Mention was also made of the provisions of Articles 133 and 134 of the Constitution which, according to him, should also be taken into consideration for determining the question regarding the violation of the equality provisions of the Constitution. Article 133 reads as follows:

"Subject to the provisions of this Constitution Parliament may by law regulate the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic:

Provided that it shall be competent for the President to make rules regulating the appointment and the conditions of service of such persons until provision in that behalf is made shall have effect subject to the provisions of any such law."

Article 134 provides as follows:

"Except as otherwise provided by this Constitution every person in the service of the Republic shall bold office during the pleasure of the President."

<u>62. None of these provisions can save an enactment of the kind under our consideration if it is in conflict with any other constitutional provision. Under Article 133 Parliament can make a law regulating the service conditions of government servants, but this power is not absolute, it is subject to the Constitution. The doctrine of holding office during the pleasure of the President is also of no avail in the present case, as the matter under challenge is the provision of an Act passed by Parliament. Besides, the pleasure doctrine is limited by the guarantee to the government servant as provided under Article 135 of the Constitution. Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the appellant, intervened at this stage and referred to two cases decided by the Indian Supreme Court.</u>

<u>63. The first of two cases cited by him. Roshan Lal vs. Union of India, AIR 1967 SC 1889 refer to the nature of legal relationship between the government and civil servants. In describing what is the relationship, Ramaswari, J. stated as follows:</u>

<u>"It is true that the origin of Government service is contractual. There is an offer and acceptance in every case. But once appointed to his post or office the Government servant acquires a status and his rights and obligations are no longer determined by consent of both parties, but by statute or statutory rules which may be framed and altered unilaterally by the Government. In other words, the legal position of a government servant is more one of status than of contract. The hallmark of status is the attachment to legal relationship of rights and duties imposed by the public law and not by mere agreement of the parties. The emolument of the Government servant and his terms of service are governed by statute or statutory rules which may be unilaterally altered by the Government without the employee. It is true that Article 311 imposes constitutional restrictions upon the power of removal granted to the President and the Governor under Article 310. But it is obvious that the relationship between the Government and its servant is not like an ordinary contract or service between a master and servant. The legal relationship is something entirely different, something in the nature of status. It is much more than a purely contractual relationship voluntarily entered into between the parties. The duties of status fixed by the law and in the enforcement of these duties society have an interest. In the language of jurisprudence status is a condition or membership of a group of which powers and duties are exclusively determined by law and not by agreement between the parties concerned."</u>

<u>The above passage clearly reveals the relationship between the government servant and the government and we respectfully agree with the aforesaid observations. The argument of the learned Attorney-General on the point of mutuality is, therefore, bereft of any substance.</u>

64. The next case referred to by Mr. Ahmed is Dinesh Chandra Sangma Vs. State of Assam, AIR 1978 SC 17, Goswami, J. observed as follows ;

"As is well known Government servants hold office during the pleasure of the President or the Governor, as the case may be under Art, 310 of the Constitution. However, the pleasure doctrine under Art. 310 is limited by Art 311(2). It is clear that the services of a permanent Government servant can-not be terminated except in accordance with the rules made under Art. 309 subject to Art 311(2) of the Constitution and the Fundamental Rights. It is also well settled that even a temporary government servant or a probationer cannot be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank except in accordance with Art. 311(2). The above doctrine of pleasure is invoked by the Government in the public interest after a Government servant attains the age of 50 years or has completed 25 years of service. This is constitutionally permissible as compulsory termination of service under F.R. 6 (b) does not amount to removal or dismissal by way of punishment. While the Government reserves its right to compulsorily retire a government servant, even against his wish, there is a corresponding right of the government servant under F.R. 56(c) to voluntarily retire from service by giving the government three months' notice in writing. There is no question of acceptance of the request for voluntary retirement by the Government when the government servant exercises his right under F.R. 56(c)."

What is to be noted in the passage quoted above is that the retirement rules which were held not to be unconstitutional have prescribed the limiting principle by the introduction of the concept of public interest", which is absent from section 9(2) of the impugned legislation.

65. Further, in repelling the contention that section 9;2) is ex-facie discriminatory, the learned Attorney-General drew our attention to the provisions of section 9(1) of the Act which enables any government servant to exercise option in retiring himself from service on completion of 25 years of service.

This shows that there is mutuality between the government servant and the Government itself in the matter of exercising option obtaining or making an order of retirement, as the case may be, when the government servant concerned has completed 25 years of service. According to him, therefore, the provisions of section 9(2) are not ultra vires the Constitution as being ex facie discriminatory.

66. The learned Attorney-General also submitted that the conferment of discretionary power did not necessarily make such power discriminatory. Finally, he contended that there was no malice in law in retiring the appellant from Government service and the order was not made to achieve any collateral purpose. Also, section 9(2) was not applied to the appellant Reliance was placed by him upon a number of decisions from Indian and Pakistan jurisdictions which, in course of my judgment, I propose to consider. It may, however, be mentioned at the outset that in the cases cited by the learned Attorney-General the decision of the Court did not turn on the question whether the Rules providing compulsory retirement were violative of the equality provisions of the Constitution the reason being non-availability of the equality clauses in the Constitution.

67. The first case referred to by the learned Attorney General is that of Jibendra Kisore vs Province of East Pakistan, (1957) 9 DLR 12. (SC 121 PLD 1957 SC 9. The observations of the Court on whose basis he tried to refute the appellant's contention have been quoted above and considered by us. He, however, submitted that if an Act laid down certain policy, its execution requires conferment of discretion on the Government or the authority concerned and, therefore, no exception could be taken to the exercise of discretion by it. In support, the learned Attorney-General referred to the following observations of Cornelius, Judge in the case of the East and West Steamship Company vs. Pakistan, (1958) 10 DLR (SC) 52=PLD 1958 SC 41 :

"Therefore, it seems to me that reference to Article 5 of the Constitution is not really relevant in the present case. It cannot be said that by leaving discretion to the Shipping Authority, he is given the position of being a law unto himself in the sense that he can decide for himself in what conditions he will grant a permit or, as the case may be, refuse a permit. There is no question of legislation at all since each case has to be considered ad-hoc in relation to the circumstances existing when it arises in the light of the requirements of the State, and in compliance with the policy laid down. That degree of description is vested in the executive inherently as a necessary condition of its existence.

69. What would be the court's duty, if the statute which confers such jurisdiction prescribes no limitations or lays down no principle for the guidance of the executive? Can its constitutionality be challenged? In answering this question, the Attorney-General drew-our attention to the principle enunciated in Dalmia's case as to the duty of the Court in deciding upon the constitutionality of a statute when challenged on the ground of conferment of unguided discretion upon the Government. The relevant observations are as follows:

"A statute may not make a classification of the persons or things for the purpose of applying its provisions and may leave it to the discretion of the Government to select and classify the persons or things to whom its provisions are to apply but may at the same time lay down a policy or principle for the guidance of the, exercise of discretion by the Government in the matter of such selection or classifications; the Court will uphold the law as constitutional.

A Statute may not make a classification of the persons or things to whom these provisions are intended to apply and leave it or classify the persons or things for applying these provisions according to the policy or the principle laid down by the statute itself or guidance of the exercise of discretion by the Government in the matter of such selection or classification. If the Government in making the selection or classification does not proceed or follow such policy that in such a case the executive action but not the statute should be condemned as unconstitutional."

<u>70. These observations do not, I am afraid, support his submission. No policy or principle for guidance of exercise of discretion by the Government has been laid down in the impugned Act. Nor has the Government laid down such principle for its guidance in the rules framed under the Act. Had such principle or policy been found in the impugned statute or rules framed thereunder, the Court might have no choice other than seeing whether the impugned action of the Government has been in conformity with such principle or policy.</u>

71. In support of his contention that a discretionary power is not necessarily a discriminatory power and that abuse of power is not to be easily assumed where the discretion vested in the Government and not in a minor official, the learned Attorney-General also relied on observations as occur in the same judgment.

"We are not unmindful of the fact that a very wide discretionary power has been conferred on the Government and, indeed, the contemplation that such wide powers in the hands of the executive may in some case be misused or abused and turned into an engine of oppression has caused considerable anxiety in our mind. Nevertheless, the bare possibility that the powers may be misused or abused cannot per se induce the Court to deny the existence of the powers. It cannot be overlooked that Parliament has confined this discretion, not to any petty official but to the appropriate Government itself to take action in conformity with the policy and principle laid down in the Act."

Reliance was placed by him on a case decided by the Supreme Court of Pakistan to show the extent of discretion exercisable by the Government and the duty of the Court when constitutionality of an Act is challenged. This case does not, however, relate to retirement rules of government servant.

72. In the case, namely, Province of East Pakistan vs. Sirajul Huq, 19 DLR (1967) SC 281, section 57 of the Electoral College Act (1 of 1964) conferred powers relating to local government which enable the Provincial Government to delimit the electoral units in the rural and urban areas into groups so that each such group is a union or, as the case may be, a town, and further it was enabled to issue notifications, constituting union councils or town committees. The aforesaid section was declared ultra vires the Constitution of 1962 and all acts done thereunder were declared to have been without lawful authority by the Dacca High Court. The decision which reversed the decision of the High Court involved the consideration of the extent of discretionary power of the government. As to the exercise of discretionary power of the government, Hamoodur Rahman, J. observed:

"The 'broad principles' upon which the grouping had to be done under this circular letter leave no room for doubt that the Provincial Government was fully conscious of its responsibilities and had no mind to disturb the limits of the existing Unions unnecessarily or to introduce any large scale revision of existing boundaries of any rural or urban Union or any Town."

So far as the Court's duty is concerned the learned Judge said:

"One of the cardinal principles of interpretation is that a law should be interpreted in such a manner that it should rather be saved than destroyed. The Courts should lean in favour of upholding the constitutionality of legislation and it is, therefore, incumbent upon Courts to be extremely reluctant to strike down laws as unconstitutional. This power should be exercised only when absolutely necessary, for injudicious exercise of this power might well result in grave and serious' consequences as had actually happened in this case."

We respectfully agree with the principles enunciated as above regarding the exercise of discretion but its applicability is confined to the facts of that case.

73. Mr. Bakr while submitting that a government servant is bound by the terms of the statute under which he is appointed and that in the present case the appellant could not complain of infringement of any fundamental right guaranteed to him referred to the case of Pannalal Binfraj vs. The Union of India 1957 SCA 660. This case related to the constitutionality of section 5(7-A) of the Indian Income Tax Act which empowered the Commissioner of Income Tax and the Central Board of Revenue to transfer any case from one ITO to another. The question raised here was whether provisions of the section being discriminatory in the nature were ultra vires the Constitution. It was observed by the Court that the power conferred was no doubt discretionary but it was not necessarily discriminatory and abuse of power could not be easily assumed where the discretion vested in top-ranking authorities, like the Commissioner of Income Tax and the Central Board of Revenue. The Court, however, held that there might be cases where improper execution of power could result in injustice to the parties, but the "possibility of such discriminatory treatment cannot necessarily invalidate the legislation and where there is abuse of such power, the parties aggrieved are not without ample remedies under the law."

<u>74. After having considered the arguments of the learned Counsel and the cases cited by him in support of his contentions that section 9(2) violated Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, I am of the view that since neither the impugned provisions of the Act nor the rules containing them provide any principle or guideline for the exercise of discretion by the Government when it proposes to retire a government servant from amongst a group of government servants similarly situated and holding similar jobs, there invariably exists the scope for arbitrary exercise of such discretion. It was not the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant that the government cannot have or claim the power to retire a government servant after the completion of 25 years of service, though the age of superannuation has been fixed at 57, but what is of importance and consequence to the government servant concerned who is proposed to be retired on completion of 25 years of service is that the discretion of the relevant authority must be seen to have been exercised on some such principles as are discernible in Fundamental Rule 56, Notes 2, East Bengal Service Rule and Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973. Where such basis has been provided by the enunciation of such principles, whether, under the Act or Rules made under an Act or even in the note to such Rules regarding the retirement of government servants, the concerned authority before exercising its discretion, has to con-form to the principles so provided therein, Such principles may be elaborately stated, as in rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1973, but even if the rules made under an Act or note appended to any rules providing retirement on the completion of 25 years merely mention that the service of such government servant who has completed 25 years is not necessary in the interest of public service or in public interest, some basis for classification or selection is discernible. Where such basis has been provided, if the government servant concerned challenges the action of government in retiring him on completion of 25 years what the Government has to do is to show that his retirement was necessary in public interest or in the interest of public service. On the other hand, the provisions of section 9(2) coupled with the omission of such basis in the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1975 leaves scope to the concerned authority to arbitrarily retire a government servant who has completed 25 years of service. Had the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Rules. 1975 provided principles as embodied in Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants ( Retirement) Rules, 1973 which were made under similar provisions of law as in section 9(2) of the Act, no challenge could perhaps have been made as to the constitutionality of the impugned provisions of this section. The existence of such principles as are found in the Rules of 1973 would have provided a complete answer to any such challenge to their constitutionality, in spite of the expression "without assigning any reason" used in section 9(2) of the Act. In such a case the authority concerned would have remained free, so as not to disclose any reason in the retirement order, but if its action in retiring a government servant was challenged as arbitrary as has been done by the appellant in the present case, the authority could have disclosed before the Court the basis of its action,</u>

<u>75. The minimum principle or guideline as has been provided in service rules as appeared from the cases cited in this judgment is that of public interest or the interest of public service. If either the impugned Act or the rules made thereunder provided such principle, the minimum requirement of law as showing the existence of some guideline for the exercise of discretion in retiring a government servant who has completed 25 years of service would, I think, be satisfied, thus making it immune from any challenge on the ground of discrimination violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. I am of the opinion, therefore, that in the absence of such a guideline either in the Act or the rules framed thereunder, section 9(2) of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act (XII of 1974) suffers from unconstitutionality and the impugned action based on it is open to the challenge of being discriminatory and in violation of the equality provisions of the Constitution.</u>

<u>76. As already observed, the impugned action was taken to circumvent the judgment of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979, and also liable to be struck down on the ground of malice in law which form the basis of the action. I declare that section 9(2) of the impugned Act insofar as it empowers the government to retire a government servant is unconstitutional and the impugned notification issued thereunder is violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution and, therefore, void.</u>

<u>For the reasons stated above, the appeal is allowed, the order of the High Court Division is set aside and the impugned order is declared to have been made without lawful authority. There will be no order as to costs.</u>

Ruhul Islam, J.—I have gone through a copy of the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother Fazle Munim, J. and I find myself in full agreement with the conclusions arrived at by him. However, I feel the necessity to add some reasons by way of clarification, as this appeal raises some important questions of great public importance.

78. Dr. Nurul Islam by filing an application under Article 102 of the Constitution in the High Court Division challenged the constitutionality of sub-section (2) of section 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 (Act XII of 1974) and the legality of the notice dated 5th June, 1980 issued thereunder by Mr. M. A. Haleem, Additional Secretary-in-charge, Ministry of Health and Population Control, retiring the appellant. from government service with immediate effect on the ground of his completion of 25 years of service. The appellant being unsuccessful in his writ petition moved this Court for leave to appeal against the order of the High Court Division when leave was granted to consider whether sub-section (2) of section 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 gives without any guideline unrestricted discretion to the authority and consequently the impugned notification was issued in discriminatory manner injuring appellant's right to public employment; and so the rule and the action are hit by Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution relating to the Fundamental Rights.

79. The appellant while holding the office of Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research was retired under sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 on the ground of his completing 25 years of service but without assigning any reason. This action according to the appellant is wholly discriminatory, illegal, ultra vires the Constitution and malafide.

<u>80. Appellant's case in short is that after obtaining M.B. degree from the Calcutta. University he joined the service of the Government of East Bengal as Assistant Surgeon on April 10, 1952. While in service, the appellant obtained T.O.D. degree from the University of Wales and M.R.C.P. degree from Edinburg and by successive promotions he became the Professor of Medicine in 1962. On the recommendation of the Public Service Commission he was confirmed as Professor of Medicine on May 10, 1963 with effect from April 24, 1963. The appellant stated that in recognition of his academic excellence and scientific contributions in medicine he was awarded F.R.C.P London under a special clause, as he was not an M.R. C.P. of London by examination. While the appellant was serving as Professor of Medicine in the Chittagong Medical College he was appointed to act as the Joint Director of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. Later on the Government by the Notification dated March 31, 1967 appointed him to act as Professor of Medicine of the said Institute in addition to his duties as Joint Director. In March, 1968 Sir James Cameron, who was the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research since establishment of the Institution in 1965, left for the U.K. and appellant was put in charge of the office of the Director and Professor of Medicine by the Notification dated January 5, 1972; and by the Notification dated November 24, 1972 the appellant was appointed as the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research with effect from January 9, 1971. Appellant's further case is that due, to his meritorious service, the Government granted him the ad-hoc rank and status of Joint Secretary in 1974; and in 1975 he was given the ad-hoc rank and status of Additional Secretary During the period of 1974-75 he was the Personal Physician of the then President of Bangladesh. The appellant stated that he completed 25 years of service on April 10, 1977 By Notification No. Per 1/1M-35/78/951 dated November 22, 1978 he was relieved of his duties and designation of Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. Legality of the Notification was challenged by filing a writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. The High Court Division by its judgment dated December 6, 1979 declared the Notification dated Nov. 22, 1978 to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect. In view of the said declaration the appellant was restored to the position held by him, that is, Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute. Appellant's grievance is that having failed to dislodge the appellant by the Notification dated November 22, 1978 the Government issued the impugned Notification dated June 5, 1980 purporting to retire the appellant from service in exercise of the power conferred under sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974. Legality of this Notification has been challenged on the ground of the order being in contravention of the constitutional protections, and also on the ground of malafide alleging that the impugned Notification is in furtherance and fulfilment of the illegal design of not only circumventing the judgment of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979 but also achieving ulterior purpose. The impugned Notification reads as under:</u>

<u>"Whereas, Dr. Nurul Islam, Professor of Medicine and Director of Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research Dacca has completed 25 (twenty five years of service.</u>

<u>Now Therefore, in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (2) of section 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Act, 1974 (Act XII of 1974) the Government is pleased to direct that the said Mr. Nurul Islam shall retire from service with immediate effect." Sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 reads as under:</u>

<u>"(2). The Government may, at any time, retire from service a public servant who has completed 25 years of service without assigning any reasons".</u>

<u>Sub-section (2) of section 9 makes a major departure from the Service Rule providing retirement of a government servant on the completion of 25 years of service under rule 342(2) of Bangladesh Service Rules. For comparative examination the relevant service Rule is quoted below:</u>

<u>"342. For officers appointed substantively to the services or appointments mentioned in rule 244 the rule for the grant of retiring pension is as follows:</u>

<u>(1) An officer is entitled, on his resignation being accepted, to a retiring pension after completing qualifying service of not less than 25 years.</u>

<u>(2) A retiring pension is also granted to an officer who is required by government to retire after completing 25 years qualifying service or more.</u>

<u>Note—Government retains an absolute right to retire any officer after he has completed 25 years qualifying service without giving any reasons, and no claim to special compensation on this account will be entertained. This right will not be exercised except when it is in the public interest to dispense with the further services of an officer.</u>

<u>The Government servant concerned should ordinarily be asked to explain his position before retirement".</u>

<u>Rule 342(2) while giving the power to the government to retire a public servant after he has completed 25 years of service, provides two important checks upon the exercise of the discretion by the authority. Firstly, the right will not be exercised except when it is necessary in the public interest to dispense with the further services of an officer; and secondly, the government servant concerned gets an opportunity to explain his position before he is compulsorily retired. The two conditions provide the necessary protection as contemplated under Article 135 of the Constitution. On the liberation of Bangladesh similar law was brought into existence, namely, the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Order, 1972 (P.O. 14 of 1972). Clause (3) of article 5 of the Order provides that the prescribed authority may, at any time, retire a public servant without assigning any reason, after 25 years of service. Although the statute provided no guideline for the exercise of the discretion to retire a public servant on the completion of 25 years of service, the government realising the necessity of some principles to provide the guidelines in the exercise of the discretion, and to avoid arbitrary action in exercise of the powers laid down some grounds by framing Rules under President's Order No. 14 of 1972. Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1973 framed under PO 14 of 1972 reads as follows:</u>

<u>"3. Government may retire a public servant after he has completed 25 years qualifying service on any of the following grounds:</u>

<u>(a) abolition of the post held by the public servant concerned;</u>

<u>(b) availability of a qualified candidate" for the post held by the public servant concerned;</u>

<u>(c) indulgence by a public servant in activities prejudicial to the interest and the fundamental principles of the state;</u>

<u>(d) bad reputation relating to morality, integrity or honesty of a public servant;</u>

<u>(e) the services of a public servant is considered not necessary in the interest of public service."</u>

<u>An order of retirement passed on any of the grounds provided in rule 3 was sufficiently guarded from being violative of the constitutional guarantee.</u>

<u>81. The impugned statutory provision provides no guideline for the exercise of authority in the matter of retiring a government servant. It does not protect the government servant from becoming a victim of arbitrary and capricious action. The statutory provision exhibits a total disregard of the constitutional guarantee provided under Article 135 of the Constitution. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, rightly submitted that the impugned statutory provision giving unqualified power to the government to retire a government servant on completion of 25 years of service, without assigning any reason, being violative of the constitutional provisions is ultra vires the Constitution; and as such the action taken thereunder is also illegal and void. He submitted that such arbitrary retirement without assigning any reason is not permissible in view of the guarantee provided under the Constitution. The unqualified and uncontrolled discretion to retire a government servant without assigning any reason empowers the authority to exercise the discretion discriminatorily. I find sufficient force in his submission that the power given to the government to retire a government servant arbitrarily without even affording an opportunity to show cause is violative of Article 135 of the Constitution.</u>

82. The government framed the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1975 under Act XII of 1974. While framing new Rules the rules framed under P.O. No. 14 of 1972 were repealed as a whole. Under the new Rules the grounds for directing retirement as provided under rule 3 of the Bangladesh Public Servants (Retirement) Rules, 1973 were totally omitted. Rule 9 of the Public Servants Retirement Rules, 1975 relates to the option given to a public servant to retire under sub-section (1) of section 9 of Act XII only, but the rule is completely silent with regard to the application of the discretion of the government to retire a public servant as provided under sub-section (2) of section 9.

<u>83. A government servant's right to continue in service is subject to the pleasure of the President. In English Common Law, a government servant, unless otherwise provided by law, holds office during the pleasure of the Crown. This principle has been recognized in the Constitution of the Republic of Bangladesh. Article 134 provides that except as otherwise provided by the Constitution every person in the service of the Republic shall hold office during the pleasure of the President. The very opening words, namely, "except as otherwise provided by the Constitution" indicate that the "pleasure of the President', doctrine is not absolute. This is subject to other constitutional provisions. Under Article 133 of the Constitution the Parliament has been given the power to regulate by law the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic. It also empowers the President to make rules regulating the appointment and conditions of service of such persons until provision in that behalf is made by or under any law. Then Article 135 provides two important exceptions. Firstly, a government servant cannot be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action intended to be taken against him. Secondly, no government servant can be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority.</u>

<u>84. Although a person in the service of the Republic holds office during the pleasure of the President, but leis service is protected under Article 135 of the Constitution, and it is also regulated by laws or rules consistent with constitutional guarantees. So, the Laws and Rules regulating appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic cannot be in total disregard of Article 135 of the Constitution which operates as an exception to Articles 133 and 134.</u>

85. The learned Attorney General appearing for the respondents could only rely upon the absolute authority of the President to retain a public servant in service. In other words, apart from referring to Article 134 of the Constitution containing the doctrine that a public servant holds office during the plea-sure of the President, he had no answer to the question. All the arguments of the learned Attorney-General advanced on this point practically centered on the authority of the Government provided under the impugned statute that is to say, it is an absolute rights of the government to retire any officer after he has completed 25 years of qualifying service without assigning any reason. He referred to the statement made in the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the government before the High Court Division, to the following effect:

"It is further stated that impugned notification was issued not with any ulterior motive or collateral or malafide purpose, but the same was issued in accordance with law."

<u>86. It has already been pointed out that Act XII of 1974 provides no guideline for the discretion by the authority. The position as stated above lends full support to the arguments of Mr. Ishtiaq Ahmed that in the absence of any principle or guideline for the exercise of the uncontrolled and unqualified discretion under sub-section (2) of section 9, provided the scope to the authority to pick and choose and to discriminate between government servants similarly placed on completion of 25 years of service in the matter of premature retirement; and such discrimination is inherent in the Act itself. Therefore, sub-section (2) of section 9 is violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution.</u>

87. Equality of citizens guaranteed under Article 27 of the Constitution: it provides that all citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law. The formula as stated in the Article contains the English concept of equality before the law and the American concept of equal protection of the laws. These are not independent or severable concepts in their application and will often be found to overlap each other. The principle on which the doctrine of equal protection of laws is founded is that persons in similar circumstances must be governed by the same laws. The legislative classification by itself does not offend against the principle of equal protection of the laws provided the law operates equally on all members of the said class or group. For valid legislation, classification must be reasonable for the purpose of legislation, should not be based on proper and justifiable distinction, should not be clearly arbitrary and should have all reasonable relation to the objects and to the public purpose sought to be achieved by the legislation. So, the prohibition against denial of equal protection does not preclude the legislature from confining legislation to a class or classes, prescribing different sets of rules for different classes. But the rule speaks of the conditions that classification or discrimination is not arbitrary but reasonable and rests on a real and reasonable relation to the legislation or the subject or subject thereof and that the legislation operates equally, uniformly and impartially on all persons or property within the same class. This rule has been consistently followed by the superior Courts of the sub-continent in testing validity of a statute. The Court has to see when a law is alleged to be repugnant to the rule of equality is what the object of the law is, what is the method provided therein for the achievement of that object and whether there is a reasonable relation between the method and the end intended to be achieved. " A law applying to one person or one class of persons may be constitutional if there is sufficient basis or reason for it"—Constitutional Law by Willis.

88. Article 29 of the Constitution guarantees equal opportunity for all citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic. This Article prohibits legislation which denies or discriminates a citizen or a class of citizens in respect of employment or office in the service of the Republic.

89. In view of the protections under the two Articles a law vesting an arbitrary discretion in the authority without prescribing the uniform rule of action or laying down a guideline or standard by which the exercise of discretion may be measured, offends against the equality of law doctrine. A law without being controlled or guided by any defined rule or specified conditions to which all similarly situated persons may conform is unconstitutional and void.

90. Sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 merely provides that government may at any time retire from service a public servant who has completed 25 years of service without assigning any reason. Rule, 9 of the Public Servants (Retirement) Rules 1975 is completely silent with regard to sub-section (2) of section 9. That the statute provides arbitrary, uncontrolled and unguided discretion, and the government is also fully conscious about that, is apparent from the stand taken in the affidavit-in-opposition. Paragraph 12 of the affidavit reflects the stand of the government. It has been categorically stated therein that "the impugned notification was issued in accordance with law." The statement nakedly reflects the view taken by the government in the matter of exercise of the power provided under sub-section (2) of section 9. It is obvious that the government having given the absolute discretion to retire a public servant, the action taken against the appellant should be presumed to have been taken in accordance with law. It further reflects the stand of the government that the government does not owe even a duty to explain to the Court to justify the impugned notification.

91. In this connection reference may be made to a decision of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Jyoti Prosad v. Union Territory of Delhi, AIR 1961 SC 1602. The Supreme Court while formulating the tests in respect of Article 14 (corresponding to Article 27 of the Constitution of Bangladesh) observed :

"The enactment or the rule might not in terms enact a discriminatory rule of law but might enable an unequal or discriminatory treatment to be accorded to persons or things similarly situated. This would happen when the Legislature vests a discretion in an authority, be it the Government or an administrative official acting either as an executive officer or even in a quasi judicial capacity, by a legislation which does not lay down any policy or disclose any tangible or intangible purpose, thus clothing the authority with unguided and arbitrary power enabling it to discriminate...…..In such circumstances the very provision of the law, which enables or permits the authority to discriminate, offends the guarantee of equal protection afforded by Article 14".

<u>92. I respectfully agree with the above view that the impugned statutory provision might not in terms enact a discriminatory rule of law but it is fraught with the inherent danger of enabling an unequal or discriminatory treatment to persons similarly placed. It is a clear case where such arbitrary and capricious action has been taken against the appellant.</u>

<u>93. The learned Attorney-General submitted that it should be presumed that the power conferred has not been abused and the authority has discharged its duties honestly and in accordance with law. The presumption that the official action has been taken in accordance with law, will not satisfy the tests to examine the constitutionality of the law. There is nothing in any part of Act XII of 1974 or for that matter in any of the rules framed thereunder, to help classification of government servants out of a number of government servants similarly placed, to whom the prevision of law may be applied. The presumption that the authority will act in accordance with the rule of law can be sustained only if there is a rule of law to guide the authority. No such principle is discernible from any part of the statute. It has already been pointed out that the statute makes a great departure from the provision as contained in rule 342 of the Bangladesh Service Rules and also from President's Order No. 14 of 1972. Thus it leads me to the irresistible conclusion that sub-section (2) of section 9 of Act XII of 1974 offends against Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. Article 26 of the Constitution declares such a statute void. Consequently by operation of the Constitution as provided under Article 26, sub-section (2) of sec. 9 being violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution, is void.</u>

94. Section 4 of Act XII of 1974 provides superannuation of a government servant at 57th year of his age, with proviso... that in case of a physician or teacher the government or authority authorized by the government may extend the service upto the age of sixtieth year. The appellant claimed that he was reasonably expecting to continue for the full term of service, and he would continue to serve for the full term but for the illegal termination of his service by way of retirement under the impugned notification. Let me examine whether premature retirement of a government servant before the age of superannuation violates the guarantee provided under Article 135 of the Constitution.

95. The appellant was holding the combined office of the Director and Professor of Medicine of the Institute of Post-Graduate Medicine and Research. An earlier attempt of the Government to separate the post of Professorship from the post of Director was successfully challenged in a Writ Petition being Writ Petition No. 571 of 1979. The appellant under the terms of his appointment was entitled to hold the combined office of Director and Professor. In compliance of that declaration the position was restored to the appellant. He was holding the combined office till he was retired by the impugned notification.

96. A person appointed substantively in a permanent post in government service has a right to hold the post until he attains the age of superannuation or is compulsorily retired as per terms of the Service Rules read with guarantee provided under the Constitution. Normally, a government servant cannot be removed from his service unless he is found guilty of misconduct, negligence, inefficiency or any other disqualification enumerated under the service rules, in an appropriate proceedings drawn up against him. Premature retirement is per se a punishment, because the government servant is deprived of his right to continue in service until he attains the age of superannuation and he also loses the benefits of service accrued to him. Termination of service before hid superannuation is undoubtedly 'removal' if not termed as 'dismissal'. It is true that a person in the service of the Republic holds office during the pleasure of the President, and the Parliament has been given the power to regulate by law the appointment and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Republic, but Article 135 provides two exceptions, namely, (i) a government servant cannot be dismissed, re-moved and reduced in rank, unless he has been given a reasonable opportunity to show cause against the action intended to be taken against him; and (ii) no government servant can be dismissed, removed or reduced in rank by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority. If the two constitutional requirements are complied with, the government servant concerned has no valid grievance to make before the Court of law. However difficulty arises only when a government servant is removed from service, not for misconduct, inefficiency, etc., but by applying provisions in the service rules or law which empowers the government to terminate service of a government servant without assigning any reason. In the instant case, service of the appellant has been terminated without assigning any reason and without giving him any opportunity even to explain his position before retirement.

<u>97. The learned Attorney-General sought to justify the action submitting that termination of service of the appellant was brought about otherwise than by way of punishment, He further submitted that since there is no stigma the action cannot be treated as a punishment. According to him, the appellant has no valid grievance to make before a Court of law, because he cannot claim the protection of Article 135 of the Constitution. In support of this contention the learned Attorney General referred to several decisions of the Indian Supreme Court laying down the principle that a government servant whose service is terminated otherwise than by way of punishment, the government servant concerned cannot claim the protection of Article 311(2) of the Constitution of India. The rule of law laid down in these decisions, in the context of the facts of these cases, does not answer the question raised in the instant case and in the background of the facts of this case. It is to be ascertained as to when an order for termination of service is inflicted by way of punishment and when it is not. It has already been stated that a government servant holding a substantive post acquires a right to hold the post until he attains the age of superannuation or is compulsorily retired, as per terms of a contract, express or implied, or a service rule. He can be removed from the post only when the post itself is abolished or he is found guilty of misconduct, negligence, inefficiency or other disqualifications in an appropriate proceeding in accordance with the service rules read with Article 135 of the Constitution. Termination of service of a government servant so appointed must be in accordance with the service rules which in its turn must be consistent with Article 135 of the Constitution. Any law or rule dealing with termination of service by retirement before the age of superannuation must be so framed as to safeguard the protections to the government servant guaranteed under the Constitution, that is, under the Fundamental Rights as well as under Article 135 of the Constitution. In support of this view reference may be made to the judgment in the case of P.L. Dhingra v. Union of India, AIR 1958 SC 36. In this case legality of the order of the General Manager of the Northern Railway reverting the petitioner from the post he was holding to his substantive post was challenged on the ground of the order being violative of Article 311(2) of the Indian Constitution. Some observations made in the judgment may be of some assistance in the present consideration of the impugned order being violative of Article 135. S.R. Das, C.J. delivering the majority judgment, observed as follows:</u>

<u>"Shortly put, the principle is that when a servant has right to a post or to a rank either under the terms of the contract of employment, express or implied or under the rules governing the conditions of his service, the termination of the service of such a servant or his reduction to a lower post is by itself and prima facie a punishment, for it operates as a forfeiture of his right to hold that post or that rank and to get the emoluments and other benefits attached thereto...… One test for determining whether the termination of the service of a government servant is by way of punishment is to ascertain whether the servant, but for such termination, had the right to hold the post.
